records.question: Who was St. Simeon the Stylite?
records.answer:
St. Simeon the Stylite, also known as Simeon el-Ăamoudi, was a remarkable Christian saint born in 390 AD in a village near Aleppo, Syria. He is best known for his unique ascetic lifestyle, which involved living on a pillar for many years, a practice that made him one of the most famous stylite saints. The term "stylite" comes from the Greek word "stylos," meaning "pillar," and refers to those who chose to live in seclusion on pillars as a form of extreme asceticism and devotion to God.

Simeon's early life was marked by a deep commitment to prayer and charity. After the death of his parents, he distributed his inheritance to the poor and joined a monastery, where he became known for his intense spiritual practices, including fasting and prayer. His dedication was so profound that he was eventually ordained as a monk by the bishop, who reportedly saw an angel standing beside Simeon during the ordination ceremony [2][4].

Seeking to deepen his spiritual life further, Simeon decided to emulate other stylite saints by living on a pillar. He constructed a pillar that eventually reached 30 cubits (approximately 52 feet) high, where he spent his days in prayer and contemplation. His elevated position allowed him to minister to the people below, drawing many to repentance and faith through his teachings and miraculous works [1][7]. He became a spiritual leader, attracting visitors from far and wide, including kings and bishops, who sought his counsel and prayers [5][7].

Simeon's life was characterized by a profound love for God and a commitment to asceticism, which included extreme fasting and self-denial. He often engaged in lengthy prayers, reportedly performing over a thousand kneelings in a single day [7]. His influence extended beyond the Christian community, as even non-believers admired his piety and sought his wisdom [2].

St. Simeon the Stylite passed away in 459 AD after a life dedicated to God, and his legacy continues to inspire many within the Coptic Orthodox Church and beyond. His feast day is celebrated on the 29th of Bashons in the Coptic calendar [5].

SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. 
Unusual and Amazing Personality: 
As much as the personality of St. Simeon (Semåan) was unique and unusual 
in its lifestyle and behavior, as much as God has confirmed its authenticity. 
Deacon Yousef Ĥabib (1909 -1981) and his brother Melika stated in the 
introduction of their book about St. Simeon, the Stylite: 
This saint, in his life and behavior, was admired, not only by the believers 
among the inhabitants of the Roman empire but by the non -believers and the 
Barbarians as well. He was greatly honored by the Persians, the Midianites, 
and the Ethiopians. The Roman Emperors sought his prayers and used to seek 
his counsel for critical issues. His biography was written by his disciple 
Theodoret who remained beside him until the end of his life. He wrote what 
he saw by his own eyes, and his testimony was confirmed by many other 
people from all categories. He stated: “Those who are under the rule of the 
Roman Empire know about the well- known Simeon, whom they indeed called 
The Wonder of the World. Yet, despite the many witnesses, I am reluctant to 
write about the strife of that saint; lest it might be difficult for the coming 
generations to believe what is written . For man usually measures everything 
according to the natural ways of things; while counting anything out of the

usual as wrong or unbelievable. But those who know the greatness of the Grace 
of God would never refuse to believe what I am saying.” 
His Upbringing: 
That saint was born in the year 390 AD in Sisan, a village close to the city 
Aleppo on the northern border of Syria, to a father called John, and a mother 
called Martha. Because of him, many strange things happened, among them in 
a dream, St. John the Baptist came to his mother, gave her the good news about 
his birth and told her about what he would become as a grownup. 
The young St. Simeon worked as a shepherd of his father's sheep. He had 
many siblings, all of whom died, except for one older brother called Samson. 
One Sunday because of the heavy snow, St. Simeon was not able to go out 
to the pastures to shepherd the sheep, so he we nt instead to attend the Divine 
Liturgy in one of the Churches; something he didn't do very often. That 
Sunday, he heard the words spoken by Jesus during the Sermon of the Mount: 
“Blessed are the pure in heart...  Blessed are the peacemakers , Blessed are 
those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” (Matthew 5:4-9) Simeon asked 
the preacher to explain more about the Christian faith, and Simeon listened 
hard. He explained to him the happiness brought by asceticism for the sake of 
the enjoyment of the joy of Christ. He talked to him about the fellowship in the 
passion of the Crucified for the sake of the eternal enjoyment of Heaven. 
From that time on, he used to go early to Church to stay a long time there, 
and sometimes he spent all night long kneeling to pray, and he used to exhaust 
himself in prayers. He often denied himself eating his ration of food to give it 
to the poor and the needy.  
When both his father and his aunt died, he and his brother inherited all their 
possessions. St. Simeon gave the land to his brother and distributed the rest of 
his inheritance on the poor and the monasteries; besides some flocks of sheep, 
he donated to the monastery he later joined. 
His Monastic Life: 
Then, St. Simeon forsook everything and set forth to the wilderness. He 
fasted a whole week while praying with tears. He approached Fr. Heliodore, 
the Abbot of a nearby monastery called Euzebona, hoping that he would admit 
him. The grace of God was so evident in his life that the Abbot of the monastery 
introduced him to the bishop just after three days. And, the bishop admired him 
and ordained him as a monk. It was said that, during praying over him, the 
bishop saw an angel standing next to St. Simeon, who told the bishop that he 
would be a chosen vessel, in whom God would pour His precious gifts. 
St. Simeon became a disciple of Fr. Heliodore for ten years. And, because 
his cousin was a monk in the same monastery and he did not go out of it for 35

DANIEL, THE STYLITE, ST. 
In the biography of St. ‘Daniel the Stylite’ (409-493 AD) and of others like 
St. ‘Simon the Stylite,’ many emphasized the challenge faced by these saints 
from even nature itself. Our sain t lived a strange life on a pillar for so many 
years. 
Writing the biography of that great among the saints reveals the depth of the 
exalted Divine love, which swallowed his heart, preoccupied his mind, and 
made him dedicate all his energies to the account of the kingdom of God. 
It was not strange that, while adoring seclusion, he loved people, sought 
their salvation, and cared to talk to them for the sake of their improvement. 
Refraining from having gifts from the elites, he loved giving; and urged those 
who listened to him to have the same spirit. 
His Monastic Life: 
St. ‘Daniel the Stylite,’ is considered the most famous among the ‘Stylite’ 
saints after St. ‘Simon the Stylite.’ He was born in the town of ‘Maratha,’ near 
‘Samosata’ in upper Mesopotamia (in Iraq), to parents who vowed him to God 
before his birth. On reaching 12 years of age, he went to a monastery close to 
his hometown, where he became a monk after several years. 
On his way to visit Antioch, the abbot of the monastery took ‘Daniel’ along 
with him. On passing through ‘Telanissae,’ they went to visit St. ‘Simon the 
Stylite,’ who allowed ‘Daniel’ to ascend to him on his pillar, blessed him, and 
prophesied that he would endure much for the sake of the Lord Christ. 
His Seclusion: 
When the abbot of t he monastery reposed, the monks intended to choose 
‘Daniel’ to replace him; but he declined. He went again to visit St. ‘Simon the 
Stylite,’ and stayed for 14 days in a monastery close to his place. Intending to 
visit the Holy Land, but the war did not all ow him to do so, he went to 
‘Constantinople’ instead, where he stayed seven days in a church outside the 
city walls. He then prepared for himself a place to live as a hermit, in which he 
lived for nine years under the care of patriarch ‘Anatolios.’ 
Dwelling on a Pillar: 
St. ‘Daniel’ intended to follow the lead of St. ‘Simon the Stylite, ’ whose 
garment he got from St. ‘Simon’s disciple after he reposed in the year 459 AD. 
He chose a location on the ‘Bosphorus Sea’ few miles from ‘Constantinople,’ 
established a pillar with a full top, then ascended on it and lived there. On 
learning that one night, he almost froze from the severe cold; the emperor 
ordered him a shelter to be built over two pillars. There, he dwelt until he 
reached the age of 84 years. During t hat time, he never forsook his support,

passages.text:
156 
 
years, St. Simeon planned to follow suit. He also used to give his portion of 
food to the poor and remained to fast for six days every week. 
Having his Eyesight Back after Losing it: 
It happened that, one day while praying, the devil appeared to him in a 
terrifying dark cloud, struck him on his eyes, causing him to lose his eyesight. 
The Abbot of the monastery felt very sad for his dilemma and intended to bring 
a physician to treat him, but St. Simeon took his permission and went to the 
tombs, where he kept praying for 40 days; and Lo! A light shone around him, 
and the saint had his eyesig ht restored, and he returned to the monastery to 
resume his worship. 
Expelling Him from the Monastery: 
St. Simeon kept progressing in his ascetic practices. He used to bind a rough 
rope around his waist so hard that it did cut wounds through his flesh, and  he 
refused to be treated. The other monks sought from the Abbot of the monastery 
to send the saint away for fear that his behavior might probably cause the weak 
to doubt themselves. The monastery Abbot went along with their request. St. 
Simeon left the mo nastery, entered a wilderness nearby, and dwelt in a dry 
well, where he spent his days praying and singing praise to God. 
Five days later, the Abbot of the monastery, in a night vision, saw men 
clothed in shining attire, seeking from him to bring St. Simeon back. The next 
day, he sent some monks to bring him back, which he barely consented to do.  
Living a Solitary Life: 
St. Simeon remained for another three years in the monastery, practicing 
strict ascetic routines. When his fellow monks kept honoring him, he was very 
uncomfortable and sought the permission of the Abbot to leave the monastery. 
He set forth to a deserted area, where he dwelt alone for another three years. 
He decided to fast every year for 40 days without any food or drinks. At the 
time his disciple Theodoret wrote his biography, St. Simeon was going through 
his 28th fasting period. 
St. Simeon considered everything as nothing, whenever he thought about 
the Crucified Lord Christ. He used to climb to the top of a high mountain and 
would sit on t he rocks with his eyes continually focused on heaven, and his 
heart is sighing with love for the Lord Christ.  
He put iron chains on his feet to keep him from much movement. And when 
Meletius, the bishop of Antioch (360-361 AD) visited him, he said to the saint: 
“These chains are for the beasts and not for humans. What bind us men are not 
iron chains, but those of love for the Lord Christ.” The saint obeyed and sought 
from a blacksmith to remove them.

His Repose: 
St. “Simeon the Stylite lived for 70 years, and God allowed him to suffer 
much through the deterioration of his physical health. And he knew that his 
departure from this world was near. The saint departed to heaven in the year 
459 AD 
Before his departure, he increased his prayers, knelt, and delivered his soul. 
So, he remained that way for some time, and his disciple did not know that he 
has already departed. On hearing about his departure, the patriarch of Antioch 
came, together with six bishops, some leaders of the army, and 6,000 soldiers 
in a grand procession to bid him farewell. During his funeral, many miracles 
were performed in the name of the Lord. 
Remark: 
There are three persons who carried the name of  Simeon el-Ăamoudi (the 
Stylite). The first is the one mentioned here, called Simeon el -Ăamoudi the 
Great. The second: Simeon el -Ăamoudi Minor, at the end of the 5 th century, 
mentioned by Fr. John of Damascus in his 3 rd sermon on the icons. And the 
third, who lived in the land of Cilicia who died by a strike of lightning falling 
on him; and mentioned by Saphronius in chapter 57 of his book: “The Spiritual 
Gardens.” 
Of His Words: 
“Whoever talks, let him utter the words of the Lord with the humility of 
heart; doing so by his works before his words.” 
 [Jesuit Fr. Botros Farmag: Pastures of the Pious in the Biographies of the Righteous; 
1877: January 5] 
 [Synaxarion: 29 Bashons and 3 Mesra] 
 
SIMON I, The 42nd POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

was a disagreement between the priests of St. Mark’s church in Alexandria and 
those of the Evangelists church in the city. The former group tended to 
recommend hegomen Yoĥanna (John) of the Enaton (Glass) Monastery for 
being a scholar and an author. In contrast, the other group recommended

SIMEON CLOPAS, THE APOSTLE 
This saint was the son of Clopas (Cleophas), the brother of the righteous 
Joseph, the fiancé of the Virgin St. Mary. He received the grace of the 
Comforter in the upper chamber of Zion, then  eventually was ordained a 
bishop of Jerusalem, after the martyrdom of St. James the Apostle. He drew so 
many Jews to faith in the Lord Christ. And through him, God performed so 
many signs. On hearing how he used to urge the people on chastity and purity, 
emperor Trajan (98 -117 AD) called him, tortured him, and ordered his 
beheading. He received the crown of martyrdom when he was 120 years old. 
 [The Synaxarion: 9 Abib] 
 
SIMEON OF MENOUF (The martyr) 
This saint Simeon (Samåan) was from the city of Menouf. He is celebrated 
by the Church on the 14th of Kiahk. He was martyred in the days of the Arabs. 
 [The Synaxarion: 14 Kiahk] 
 
SIMEON, THE ARMENIAN BISHOP (The martyr) 
He was a bishop on Persia, and he was martyred along with 150 other 
martyrs. He lived in the days of King Shapur II (309-379), the son of Hormizd 
II, the king of Persia. This king treated the Christians oppressively, cruelly and 
unjustly. Simeon wrote to the king a message in which he said: “Those whom 
the Lord Christ purchased by His precious bl ood to save them from the 
servitude of evil should never serve those who break the law.” On reading this 
message, the angry king called the saint, put him in chains, and cast him in 
prison. There, finding some prisoners who worshipped the fire, he taught them 
and preached them. They proclaimed faith in the Lord Christ before the 
governor, who ordered to cut their heads by the sword; and did the same to the 
saint. In this way, all of them received the crowns of martyrdom. 
 [The Synaxarion: 19 Baramouda] 
  
SIMON THE CANANITE, THE APOSTLE 
This apostle was called Nathaniel and also Simon the Zealot. He was born 
in Cana of Galilea. He was a scholar in the Law and the prophets; he was so 
jealous to be called The Zealot; he was righteous, pious, and never came to 
compliment anyone at the expense of the truth. When Philip the Apostle came 
to tell him: “We have found the Christ about whom Moses the prophet wrote,

passages.text:
157 
 
A Wonder-Maker: 
As many miracles and signs were performe d on his hands, in the name of 
God, multitudes came to him from Persia, Ethiopia, France, Spain, England, 
and Italy, to seek counsel and healing from St. Simeon. Kings and bishops 
came from Europe to ask him about specific issues, which he answered 
according to the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and many people put his portrait 
in their houses for a blessing. As testified by his disciple Theodoret, who saw 
it by his eyes, being burdened by having his hands kissed and his robe touched 
for blessing by many, he made for himself a six cubits (1 cubit=1.73 feet) high 
pillar; increased it by six cubits, then by 8 cubits more, to reach 30 cubits high 
[= 52 feet]; with a top circle of 6 spans (1 span=9 inches) wide [= 4.5 feet], 
surrounded by a low fence to keep him from falling off. 
St. Simeon drew many believers to repent. He had a fantastic influence on 
pagans who proclaimed their faith in the Savior of the world. And, he was the 
cause of comfort to so many who came to listen to his sermons. 
The Repentance of a Thief: 
Antiochus Agonatus, the head of a gang of thieves, had such a very strong 
body, that he was feared even by soldiers. When he went too far with his 
crimes, a large regiment of soldiers was sent to chase him. Finding him in a 
night club, once he raised hi s sword, they were so terrified that he could flee 
away. By the grace of God, he went to St. Simeon to present repentance with 
tears. When the soldiers came to arrest him and asked the saint how he would 
protect such a criminal, He answered them that the t hief came to him seeking 
the mercy of God and offering repentance. 
When the soldiers withdrew, the saint sought from the thief not to resume 
his crimes. The thief cried out, exploring the mercies of our Lord Jesus Christ, 
raised his hands toward heaven, and said: “O my Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of 
God, receive my spirit.” Crying for two hours, the saint and all who were 
present, were so impressed that they all cried when they saw the thief lean his 
head on the pillar, and then deliver his soul. 
A Man of Prayer: 
Once his disciple was watching the saint praying and started to count the 
number of times of his kneeling (metanoias). The disciple scored 1,240 
metanias that the saint did, then he stopped counting. 
It was said that when an elite came to visit the saint, the man implored him, 
saying: “In the name of Him who incarnated for our sake, I beg from you to 
tell me; Are you a human or of another creation, which appears as human?” 
Here, the saint sought from his disciple to bring a ladder and to let the man

150 
 
Having benefited from this teaching, the brother  started to work by his own 
hands to give alms from what remains from whatever he was earning. 
Cotelerius narrated to us so many stories about this St. Silvanus. Among 
those was that he once woke up from his sleep terrified, for he dreamt that he 
found him self in eternity and saw many of the monks in hell, while many 
laypeople were in heaven. This father also made so many beneficial statements 
about spiritual strife. When St. Silvanus consummated his strife in right old 
age, God let him know the time of his departure from this world. He called the 
monks close to him, got their blessings, and sought from them to remember 
him in their prayers; then, he reposed in peace. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 670] 
 
SIMEON BARSABAE, THE BISHOP AND HIS 
COMPANIONS (The martyrs) 
His Arrest: 
This saint was the bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon in Persia. He was also 
called Barsabae. When king Shapur II (309-379) gave the order to arrest him, 
the soldiers chained him and brought him up to be tried before ma licious 
governors. He refused to worship the sun and firmly testified with a loud voice 
to the Lord Christ. He was imprisoned for a long time, along with hundreds of 
believers among them were bishops, priests, and deacons of different ranks. 
His Support for the King’s Counselor: 
Among those arrested was Usthazanes (Chusdazat), the king's counselor, 
who had weakened earlier and denied his Christian faith. However, later on, 
he repented on the hands of bishop Simeon and were arrested and condemned 
to death. He was steadfast until he was martyred. On the next day, it was the 
memorial of the passion of the Lord Christ, and all the others were condemned 
to death and their heads were cut off by the sword in front of St. Simeon. The 
saint zealously encouraged every  one of them to receive his crown of 
martyrdom. Finally, he was martyred in the same way, in the year 341 AD. 
Among those tortured and martyred at that time, were the two priests: 
Abdechalas (Abdella/Abdhaihla) and Ananias (Hannanja), together with 
Pusicius (Pusai), the overseer of the king's workers. Because he kept 
encouraging the priest Ananias to stand firm before the persecution, Pusicius 
was killed in a wrong way. His tongue was cut off, then his head, and after him, 
his virgin daughter Askitrea was slained too. 
 [Butler, April 21]

of Alexandria, Behira and Marriot. Then, he returned to Alexandria to cause so 
many troubles to Pope ‘Agathon,’ and requested from him annual taxes and 
burdened him with paying the expenses of the crews of the fleet. 
The pope was committed to staying in his cell day and night; because 
‘Theodosius’ has ordered his followers, whenever they see the pope stone him 
to death. The pope, nevertheless, while not ceasing to pray for his sake, kept 
working from his cell and ordaining pious and God-fearing priests. 
When the pope reposed in the Lord in the year 677 AD, after 17 years on 
the Papal throne, ‘Theodosius’ hastened to close and seal the doors of the 
Patriarchate. The congregation was provoked to anger, and the elders resorted 
to the governor of the city of ‘Sacha’ to intervene to lift that burden up from 
the people. In the meantime, God struck ‘Theodosius’ with dropsy, and he died 
after suffering bitter pains. The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of the repose 
of Agathon, the Pope, on the 16th of Baba. 
 
AGATHON, THE STYLITE, ST. 
His Monastic Life: 
He was born in the town of ‘Tanice’ in the Menzallah lake region, to pious, 
almsgiving, God -fearing parents. His heart was inflamed with the love of 
monasticism and dedicating all his energi es to worship. When he reached 35 
years of age, he had ordained as a priest and ministered to the people of God 
with sincere love; yet his heart remained inflamed with a desire for a life of 
contemplation and asceticism. 
God granted him his heart ’s desire; he set forth to the region of Marriot, 
then to the ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disciple for three years to the saintly 
Fathers: ‘Abraam and Gawargy.' Everybody because of the strength of his 
spirit and virtues loved him. Then, St. Yoannes, the Father of Scetis and a group 
of saints, prayed on him for three successive days and put on him the angelical 
‘Eskeem’ belt. Then, he struggled even more in his monastic life with extended 
fasting and unceasing prayers. 
Setting Forth to Sacha: 
Longing to imitate St. S amaan the Stylite, he sought the counsel of the 
Fathers in the wilderness who approved his idea and prayed for him. He set 
forth to the desert near ‘Sacha,’ where the believers built for him a dwelling 
place in the form of a pillar, which he ascended. 
There, he ministered to the people by his prayers and counsels with an open, 
loving heart and with his pure soul. God granted him the gift of performing 
miracles, of which we may mention: 
1- In his days, a man showed up possessed by a stubborn evil spirit by whic h

passages.text:
186 
 
to proclaim his faith in the Lord Christ and not to persecute any Christian. 
Receiving the Christian Faith: 
Sosenius called a priest, sat with him to inquire about what he did not know 
about the facts of the Christian Faith. He was so satisfied and rejoiced by the 
priest's answers and asked to be baptized. When Sosenius' father noticed his 
delay in fulfilling the commands of the emperor and coming to know of his 
son's intention to proclaim faith in the Lord Christ; he was provoked to anger, 
and reported him to the emperor. The emp eror gave the command to punish 
him, in an attempt to make him change his mind. 
His Torture and Martyrdom; 
Sosenius endured so many kinds of torture, and the Lord kept strengthening 
him. Finally, the emperor ordered cutting his head off. About 1,100 person s 
assembled around him, amazed at his courage, his steadfastness in faith, and 
being happy to be martyred. They all approached the swordsmen and 
proclaimed their Christian faith. Therefore, the soul of the saint did not set 
forth alone, but in a huge proce ssion of martyrs, to bring joy to the Celestials 
and to enjoy the fellowship in the Heavenly glories. 
The Church celebrates this joyful procession on the 26th of Baramouda. 
 
SOSENIUS, THE EUNUCH, ST. 
St. Sosenius (Sousenyos/Sisinnios) was one of the men in the royal court of 
Emperor Theodosius II (402 -450 AD). He was full of mercy, grace, and 
wisdom. When the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus was held in 431 AD 
to try Nestor, this saint was servicing St. Cyril the Great and the other saintly 
bishops of the Council, who were invited by the emperor. When it happened 
that Sosenius fell severely sick, St. Cyril prayed to God on his behalf, and he 
was healed temporarily from his sickness. Then, he got up and hastened to 
distribute all his possessions on the p oor and the needy; and later, he reposed 
in peace. St. Cyril prayed over his body and set a memorial day in his name. 
The Coptic Church commemorates his departure on the 21st of Abib. 
 [Synaxarion: 21 Abib]

records.question: Who was St. Barbara the martyr?
records.answer:
St. Barbara is a revered martyr in the Coptic Orthodox Church, known for her steadfast faith in Christ despite severe persecution. Born in the early 3rd century AD in the village of Gamis near Nicomedia, her father, Dioscorus, was a pagan who built a high tower to isolate her from the outside world and filled it with idols and entertainment to prevent her from encountering Christianity. However, Barbara was deeply contemplative and, inspired by her Christian servants, she eventually embraced the Christian faith and was baptized secretly, dedicating her life to God and vowing to remain a virgin [2][10].

Her faith led to a dramatic conflict with her father. When he discovered her conversion and her destruction of the idols in her tower, he became furious and sought to have her tortured. He brought her before the governor, Martinianus, who initially fell in love with her beauty and offered her honors if she renounced her faith. However, Barbara remained resolute, openly declaring her commitment to Christianity and refusing to worship the idols [1][10]. This defiance resulted in brutal torture, including whippings and being subjected to various forms of torment, yet she remained unyielding, praying to God for strength and healing [1][3].

Remarkably, during her imprisonment, Christ appeared to her, healing her wounds and filling her with divine light, which astonished the governor when he summoned her the next day. Despite her miraculous healing, the governor escalated her torture, ultimately ordering her execution. St. Barbara was beheaded, and her martyrdom is commemorated on the 8th of Kiahk in the Coptic calendar [1][2][3]. Her story is a powerful testament to faith and endurance in the face of persecution, and she is celebrated as a saint in both the Eastern and Western Christian traditions.

St. ‘Barbara’ was then whipped until her b lood started pouring. They also 
tore her flesh by hitting her with sticks full of sharp nails. During that time, she 
kept silent and continued praying to her God. Then, they clothed her in rough 
sackcloth over her torn body full of wounds, and she was cast  in a dark 
dungeon. 
While she was suffering from her wounds, the Lord Christ appeared to her 
in the dungeon, comforted her, and healed her completely. 
When the governor called for her on the next day, he was astonished to find 
her exultant with no traces o f any wounds on her body. He grew much more 
violent and sought from the executioners to comb her body with sharp iron 
combs, to put flames on her sides, and to cut off her breasts. Then, he ordered 
them viciously to lead her naked along the streets of the town. At this point, 
she cried out to the Lord to cover her nakedness, and God responded by 
engulfing her in Divine light. 
On seeing her amid her incredible sufferings, a girl by the name of ‘Juliana’ 
bitterly cried; and the governor ordered to torture her along with St. ‘Barbara,’ 
and to cast them together in the same dungeon. There, they kept praying all 
night long. 
Their Martyrdom: 
Governor ‘Martinianus’ gave the command to cut the heads of the two saints 
by the sword. While being lead to the arena outsi de the city, they kept on 
praying. And once they arrived there, ‘Dioscorus’ sought from the governor to 
let him kill his daughter by himself, and he was allowed. So, both St. ‘Barbara’ 
and St. ‘Juliana’ finally received the crowns of martyrdom. Their bodies were 
placed in a church outside the city of ‘Galatia.' 
St. ‘Barbara's father perished shortly after their martyrdom, and so did the 
governor who tortured her. The water of the basin that had the cross over it in 
the bathhouse had the power to heal everyone who washed with it. 
The body of St. ‘Barbara’ is kept now in a church under her name in Old 
Cairo. And, according to some historians, she might have been martyred in 
Heliopolis, Egypt. 
 
BARBASYMAS, THE BISHOP , ST. 
(The martyr) 
St. ‘Barbasymas’ (Barba'shmin) succeeded his brother St. ‘Shahdost’ as a 
bishop on the diocese of ‘Seleucia-Ctesiphon’ in the year 342 AD. 
This saint was inflamed with zeal on faith and the care of God’s people, and 
this stirred up the devil to consider him of being an enemy of the  Persian

they allowed those two hermits to worship another God on that same mountain. 
Forty young pagan men dedicated themselves to kill the two hermits, but God 
kept them safe and hid them away from their sight. 
Their Martyrdom: 
Then, it happened that ‘Maximianus, the partn er of Emperor ‘Diocletian,’ 
came to Egypt to supervise by himself the persecution and to enjoy seeing by 
his own eyes the shedding of the blood of Christians. 
The priests of the great idol went to complain to the emperor about what 
took place, and how thei r god declared his anger because of the presence of 
those two hermits on their mountain. At the same time, the Archangel 
‘Michael’ appeared to the two saints to tell them that the emperor would be 
seeking them and that the heavenly crowns were prepared for  them. The two 
saints then set forth from the mount to the messengers of the emperor and went 
with them to proclaim their faith before him. He gave the order to cut their 
heads off, and they received the crowns of martyrdom on the 7 th of the month 
of Kiahk. 
 [The Synaxarion; Edition of Rene Basset] 
 
 
BARBARA, ST. 
(The martyr) 
Saint ‘Barbara’ has gotten great fame in the East and the West; she endured 
so much to hold dearly to her faith. The Coptic Church celebrates her feast on 
the 8th of Kiahk and the Western Church as well as the Greek Church on the 
4th of December. 
Her Upbringing: 
She was born in the village of ‘Gamis’ near the city ‘Leopolis’ in 
‘Nicomedia,’ at the beginning of the 3rd century AD, during the days of 
Emperor ‘Maximinus I ’ (235-238 AD). He r father ‘Dioscorus’ was a firm 
believer in his pagan worship and strongly hated Christians.  
On seeing how beautiful she was and worrying about the corruption of that 
time, her father built for her a high tower and surrounded it by guards, and 
filled it with idols and all kinds of entertainments. He also provided her with 
great teachers who cared for her advanced learnings. 
‘Barbara’ having been a lover of meditation, she used to lift her eyes to look 
at the sun, the moon, and the stars, praising the God who created the earth with 
everything on it for the sake of humans. 
One day, some of her Christian servants told her so many good things about

Her Persecution: 
On failing to convince St. Juliana with showing his compassion,  the 
governor started to use violence and torture with her. Six of his shrewdest men 
whipped her until they were utterly exhausted. During all that time, she did not 
cease to repeat: “O my Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, Come to my help.” 
They beat the saint harshly for a long time, but after each beating , she 
received healing and new strength from God . Her punishment took place 
before a large number of people. Of these, 500 men and 150 women came to 
confess Christ after witnessing the courageous holy virgin miraculously healed 
from her severe wounds . They were all beheaded and were baptized in their 
blood. Then, the governor commanded to cast her into prison. 
There, she confronted and fought against Satan face to face, and prevaile d 
over him. Satan took the form of an angel of light, and tried to convince her to 
forsake her faith, and submit to the will of her father in the flesh and to the 
governor who tortured her. (Because of that, her old icons portrayed her tying 
a winged Satan with chains). Then, they continued her torture . They tore her 
flesh with iron claws and immersed her in boiling water . However, these 
tortures did not harm her. Finally, St. Juliana was sentenced to death and earned 
the crown of martyrdom by having her head cut off around the year 304 AD. 
 [Butler’s The Lives of the Saints: February 16] 
 
JULIANA (The martyr) 
St. Juliana (Yuliana) was present at the time when governor Marcianus was 
torturing St. Barbara in the days of Emperor Maximianus in the 3 rd century 
AD. Juliana was so impressed, and believed in Christianity when she saw how 
the Lord Christ comforted and strengthened St. Barbara. Getting to know that 
Juliana converted to Christianity, governor Marcianus ordered cutting off her 
head on the 8th of the Coptic month of Kiahk. A church was built on the location 
where she was buried and was dedicated on the 26 th of Kiahk. Her biography 
could be found together with that of St. Barbara under the letter ‘B’:  St. 
Barbara. 
 
JULIANUS OF ANCYRA (The martyr) 
This St. Julianus was a priest in Ancyra at Galatia. He was martyred during 
the persecution by Emperor Licinius I (E: 308-324 AD) at the beginning of the 
4th century AD. His memorial is celebrated by the Western Church on the 13th 
of September every year.

way, this monk was able to overcome the adversary thoughts. 
5. Controlling the Mind: The saint was asked: “How could man reject the 
talk of laymen in temporal issues; and how could he keep his mind with God , 
as it is written?” She answered: “This is like sitting at a banquet with many 
kinds of foods. If you eat with greed and covetousness, you would be guilty. If 
you eat without greed or covetousness, then you are not guilty. It is the same 
if you listen to the talk of laymen, but keep your heart with you, and have no 
pleasure in what being said. you would be unharmed.” 
6. The Features of a Teacher: It is befitting of a teacher to be a stranger to 
the desire of authority, pride and vainglory; lest he would pr obably fall by 
flirtation and lose his vision by gifts. But it is befitting of him to be 
longsuffering, meek and humble, as much as he can, and does not seek 
appearances, but cares for all and loves everyone. 
7. Enduring Tribulations: Let us try to enter t hrough the narrow door. For 
unless a tree endures the tempests of winter, it would not be able to produce 
fruit. For us, this age is like a stormy winter; it is only by enduring the 
tribulations and the temptations, we would inherit the Kingdom of Heaven. 
8. Sanctification of the Body: In a debate concerning the body between a 
Christian and a Mani -follower, the Christian said: “By letting the body walk 
according to the Divine law, you will find it on the side of its Creator.”  
 
THEODORA, EMPRESS 
This saint Theodora (~500-548 AD) was the wife of Emperor Justinian I 
(527-565). She was one of the most prominent women of the old , known for 
her beauty, iron will, riches and firmness, along with her broad knowledge. 
In the year 523, Justinian married her, and in the year 527, she was crowned 
as an empress. She had an active role in the theological debates and was very 
vibrant in other activities . Contrary to her husband, she loved St. Severus of 
Antioch and supported the non-Chalcedonian Egyptian Church. 
She had a significant role in the ethical reforms, cared for pious works, and, 
together with her husband, they cared for building churches and hospitals. 
She reposed in the year 548 AD. Her portrait in the mosaic was found in the 
Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna. 
   [Cross: Dictionary of the Christian Church, p. 1358]

to deny his faith, along with 16 of his priests. Then, they were cast in a dark 
prison. Now and then, they were whipped and insulted, in addition to suffering 
hunger, thirst, and disgusting smell. 
St. ‘Barbasymas’ and his companions endured the sufferings for 11 months, 
as though saying together with the apostle ‘Paul’: “Who shall separate us from 
the love of Christ? Shall tribulation or distress, or persecution, or famine , or 
nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35).  
When they were called before the crowds, their appearance was so distorted 
and altered that no one could recognize any of them. The king presented the 
saint with a golden vessel containing 1,000 pieces o f gold and promised to 
make him a governor if he worshipped the sun. The saint answered him that if 
he preferred gold or even the whole empire over His Holy Commandment, he 
would not be able to stand before the Lord Christ in the last day, nor would he 
endure His rebukes. The saint proclaimed his readiness to suffer death with joy 
for the sake of his Savior. All of them were then condemned to death by having 
their heads cut off on the 14th of January 346 AD in ‘Karka d’Ledan’ in ‘Beth 
Huzaye.' 
 [Asseman: Acts Martyrum Orientalium; I; pp. 111–116] 
 
 
BAR-DAISAN (BARDESANES) 
We introduce this personality who lived in the period 154-222 AD, because 
of its importance.  
He was a citizen of Ede ssa (El -Roĥa) in Syria, who converted to the 
Christian faith in the year 179 AD. Then, he got back to fall into the 
Gnosticism, considering the body of Christ as an illusion and that there would 
be no resurrection of the bodies. He managed to attract a multitude of disciples. 
He was supported by his own son ‘Harmonius,’ who helped him by presented 
his doctrines in the form of several beautiful songs of praises; in such a way 
that some considered him as the father of the Syrian praises. 
[Smith and Wace: Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. 1, p. 250 f] 
 
BARHADBESABA, ST. 
(The martyr) 
In the year 340 AD, the Church of Persia fell under a violent wave of

her torture, and then he ordered to cut her head off . At that moment, a lighted 
dove came down on her head, which made many of those present proclaim 
their faith in the Lord Christ. 
 [Butler: September 7] 
 
REGULUS, THE BISHOP , ST. 
St. Regulus (Rieul) is the intercessor of the city of Senlis . He is said to be 
the first bishop in the city , for he lived in the 3 rd century. After that , the 
Cathedral of Senlis was burnt out with all the records of its former bishops . It 
is said that after he proclaimed his faith in the Lord Christ, he set forth to 
France where he preached Christianity. And, he went to Paris to search for the 
relics of the martyrs: St. Denis, St. Rusticus, and St. Eleutherius. Then, he took 
upon himself to convert the inhabitants of Senlis; to Christianity . He reposed 
around the year 250 AD. 
  [Butler: March 30] 
 
REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine . When she was 12 
years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249 -
251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her 
beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making 
her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of 
fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing 
praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she 
holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her 
head off, she walked wi th them singing praise . Finally, when she was 
beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, 
flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she 
was honored by several dioceses. 
 [Butler: October 8] 
 
RESTITUTA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady St. Restituta was a Roman virgin of noble origin, and was 
martyred in the year 271 AD in the town of Sora in Italy. She became the patron 
saint of that city where she was buried . It was said that the Lord Christ 
appeared to her and instructed her to go to Sora, and an angel led her to that

AD by the king of Persia ‘Shapur II’ (309-379 AD), that Father was put under 
arrest along with his monks . They were led in chains to the city of ‘Istakhr,’ 
near the remains of the city of ‘Persepolis.’ 
The governor of the province tried hard to make those men deny their 
Christ. He used every fierce mean against them, but he failed utterly. He found 
them consistently testifying to their Christ with joy. So, he issued his order to 
cut their heads off. The pagan mob became exulted while watching them being 
led to the arena of martyrdom.  
It happened that a rich man was on hi s way out of the city with his family, 
and they passed by the execution arena . There, the rich man noticed how St. 
‘Barsaba’ was getting hold of each of his men, to deliver them by himself one 
after the other to the swordsman, as though he was offering a sacrifice to God.  
Suddenly, the rich man saw a splendid Cross shining over the bodies of the 
martyrs and his soul got enflamed to partake of their glories. He whispered in 
the saint' s ear , and the later got hold of him an d delivered him to the 
swordsman. Then, he went back to consummate his work with the rest of his 
men; then, with joy, he approached the swordsman. 
On seeing that, the wife and children of the rich man hastened to have their 
portions with that holy congregation. 
              [Butler’s Lives of Saints, Dec. 20] 
 
BARSAS (BASSAS), BISHOP 
He was a bishop of Edessa (El -Roĥa) in Syria and was exiled to the island 
‘Aradus’ by the Arian Emperor ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD), and when he found 
favor in the sight of the people there, who loved him in the Lord; the emperor 
moved him again to the city of ‘Oxyrynchus’ in Egypt . As he gained 
considerable fame there, he was removed from there and was sent to a deserted 
wooded island in the N ile called ‘Philae (the Elephants), ’ near the city of 
‘Aswan.’ There, the saint reposed in the Lord. 
     [Baring–Gould, Lives of Saints, Jan. 30]

(The martyr)

strive in his worship with many metanoias and continuous prayers and would

established on her name. She was the daughter of a prince of Galicia in Spain. 
She was baptized without her father’s knowledge and dedicated her virginity 
to the Lord. And, she had to flee away from her father’s house, when he tried

BARLAAM AND JOSAPHAT, SS. 
These two saints were added to the Roman martyrology; but some Western 
scholars had doubts on the authenticity of their biography, which was among 
the writings of St. ‘John of Damascus’ (675-749 AD). 
Those two saints were born in India on its border with Persia (Iran) . 
‘Abenner’ was a pagan king of India, and he hated the Christians and 
persecuted them. When someone prophesied that the son of King ‘Abenner’ 
whose name was ‘Josaphat’ would become a Christian, ‘Abenner’confined him 
since his childhood in a palace to keep him from any encounter with Christians 
or to have any knowledge of the Christian faith, but the son managed to escape 
from the palace and met with a hermit named ‘Barlaam,’ who pretended to be 
a trader of precious pearls. He talked to the boy about the Christian faith until 
he embraced it. On hearing this, the king came to be intensively grieved; but 
failed to change his son's mind, and he came to accept the Christian faith. The 
king set his son as a partner on the  throne but his son didn't remain for a long 
time, as he chose instead to set forth to the wilderness to live with the hermit 
St. ‘Barlaam.’ 
This incident most probably was written to glorify the monastic life, and it 
included three sides: the story -telling side; interpretations of the Christian 
faith; and quotations from a book about the early Christians. 
These two saints are remembered on the 27th of November. 
[Cross: The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, pp. 132-133] 
 
BARLAAM 
(The martyr) 
He was m artyred in the days of Emperor ‘Diocletian’ ( 284-305 AD). 
‘Barlaam’ was a simple farmer from ‘Cappadocia Caesarea,’ who, by his faith, 
managed to testify to the Lord Jesus Christ before the rulers. 
When the fire of persecution was i nflamed, he was arrested along with a 
significant number of Christians . They were chained and brought forth to the 
court of justice. The judge asked him about his name, work , and faith, and he 
mocked the saint as an illiterate man who did not know much in his life except 
the bull that pulled his plow and the land he planted. On seeing how he held so 
fast to his faith, he threatened him by severe punishments, for which the poor

area, somehow, she got the chance t o see him. Talking to her about the Holy 
Scriptures, she came to love the Lord Christ with her whole heart. Then, 
without the knowledge of her father, she managed to get baptized. Having her 
heart inflamed with the love of God, she vowed her life for Him and longed to 
live as a virgin dedicating her life to worship. 
Many proposed to marry her; among them was a rich young man, the son 
of a prince. Her father came to tell her about the good news, thinking that she 
would be exultant by it. However, she wisely declined the offer saying that she 
was not ready to get married. As her father was leaving the next day for 
business out of town, he postponed the whole issue until he would return, 
hoping that she would change her mind by then. 
During this time, a luxurio us bathhouse was being built at her father ’s 
house. By his orders, the workers prepared to put two windows on the south 
side. But ‘Barbara,’ taking advantage of her father ’s absence, asked them to 
make a third window, thereby forming a Trinity of light. Sh e turned the 
bathhouse into a place to worship God with prayers, fasting, and unceasing 
watching the nights. She destroyed all the idols in her tower; set a cross on the 
basin of the bathhouse, as well as on the top of the tower. 
And, as the doxology dedic ated to her says: “The light of the Holy Trinity 
shone on that virgin St. ‘Barbara,’ the bride of Christ.” 
Facing the Cruelty of her Father: 
Returning from his trip, her father noticed all those changes in her and the 
place. Enquiring from her about the reason, she started preaching him the faith 
in the Holy Trinity, and how he should believe in the One God of the three 
Hypostasis. He rebuked her in great anger; however, she did not care for his 
reaction. And, she openly and declared her faith and told him about her 
intention of keeping her virginity. The father in a fury jumped on her, pulled 
her by the hair, and was about to strike her with his sword, but she escaped 
from him and ran through the gate of the palace. While chasing her, it was said 
that rock on her way split open to let her pass through it, then returned to its 
original form to block her chasing father. When he finally found her hidden in 
a cave, he jumped on her like a wolf on a lamb, violently beating her and put 
her in a dark dungeon in his palace.

Her father ‘Dioscorus’ relayed the problem with his daughter to the 
governor ‘Martinianus,’ and sought from him to torture her. However, when

records.question: Who was St. Paul the First Hermit?
records.answer:
St. Paul the First Hermit is recognized as the first known Christian hermit and a significant figure in the early monastic movement. Born in Alexandria around 228 AD, he inherited a substantial fortune from his parents. However, following the death of his father, his older brother Peter conspired to take the majority of the inheritance, prompting Paul to flee into the wilderness around the age of 16 during the persecution under Emperor Decius (around 250 AD) [5][10].

In the wilderness, St. Paul lived a life of extreme asceticism, dedicating himself to prayer and solitude. He is said to have lived for nearly ninety years in the desert, sustained by divine providence; a raven brought him half a loaf of bread daily, which he supplemented with dates and herbs [5][10]. His life of solitude and prayer exemplified the monastic ideal of seeking God in isolation from worldly distractions.

St. Paul is also known for his encounter with St. Anthony the Great, who is often referred to as the father of monasticism. This meeting was significant as it highlighted the spiritual bond between the two saints and the impact of their lives on the monastic tradition. St. Anthony, upon learning of St. Paul, sought him out and found him living in a cave. Their conversation was marked by mutual respect and admiration for each other's spiritual journeys [2][10].

St. Paul's legacy is profound; he is celebrated not only for his personal holiness but also for laying the groundwork for the monastic life that would flourish in Egypt and beyond. His life inspired many others to pursue a similar path of asceticism and devotion to God, leading to the establishment of monastic communities that emphasized prayer, worship, and communal living [5][6]. His feast day is commemorated in the Coptic Church, reflecting his enduring influence on Christian spirituality.

A group of ninety-seven confessors: men, women , and children, were 
brought to the governor , and  he ordered  the executioners to burn the  
believers' left feet using red hot heated iron and to pluck out their right eyes 
then sear them with red hot metal. Afterward, he sent those courageous 
confessors to work as slave laborers in the mines of Lebanon. 
Another group from Gaza was arrested while gathering in prayer and 
listening to the Word of God. Among them was a girl named Thea (Tia), who 
rebuked the governor when he threatened to have her raped in public , and he 
ordered that she would be whipped and t ortured. When another girl from 
Caesarea of Palestine, named Valentina saw that, she rushed through the 
crowd to tell the governor: “Until when will you torture my sister?”  She was 
arrested and was taken to the temple of the idols . There, she kicked the al tar, 
and the governor ordered tying the two girls together and burning them alive. 
At the same time, the head of a Christian man name d Paul (Paulus) was 
cut off because he held fast to his f aith. That man showed an amazing love in 
the moments before his ma rtyrdom. After he requested the permission of his 
executioner, he stood up and with contrition prayed with a loud voice to God 
for his companions to support them in the moments of their s uffering; for the 
spreading of f aith; for t he sake of all who were pr esent and for that of the 
emperor, the governor and all the officials.  
His sufferings drew him to think not of himself but of the others, even the 
opponents and the persecutors, to pray to God to grant them Salvation. 
 [Eusebius: Ecclesiastical History, ch. VIII] 
 
PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA 
Through Divine care , St. Abba Anthony the Great the Father of the 
Monastic family and its founder in the whole world, encountered this St. Paul 
who preceded him by long years in monastic life in the wilderness, where no 
one but God knew anything about him . God kept sustaining him by half a 
loaf of bread, carried to him by a raven every day all along many decades; in 
which God smelled the sweet fragrance of his prayers and praise, to call him: 
“My beloved Paul.” 
His Upbringing: 
St. Paul the 1st hermit was born in Alexandria around the year 228 AD. His 
father passed away leaving a great wealth for him and for his older brother 
Peter. However, Peter conspired to acquire the greater portion of the 
inheritance for himself, and  when the disagreement escalated between the

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 381
passages.text:
381 
 
AD; St. Abba Bishoi fled the area and went to mount Anesna in Upper Egypt. 
There, he met with Abba Paul the H ermit and they both had an amazing 
spiritual friendship, that an angel appeared to St . Paul, saying: “ Your body 
will be with that of Abba  Bishoi.” (The two bodies are still together in one 
tube in the Monastery of Abba Bishoi up to this very day) . It was said that 
later on when the bishop of Anesna  decided to move the body of Abba  
Bishoi; his boat did not move until a hermit name d Jeremiah told them about 
the promise of the Lord to Abba Paul, so they brought the body of Abba Paul 
to the boat and they moved them together to the Monastery of Abba  
Shenouda in Akhmim . Later on, the bodies of these two saints were moved 
again together in the days of the 52 nd Pope Yusab I in the 9th century (831-
849 AD) to the Monastery of Abba Bishoi in the Scetis. 
The bodies of the two saints were kept in one tube; and this is a testimony 
of the spiritual friendship full of love that bound the two saints together; that 
even death could not separate them. This is not on the le vel of this mortal 
world but the level of the Eternal glory of both the body and the soul. 
Abba Paul was known for his great love of worship, particularly for the 
perpetual prayers, as well as his serious asceticism, that his disciple Ezekiel 
told about him that he faced death six times because of his harsh asceticism. 
He lived in solitude as a herm it, in perpetual strife, that the Lord  Jesus 
Christ appeared to him saying: “ Enough labor, My beloved Paul”.  St. Abba 
Paul answered Him: “ O my Master, let me exhaus t my body for the sake of 
Your Name; as You have done for the sake of mankind. Even though You are 
God, You delivered Yourself for our sake, we who are unworthy.” 
 [O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt; p. 223-4] 
 
PAUL THE GREAT, ST. 
St. Paul the Great once said: “The monk who cares for the few things he 
has in his cell, will be mocked by the demons . Personally, I suffered from 
such a situation.” This St. Paul (Boulus) was from Galatia, a Roman province 
in Anatolia (modern central Turkey). 
[Boulus the Confessor: cf. the Biography of ‘Ur’ (Hur), Isaiah, Boulus & Nobi] 
 
PAUL (The martyr) 
The historian Eusebius mentioned the details of what  he witnessed of 
violence and brutality in Caesarea of  Palestine against the believers , in the 
year 324 . These tortures were inflicted by the governor of Palestine 
Firmilianus, the successor of Urbanus, in the days of E mperor Maximinus II

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 384
passages.text:
384 
 
of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St . Anthony what to 
do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on 
the ground and they dug the grave with their claws ; according to St. Antony's 
directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body. 
St. Anthony carried the garment of palm t ree fibers and presented it to 
Pope Athanasius who gr eatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every 
year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany , and Resurrection . Many signs 
were shown by that garment. 
In the location where St . Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery 
was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise 
for the Lord. 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.” 
 [The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25] 
 [Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

passages.text:
385 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
One of the desert fathers told this story about a monk by the name of Paul  
(Boulus) from somewhere in Lower Egypt and he lived in Thebes:  
He used to hold a serpent by his bare hands and split it into two . Some of 
the brethren made metanoia before him, and said: “Tell us brother; what did 
you do that made you qualified for such a marvelous grace ?” He answered 
them: “Forgive me, fathers. Once the man acquires purity, everything would 
submit to him and obey him. Like the way , Adam was in Paradise before he 
disobeyed the Divine commandment.” 
 [Light Publications: Sayings of the Elder Fathers, 1983, p. 258 (Arabic)] 
 [Bendicta Ward: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers] 
 
PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST. 
This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of 
God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 
60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer 
who got married to a very beautiful girl . After living together for so many 
years, he started to take notice o f so many rumors about his wife' s evil 
behavior. However, whenever he inquired fr om her about the matter, she 
would pretend to be a pure woman . Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the 
evil act . On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba 
Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples. 
Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony 
advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be 
difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age . Before his 
persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in  the valley to practice 
with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not 
leaving that mountain. 
Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; 
and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance , and obedience . Among 
those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching 
him lest he would collapse. He s ought from him to  remain a whole week 
outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without 
leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, 
to loosen it and weave it anew . In all that he was obedient, worked with joy 
and extreme simplicity. 
On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted 
him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way 
between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

passages.text:
Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church – Volume 1  
666 
In the apostolic age, many practiced a kind o f monasticism, seeking to enjoy the 
perfection of the Gospel. The eschatological direction of the Church made the believers long 
for the coming of their Bridegroom, so some preferred to live a life of virginity, consecrating 
all their time for worship to p repare themselves for the heavenly wedding. In the second 
century, the Christian virgins in Smyrna and Corinth used to walk in liturgical processions 
behind the priests and in front of the widows. Moreover, many groups of virgins were found 
living in Alexandria and in many cities around the world. Articles about virginity represented 
an essential aspect of the writings of the Church Fathers in the first three centuries. 
Virgins used to live together, while men preferred to leave the cities to live in simple huts 
in villages and were often called “consecrated.” Some people felt a thirst for the angelic life 
so they fled to the wilderness. We know of only a few of these, such St. Paul the Hermit who 
lived in the wilderness for almost ninety years (between 250–340 A. D.). 
St. Anthony established the monastic movement and is considered the father of all monks 
in the entire world, even though many preceded him. This is because of his strong relationship 
with St. Athanasius, who wrote about him to the Roman world. It is also because he opened 
his cave after twenty years of solitude to disciple monastic leaders, converse with 
philosophers in the simplicity of his faith, and receive rulers. He had an active role in the 
Church and went to Alexandria to support the martyrs and stand against the Arians. 
St. Pachomius, founder of cenobitic monasticism, felt that the order of solitude may not 
work for all those who want to become monks, so he started a monastic community within 
the walls of monasteries, and the hermits praised him for doing so. 
St. Macarius the Great, St. Ammonas and others started the order of communities (or the 
semi-eremitical order). Many came from around the world to practice the ascetic life in 
Egypt, and to write about it and take these orders back to  their countries. It is important to 
note that the leaders of the three orders were not biased for their monastic styles, but instead 
they used to visit each other and praise each other’s orders. 
The monastic movement of women started side by side with tha t of men, and monks 
helped build convents. Female leaders arose and had great influence, like Amma Sarah, 
Amma Theodora, and Amma Syncletica. Moreover, some Egyptian and foreign women were 
disguised in the apparel of men and led ascetic lives in monasterie s of men, and their 
asceticism, struggles, and spirituality exceeded many. 
875. Who were the most important monastic leaders? 
St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit):  St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 
375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and 
Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his 
parents. During the persecution of  Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness 
after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years

passages.text:
380 
 
West (Gaul, Britannia, and Hispania) was for Constantine II (337 -340 AD). 
Emperor Constantius II  was inclined toward Ariani sm, so he exiled the 
patriarch Paul I to set Eusebius of Nicomedia  in his place on the throne of 
Constantinople. However, Eusebius died in the year 341 AD and the church 
was saved from his evil plots. While the Arians set the deacon Macedonius as 
his successor; the Orthodox congregation brought back their legal patriarch . 
When the two factions fought against one another, with dead and wounded on 
both sides; the emperor sent his high army commander to establish peace, but 
when he was killed, the emperor came by himself and forgave everybody. Yet 
because of his inclination toward the Arians, he exiled the patriarch Paul I for 
the third time. 
The Arians found their chance to spread their heresy; and Macedonius 
spread a new heresy, by which he denied the Divinity of  the Holy Spirit . 
Patriarch Paul I feeling his responsibility toward his people ; he had to return 
to Constantinople to hold th e congregation on the Orthodox F aith and to 
counter the other vanities. When the emperor heard about that, he sent some 
people to get hold of him in secret, and he was taken in chains to be exiled in 
Singara in Mesopotamia. Then, he was taken back to Homs  (Emesa) and was 
left there. During all that, he suffered his fourth exile with thanksgiving. 
When the Pope of Rome Julius I  (337-352 AD) heard about St . Paul's 
latest exile; he sought the help of Constans I the emperor of Italy and Africa. 
That emperor loved the c hurch, and he intervened with his brother 
Constantius II  to bring back the exiled bishops . Then, he held a Church 
Council in Sardica headed by P ope Julius I in the year 343 A D, in which he 
excommunicated Macedonius and the Arians . Constantinople received its 
patriarch with great joy, and St. Paul I did his best to shepherd his flock. 
When emperor Constans I was assassinated, the Arians found their chance 
to slander Pope Paul I and to accuse him of heresy and evil practices . They 
eventually managed to get hi m exiled for the fifth time to Cucusus  in the 
mountains of Cappadocia ( in Armenia Minor), where he reposed in the Lord 
in the year 351 AD, as a result of what he suffered of labors, hunger , and 
thirst; enduring them all with joy. 
The Latin Church celebrates his feast on the 7th of November. 
 
PAUL OF TAMOUH, ST. ABBA 
The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of this saint on the 7th of Baba, and 
seeks his prayers in the commemoration  of the saints in the Liturgy, along 
with St. Ezekiel his disciple.

337 
 
memorial on the 2nd day of the Coptic month of Mesra.  
 
PAESIUS (The martyr) 
Paesius and Paesi were among the common names of the early monks and 
martyrs. We can mention few of them: 
1- St. Paesius: an Egyptian martyr who offered his life together with others 
as a sacrifice to God in the 2nd year of the persecution stirred up by 
Emperor Diocletian  (284-305 AD).  They were tortured by Urbanus, the 
governor of Caesarea of Palestine [Eusebius: Martyrs of Palestine]. 
2- Martyr Paesi  (Paesius/Isi): brother of martyr Takla; two Egyptians (8 
Kiahk) from Abisir, west of El-Ashmonein (see Isi). 
3- St. Paesius, brother of Abba Isaiah, the Scetic (see Isaiah). 
4- St. Paesius, brother of Abba Bemen, the hermit; also called Paul, one of 
seven brothers. 
5- St. Paesius, brother of Abba  Paul and Abba Bishoi. Sometimes the name  
Paesius is mentioned instead of Bishoi. 
 
PALAMON, THE HERMIT, ST. ABBA 
This saint Palamon was mentioned on the 20 th day of Toba in the 
Synaxarion published by Rene Basset . He is a different saint from  Abba 
Palamon, the mentor of St. Pachomius, the Father of the Koinonia.  
In the Eastern Wilderness: 
We do not know a lot about this saint, except for his story , which showed 
the bitter war that Satan would raise against everyone, particularly those who 
achieve a high spiritual level . This father was earnest in his spiritual strife, 
never known to laugh since his youth . Yet the enemy planned to push him to 
the pit to destroy him completely if it was not for the e levated care of God 
Almighty. 
It was said that he once came out from his cave on the eastern side of the 
mountain, carrying a little of his handwork to sell it i n the countryside . It 
happened that he lost his way in the middle of the wilderness and could not 
find any sign that would lead him in the right direction . He remained that 
way for a whole week without food or drink in the deadly heat of summer . 
When he was on the brink of death, he cried out loud: “My Lord Jesus Christ, 
help me .” He instantly heard a voice telling him: “Have no fear, for the 
enemy will have no power on you because you remember Me . Get up, walk 
toward the south, until you meet a true elder monk named Thallason, as solid 
as a stronghold . Tell him about how Satan seduced you and about the great

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 379
passages.text:
379 
 
Berba (pagan temple) and a fire was ignited underneath them . However, they 
were not harmed and the fire almost consumed  the temple. Here, the priests 
of the idols intervened and begged the governor to get rid of them by having 
their heads cut off, which he did . Afterward, God performed so many signs 
and healings from the bodies of these two saints. 
 
PAUL I, THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE 
With jealousy on the Orthodox Faith, St. Paul I, the patriarch of 
Constantinople (337-351 AD) stood against the Arian heresy that denied the 
Divinity of the Lord  Jesus Christ. He had a close relationship with  the 20th 
Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD) and the Pope 
of Rome, St. Julius I (337-352 AD). St. Paul I  was exiled five times during 
his patriarchate, these were plotted by Eusebius of Nicomedia and 
Macedonius, the denier of the Holy Spirit. 
This saint was bo rn in Thessalonica at the end of the 3rd century. He was 
raised on lovi ng God and holding fast to the f aith. When he moved to 
Constantinople, its p atriarch Alexander (314 -337 AD) ordained him as a 
priest, after observing how he led a tru ly pious life, along with great 
knowledge and strong faith . As a priest, he was loved by the congregation , 
and when the patriarch felt that his departure was close, he gave his counsel 
to choose the priest Paul (Boulus) as his successor. 
His Patriarchate:  
St. Paul was chosen as an archbishop of Constantinople in the year 337 
AD. This was the start of his struggle in bearing his Cross . His troubles were 
mainly caused by the heretics who focused on opposing him until the 
moment of his departure from this world . Eusebius of Nicomedia, w ho was 
cherished by the emperor's sister, was able to convince E mperor Constantine 
the Great (306 -338 AD) to exile th is saint after he and his collaborators 
presented so many false claims and reports that stirred up the emperor against 
him. However, after his exile, they tried to convince the emperor to get 
another patriarch to replace him; but Constantine refused to do so . The saint 
remained in exile until  Emperor Constantine passed away in the year 338 
AD, then he returned to his  throne; as did St . Athanasius the Apostolic, St. 
Eustathius of Antioch, St. Marcellus bishop of Ancyra and others. 
His Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Exiles: 
Before he died, E mperor Constantine the Great divided his empire on his 
three sons: The East an d Constantinople  was the portion of Constantius II 
(337-361 AD); Italy and Africa that of Constans I (337 -350 AD); and the

passages.text:
383 
 
two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court . However, on his way 
to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened 
to be passing by . St. Paul asked himself: “Has t hat rich man taken anything 
from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he 
totally despised the temporal life . His heart was so i nflamed with the Eternal 
inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and  
entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking 
the Divine guidance. 
Then, an angel appeared to St . Paul and guided him to the wilderness in 
the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea . There he 
lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself 
in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration 
of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven . The saint lived 
all that time on that bread with s ome dates from the palm trees or herbs from 
the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring. 
An Encounter with Abba Anthony: 
One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to 
dwell in that wilderness . Then, an  angel of the Lor d appeared to Abba  
Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the 
world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers , God has 
lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain. 
On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St . Anthony set forth  with Divine 
guidance, to the cave of St . Paul. When he got there, St . Paul called him by 
his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their 
lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual  but carrying a whole loaf of bread . 
St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all 
along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, 
but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.” 
At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to 
bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius 
the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching . Abba 
Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment , and headed back to 
St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his s oul to 
Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God. 
On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling . 
For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to 
finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely 
mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.  
When St. Antony wanted to bury St . Paul, he wondered how he could dig 
the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body

records.question: Who was St. Abanoub, and how old was he when his parents died?
records.answer:
St. Abanoub was a young Christian martyr from Nehissah, in the city of Talkha, who lived during the 4th century. He was raised by pious parents who instilled in him strong Christian values and a love for God and the Holy Bible. Tragically, he lost both of his parents when he was only 12 years old, which deeply affected him, earning him the title "the lamented boy" due to his prolonged sorrow over their loss [1].

Despite this early grief, St. Abanoub demonstrated remarkable faith and courage in the face of persecution. After hearing a sermon encouraging Christians to endure suffering with joy, he felt inspired to openly declare his faith. This led him to confront the local governor, where he faced severe torture for his steadfastness. Throughout his trials, he was reportedly supported by divine interventions, including the presence of Archangel Michael, who healed him during his tortures [2][4]. Ultimately, St. Abanoub was beheaded for his faith, and his martyrdom is commemorated on the 24th of Abib [2]. 

In summary, St. Abanoub was a courageous young martyr who was only 12 years old when he lost his parents.
