her that her salvation is near. On the next day, the governor ordered to resume 
her torture, and then he ordered to cut her head off . At that moment, a lighted 
dove came down on her head, which made many of those present proclaim 
their faith in the Lord Christ. 
 [Butler: September 7] 
 
REGULUS, THE BISHOP , ST. 
St. Regulus (Rieul) is the intercessor of the city of Senlis . He is said to be 
the first bishop in the city , for he lived in the 3 rd century. After that , the 
Cathedral of Senlis was burnt out with all the records of its former bishops . It 
is said that after he proclaimed his faith in the Lord Christ, he set forth to 
France where he preached Christianity. And, he went to Paris to search for the 
relics of the martyrs: St. Denis, St. Rusticus, and St. Eleutherius. Then, he took 
upon himself to convert the inhabitants of Senlis; to Christianity . He reposed 
around the year 250 AD. 
  [Butler: March 30] 
 
REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine . When she was 12 
years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249 -
251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her 
beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making 
her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of 
fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing 
praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she 
holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her 
head off, she walked wi th them singing praise . Finally, when she was 
beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, 
flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she 
was honored by several dioceses. 
 [Butler: October 8] 
 
RESTITUTA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady St. Restituta was a Roman virgin of noble origin, and was 
martyred in the year 271 AD in the town of Sora in Italy. She became the patron 
saint of that city where she was buried . It was said that the Lord Christ 
appeared to her and instructed her to go to Sora, and an angel led her to that

164 
 
Earlier on, Genevieve 's poor parents received the Christian faith and 
forsook the idol -worship. Then, her father needed her to shepherd his s mall 
flock of sheep, in which the girl found a great chance to spend the whole day 
on the pasture land, practicing a life of prayer and worship of her beloved 
groom Jesus Christ . On the other hand, Genevieve 's mother tried to let her 
daughter stop spending  long hours worshipping God, with no avail . It 
happened that on a feast day, intending to punish her daughter for disobeying 
her, she ordered her to stay home and not to accompany her to church. Pleading 
with her mother with tears, not to deny her the enjo yment of the feast of her 
heavenly groom, the mother in anger, slapped her daughter on the face . In 
return, she was inflicted by blindness for two years. Then, with a contrite soul, 
she gave her daughter some water, asked her to pray o ver it, and then washed 
her eyes with it and God healed her on the spot. When her parents passed away, 
Genevieve went to live with her God-mother in Paris, where she dedicated all 
her time praying and helping others . Yet, she was subjected to ridicule and 
scoffing, even after St. Germanus visited her once again. 
Her Severe Illness: 
Genevieve was inflicted by a severe illness that left her in a coma that lasted 
for three days, and she was on the brink of death . However, God gave her a 
night vision to comfort her, in which she saw the saints in their glory and the 
wicked in their sufferings. She saw her soul had set forth as though to Mount 
Golgotha, to see the Lord  Jesus Christ crucified . This vision became so 
engraved in her heart and gave her the support she needed in her strife.  
Once more, she was inflicted by leprosy , and she was abandoned by 
everyone, but God healed her to become a guide to the virgins in Paris. 
Knowing the Inner Thoughts of Others: 
For her great love of the salvation of her brethren, God granted her the grace 
of understanding the inner thoughts of others and what was going on in their 
minds, and she used that to exhort them to repentance . A girl who vowed 
virginity fell into the sin of adultery, on meeting with the saint, who exhorted 
her to repent. The girl perceived that the saint had complete knowledge of the 
place, date, and time of her sin, and the girl felt shame and did repent sincerely. 
Building a Church: 
Saint Genevieve once revealed to some priests her longing to build a church 
in the na me of St. Dionysius , the martyr. They explained to her that they 
couldn't do that without having the needed building materials. Yet, the next 
morning they, miraculously found all the building materials required in a forest 
nearby, which they used to build that church.

passages.text:
651 
 
of her happiness. She answered that she was exultant because God used her to 
save the two sisters from the captivity of the devil. 
Finally, when the governor ordered to cut her head off, she cried out, saying: 
“I thank You, O Lover and Savior of the souls for inviting me to Your Heavenly 
Paradise.” 
With the Noble Young Man Theophilus: 
On her way to execution, a lawyer by the name of ‘Theophilus’ approached 
her, and mockingly asked her: “Where are you going , ‘Dorothy’?” She 
answered him: “I am going to the Garden of my Groom .” Then, he, with a 
scoff, said to her: “I seek from you, O bride of Christ, to send me some roses 
and fruits from the Garden of your Groom .” She answered him: “I shall 
certainly do as you requested.” On reaching the arena of martyrdom, a peasant 
child approached her carrying a plate containing three fruits and three roses 
with green leaves, even though it was winter. She said to him: “Please go and 
present them on my behalf to the lawyer ‘Theophilus’ and tell him that these 
roses and fruits are from the Garden of Jesus, my Groom.” The child went his 
way, and she approached the swordsman to enjoy the crown of martyrdom 
around the year 303 AD. 
In the House of Theophilus: 
While ‘Theophilus’ was at home narrating to his friends what he had done, 
and how he had scoffed the virgin ‘Dorothy;’ behold, that chi ld came in and 
presented to him the plate of roses and fruits, saying: “This is a gift for you 
from my sister ‘Dorothy,’ she plucked from the Garden of her Groom.” Then 
the child immediately disappeared. ‘Theophilus’ was amazed and cast himself 
on the ground, thanking God for His work with him, and before all those who 
were present, he confessed that the Lord Christ was his God and the Savior of 
the whole world . Then, he shouted aloud: “Blessed are You Jesus, my God, 
Groom of ‘Dorothy;’ and blessed are all those who believe in You, and who 
die for the sake of faith in You.” 
When one of those present hastened to inform the governor what had 
happened, he did not believe until he called ‘Theophilus,’ who confessed his 
faith before him . Then, he was put under severe torture and was finally 
crowned with the crown of martyrdom. 
It was said that ‘Dorothy’s body was carried to Rome, where it was kept in 
a church carrying her name, on the banks of the River ‘Tiber.’  
It became a tradition to paint the p ortrait of the saint carrying roses and 
apples, and in the celebration of her feast, a special rite is practiced to bless the 
roses and apples. 
 [Butler: The Lives of the Saints, February 6]

242 
 
This saint Theodora was a woman who dedicated her life and energy to 
serve the martyrs during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian 
(284-305 AD), And when the available cemeteries were all filled by the tombs 
of the martyrs; she had them buried in her land on Flaminian Way, about 26 
miles from Rome . In that land, she hid the martyrs Abundius , the priest, 
Abundantius, the deacon, Marcianus, and Joannes. 
The West celebrates this saint’s feast on the 17th of September. 
 [Henry Wace: A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Literature, Sects & Doctrines; 4 
Vol.; London 1877-1887] 
 
THEODORA, THE CANONESS 
This saint Theodora was a Church woman (Canoness), to whom St. Basil 
the Great wrote a magnificent letter (# 173 [302]), in which he explained the 
strength of the rules of the Evangelical life which she adopted . And, he 
apologized to her that he ceased from writing more in his letter, lest it w ould 
probably fall in somebody’s hand, and he would read it. 
[New Advent; Fathers of the Church; Letters of St. Basil of Caesarea: 173]  
 
THEODORA, THE REPENTANT, ST. 
This is the story of an innocent God -loving soul, which, due to the lack of 
discernment, might drop and fall to the bottom . It is the story of the human 
being who is eager to have everybody saved, no matter how bad his/her sins 
were, to be installed as a holy son/daughter of the Mighty God. Theodora was 
the second Magdalene who knew, by her love for God, how to trample the sin 
under her feet, to live a holy life for Him. 
The Happy Wife: 
This saint Theodora was brought up in the 5th century in the days of Emperor 
Zeno (474-491 AD) of a noble family , and she had great beauty, piety , and 
wealth. She was married to a rich and pious young man, and she lived with 
him a life of peace and joy . Amid the riches and the multitudes of banquets, 
she got acquainted with a rich young man who admired her wisdom and well-
balanced nature. Her husband noticed this admiration but was sure of the purity 
of the young man . But, with time, the devil started to plant the seeds of evil 
thoughts in him toward Theodora, which he tried hard to fight for his respect 
for her. However, with the growing temptation and at the prop er chance, he 
revealed to the lady how he felt towards her. Because she thought he was pure 
in mind, she was shocked to hearing what he said. However, with time and the

DOROTHEUS, ST. 
(The martyr) 
This St. ‘Dorotheus’ was a priest in the city of ‘Tyre’ in ‘Phoenicia’ 
(nowadays Levant). Probably, he became the bishop of that city. 
When Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) stirred up persecution against 
Christians, he suffered much in his city, was exiled for a while, and then came 
back to his diocese. In that period, he attended the Nicene Ecumenical Council 
in the year 325 AD . And when Emperor Julian the Apostate ’ (360-363 AD) 
reigned and renewed persecution against Christians, he exiled again to 
‘Odyssopolis in ‘Thrace’ (nowadays the port of ‘Varna’ in Bulgaria). 
Even in his exile, he was not left alone in peace. Although he was over 115 
years o f age , he was arrested and was beaten so fiercely that he became a 
martyr at the age of 117 years in the year 362 AD. 
[Butler: The Lives of the Saints, June 5] 
 
DOROTHY, THE VIRGIN, ST. 
(The martyr) 
The Virgin Bride of Christ: 
‘Dorothy’ (Dorothea) was a virgin in ‘Caesarea of Cappadocia,’ daughter of 
an elite Roman judge by the name of ‘Tadoros’ and his wife ’s name was 
‘Theodora.’ When the persecution against Christians got intense, they fled 
from Rome to ‘Cappadocia’ and resided in the city of ‘Caesarea.’ There, God 
gifted them with their daughter ‘Dorothy,’ and they were greatly comforted. 
The blessed girl exalted in virtue, particularly in humility, meekness , and 
chastity. Besides her God-given gifts of beauty and prudence, she had a well -
developed mind and was unique in her time. Many proposed to her in marriage, 
but she declined , for her heart was so kindled with love for her Heavenly 
Groom that she vowed to keep her virginity. Out of admiration, everybody used 
to call her “The Bride of Christ.” 
With Governor ‘Sopricius’: 
The fame of ‘Dorothy’ spread fast, and when governor Sapricius (Fabricius/ 
Apricius), came to visit ‘Caesarea,’ some people informed him of her great 
beauty and prudence  and told him that she was keeping Christians from 
worshipping the gods of the emperor . ‘Sapricius’ called her to appear before 
him, and once he talked to her, he felt that she was unique. The governor asked

passages.text:
165 
 
God also granted the saint the grace of casting demons out  and performing 
miracles. This given powers made some je alous people accuse her of 
deception. However, St. Germanus came to her defense. 
Attempting to Burn her Alive: 
It was said that the heathen king Attila the Hun  (434-453 AD) , after 
defeating Austria, headed toward France with an army of half a million 
soldiers. When he came close to Paris , the people planned to flee away to the 
surrounding fortified cities , but St. Genevieve convinced some women that 
Attila would not touch Paris . They, in turn, convinced their husbands to stay . 
However, some people thought that she was a sorcerer, and they plotted to burn 
her alive. Again, St. Germanus sent his deputy from Italy, a pious priest, to act 
in her defense, mainly that her prophecy was realized. 
Her Courage and Love for the Others: 
Another king of the Salian Franks  by the name Childeric  I (458-481 AD), 
came and put Paris under siege. This led to such a great famine that many poor 
people died on the streets . Greatly distressed for the news, Genevieve led a 
caravan of more than ten boats loaded with wheat, across the river to bring 
food to the inhabitants suffering from hunger , and out of her great love and 
compassion on people, she twice bravely sought from king Childeric  I to 
release the war captives, and twice she got her request. 
With Selinia: 
Genevieve once encountered a girl of a noble family, by the name Selinia . 
Talking to her about the virgin life and how the virgins were like angels , the 
girl broke her betrothal with a wealthy young man to lead a life of virginity. In 
retaliation, that young man intended to kill both girls , but they fled and took 
refuge in the church, where the closed gate opened for them then closed behind 
them in a miraculous exalted way. 
Her Asceticism: 
St. Genevieve only ate on Sundays and Thursdays, only bread of barley and 
boiled beans, and drank only water. She clothed herself with sackcloth, slept 
on the bare ground without a mattress a fter spending several hours praying at 
night. Finally, she reposed in peace around the year 500 AD. 
Among the miracles that happened after her departure to heaven, which 
reflected her intense love and compassion on people, was one that took place 
in the year 1129 AD, when a plague spread in France. The people carried the 
saint's coffin and paraded along the streets of the city, and the plague stopped 
at once. The church there, still celebrates the anniversary of that miracle up till

evil people set up against him and managed to expel him from there. So, he 
built another monastery at ‘Gormon’ on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, 
where he reposed in the year 430 AD 
He was famed for establishing in his monasteries a large Choir, which was 
divided into several groups. These groups would rotate throughout the day, 
each new group relieving the one before it, to create uninterrupted prayer and 
worship twenty -four hou rs a day without ceasing. Hence, they were called 
‘Akimetes’ or ‘Acoemetae,' meaning (The Sleepless Ones). 
 [Butler’s Lives of Saints, Feb. 23]  
 
ALEXANDER OF CAPPADOCIA 
(The martyr) 
Among many strangers who came to Milan in the days of Emperor 
Theodosius the Great ( 346-395 AD) were three men from Cappadocia: 
‘Sisinnius,' ‘Martyrius’ and his brother ‘Alexander.' They were so appreciated 
by St. Ambrose to recommend them to St. ‘Vigilius,’ Bishop of ‘Trent,' to 
designate them for preaching mission. They were sent to preach in ‘Tyrolese 
Alps,' where they faced so much trouble, although they managed to gain so 
many souls to the Lord Christ. 
When the pagans observed how those three men have converted a large 
number of the inhabitants to Christianity, they attacke d the church and 
violently continued beating the three saints. The first (a deacon) reposed within 
few hours, the second (a reader) managed to crawl into a garden nearby and 
was found the next day, to be dragged by his feet on the rocky road to be 
severely bruised and eventually to repose. 
Then, when the third (Alexander) fell into their hands, they tried to provoke 
him to deny his faith. They burned the bodies of his two companions in front 
of him. However, St. Alexander did not change his stand, so they b urned him 
alive. The believers gathered their burnt relics and carried them to Trent. St. 
‘Vigilius’ built a church on the location where they endured the sufferings. St. 
Ambrose, St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine mentioned these saints in 
their writings. 
 [Butler’s Lives of Saints, May 29] 
 
 
ALEXANDER OF THEBES 
(The martyr)

119 
 
because his lack of wisdom and discernment, fell from a considerable height 
and was about to perish, except for God’s care that had tender mercy upon him 
and saved him to resume his holy journey through the tribulation. 
St. ‘Palladius’ gave the following account:  
“I, myself, gained benefit from the experience I had with the blessed 
Albinus; when we set forth to ‘Scetis.' We had still 40 miles to travel to reach 
‘Scetis,’ during which we ate twice and drank water three times. However, he 
tasted nothing all along the journey, but walked on his feet, reciting verses from 
the Holy Bible, which he knew by heart; he sang 15 psalms with the Beatitudes, 
recounted the epistle to the Hebrews, the book of the prophet Isaiah, a part of 
the text of the prophet Jeremiah, the gospel of Luke and the book of proverbs. 
Even so, we could not catch with him.” 
“Yet, that man was tempted by lust, as if by fire. He could no longer stay in 
his cell, so he descended to Alexandria. All that happened because of his 
pride. However, by a Divine plan, according to the saying: (A nail could be  
pushed away by another nail), that although he chose to submit himself 
willingly to his lack of discernment, he found involuntary salvation afterward. 
In Alexandria, he started to go to the theaters, did not cease to drink wine in 
bars and has fallen into the love of women. Finally, he had another affair with 
one of the famous harlots, but the Divine Providence allowed for him to be 
inflicted on his private parts with a disease that lasted for six months. After he 
was healed, he was awakened up and remembe red his past Divine career, so 
he hastened to go back and confess all his sins to the Scetis ’ Fathers. He did 
not cease weeping in repentance and went back to his earlier ascetic life. 
However, a few days later, he departed from this world.” 
 [Budge: Paradise of Fathers, V. 1; pp. 134-5] 
 
ALEXANDER AKIMETES, ST. 
This saint was born in Asia Minor and was educated in Constantinople, 
where he received the Faith through his love of reading the Holy Bible. He 
then went to Syria to practice ascetic life. He pract iced the experience of 
fellowship than that of seclusion, and after 11 years of his monastic life, he 
dedicated himself to preaching in Mesopotamia (Al -Missa). And, it was said 
that he was the one who brought ‘Rabulas’ to the Faith, who became the bishop 
of Edessa (Al-Roha) later on. 
He established a vast monastery near the Euphrates. However, he did not 
stay long there, for he took a large number of its monks and went to Antioch 
for a while; although, his visit stirred up so many troubles. So, he finally h ad 
to leave and establish a new monastery in Constantinople. Once more, some

245 
 
AD. In the Roman Martyrology going back to the 8th century AD, A story was 
mentioned concerning St. Mark the Evangelist  and those two saints  that 
seemed to have taken place before he established the Seat of Alexandria. That 
account says that St. Mark went from Rome to preach the Gospel in Aquileia, 
North-East of Venice. He complemented his preaching by performing some 
miracles, and many people there were converted to Christianity.  Before St. 
Mark left the town, he ordained Hermagoras as a bishop and Fortunatus  as a 
deacon to take care of the believers. They kept preaching in the area until  
Christianity spread all around. 
Emperor Nero  (54-68), who hated the Christians, also sent his deputy 
Sebastus to Aquileia, to put his orders into action against the Christians there. 
He put Hermagoras  under arrest, tortured him , and cast him into prison . At 
midnight, a splendid heavenly light shone inside the prison , which impressed 
the jail -keeper in such a way that he be lieved in Christ and ran all around 
screaming: “Great is the God of Hermagoras! Come and see his wonders. ” 
When a multitude came to the prison, they saw the light and believed . At this 
point, Sebastus sent his swordsman and cut the heads of the bishop and his 
deacon in the darkness of the night. They received the crowns of martyrdom. 
 [Baring-Gould: Lives of Saints: Vol. 7, July 12] 
 
HERMAS, ‘THE SHEPHERD'S AUTHOR 
In the Muratorian Canon1, it was mentioned that Hermas, the author of the 
book ‘The Shepherd,’ was the brother of the first bishop of Rome, Pius I (140-
155 AD) . Origen (184 -253 AD)  believed that he was the same Hermas 
mentioned by St. Paul the Apostle (Rom. 16:14). In talking about himself, 
Hermas says that He was a slave, sold in Rome to a Roman lady called Rhoda. 
He began to love her as a sister. Then, seeing how beautiful she was, he desired 
to have her as his wife (Herm.Vis. 1:1). After she set him free, he became rich 
by working as a farme r and a merchant . He ended up marrying a talkative 
woman, and he became indifferent in caring  for his family . His children 
plunged into evil (Herm.Vis. 1:3), and because of them , he became poor 
(Herm.Vis. 1:2 , 2:3, 3:6). Sometimes, Hermas  portrayed himself as being 
virtuous, chaste, simple, and free from all evil desires (Herm.Vis. 1:2). At other 
times, he portrayed himself as a liar and a hypocrite (Herm.Vis. 3). At the time 
of persecution, he and his wife held fast to their faith. However, their children 
denied their faith. Enthusiastic about repentance, Hermas authored his book 
                                                 
1 The ‘Muratorian Canon’ (also called the ‘Muratorian Fragment’) is an ancient list of New Testament 
books—the oldest such list... The original document, which was written in Greek, is dated to around 180 
AD and lists 22 of the 27 books that were later included in the New Testament Bible...

Gaining the Blessing of the Holy Land: 
St. Hilarion kept on moving around in the Sinai desert . Then, he set out to 
get the blessing of the Holy Land , which was sanctified by the Lord  Jesus 
Christ, who lived there for a while . He also visited the monasteries there, 
enjoyed the encounter with the saintly monks and nuns, in whom he smelled 
the sweet fragrance of Christ.  
Father of the Monks: 
However, during his wandering in that area, a high number of young men 
gathered around him seeking to be his disciples, since they were impressed by 
his imposing role model of holiness, love, and humility, which were planted in 
him by Abba Anthony.  
So, as the monks gathering aroun d him increased in number, St. Hilarion  
built monasteries for them. He became a father for all of them and kept visiting 
every monastery once every year to guide the monks and to hold them fast unto 
Faith. He became so burdened with labor, especially with the increasing crowd 
of those who came to seek his prayers and blessing. 
The Saint Gets Attacked: 
It happened one day that Hilarion was attacked by armed robbers while he 
was kneeling to pray. When he disregarded them and kept on praying , they 
asked him: “Don’t you fear us?”  He answered, saying: “He who possesses 
nothing would fear no one !” When they added: “We could kill you!”  He 
answered them: “I don’t fear death  because I am always ready for it!” 
Perceiving the true faith through him, they were filled with fear and repented 
before him. St. Hilarion was attacked several times by the devi l: once in the 
form of women to corrupt the purity of his mind . Other times in the way of 
wild beasts to terrify him . Yet, he kept being armed with prayers and making 
the sign of the Cross on himself and managed to live in the peace of God. 
God's Miracles performed on His Hands: 
In the city of Eleutheropolis (Beit Guvrin near Hebron), a barren 
noblewoman came to seek his prayers to ask God to give her a child. Running 
away from her, she kept chasing him while bitterly weeping . He finally had 
compassion on her, blessed her, and told her: “My daughter, be sure that God 
responded to your request.” The following year, she came to him carrying her 
child, and the news spread all over the area. 
When the miraculous works of God kept happening again and again through 
this saint, multitudes of people came to seek his prayers . Many pagans 
proclaimed their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, and a lot of believers asked him

390), to whom the later sent several  letters. He was raised in the city of 
Arianzos. A s his piety became apparent since his childhood, St. Gregory 
brought him over to keep his company in Constantinople in the year 379. 
However, they were poorly received by the Arian monks and the mobs, who 
onetime forced their way on an assembly while holding the Holy Eucharist and 
threw stones on the priest. It seemed that Theodore was so upset and could not 
forebear that violence, the way St. Gregory did, that he planned to complain to 
the authorities a bout those wicked people . But St. Gregory wrote him a 
marvelous long letter, to show him that forbearing the wicked is stronger than 
avenging them [Letter 81]. It seemed that he was ordained as a bishop on Tyana 
after the year 381 AD; since his predecessor bis hop, Epherius attended the 
Council of Constantinople in the year 381 AD. 
On returning to his hometown , Arianzos, St. Gregory of Nazianzus, 
exchanged with bishop Theodore several letters that bore feelings of friendship 
and love. And St. Gregory invited him to partake of the celebration of the feast 
of the martyrs [Letter 90]. However, because he was not feeling physically 
well, he could not attend [Letter 221].. 
According to St. Palladius, bishop Theodore was invited to attend a Church 
Council that was assembled for the purpose of sending St. John Chrysostom 
into exile. However, once he got to know the real situation when he arrived at 
the site, he left without attending the Council. He went back to his diocese, St. 
Palladius described him as wise, revered, and compassionate. 
 
THEODORE, DISCIPLE OF AMMON, ST. 
This St. Theodore was often commended by pope Athanasius the Apostolic 
(328-373), who said about him: “A saintly pure man who chose to be unknown 
among the saints of God.” He was so admired by so many saints that whenever 
St. Ammon was mentioned, Theodore, his firstborn disciple , was also 
mentioned. According to St. Pachom, he was the life -companion of Abba 
Ammon. St. Ammonius, the companion of the great St. Ammon, and one of 
his early disciples, who was originally from Tabensin, then became its bishop, 
later on, was assigned by Pope Theophilus (385-412) to write St. Theodore’s 
biography. St. Theodore lived together with Abba Ur in a shared life . And it 
was said that while they were both occupied with painting a cell with  plaster, 
one of them asked the other: “If the Lord Christ visits us at this hour, what shall 
we do?” And, right away , they cried, abandoned what they were doing , and 
each of them returned to his cell.

passages.text:
246 
 
“The Shepherd” to urge the sinners to repent. He pointed out that the purity of 
the Church was in danger, because of the spread of sin, and that the end was 
close at hand. 
 “The Shepherd” Book: 
Some Church Fathers considered this book as an essential Church 
document, while some other Fathers underestimate at its worth . The book 
cared for the educational aspects more than the theological ones . It draws 
attention to the simplicity of the Christian life, its socialistic nature , and the 
depth of its spirituality ; yet vaguely and incompletely way. In the book, the 
writer used to stir up a problem and start giving a point of view; but before 
completing it, he would move on to another point. However, the book provides 
us with a costly material about the condition of the Church during the 1 st half 
of the 2nd century AD. The book is counted as a self-evaluation by the Church 
of Rome.  The book consists of five “Visions,” 12 “Commandments” 
(mandates), and 10 “Parables” (similitudes 
[Fr. Tadros Malaty: Introduction to Patrology, Pt. 1: Start of Christian Literature, 
Apostolic Fathers] 
 
HERMES, BISHOP OF SALONA (The martyr) 
St. Hermes was the bishop of Salona, the capital of Dalmatia1. Some people 
believe that  he was probably the same Hermes mentioned by St. Paul the 
Apostle in his epistle to the Romans (Rom. 16:14). It was believed too that he 
succeeded Titus as a bishop on Dalmatia, he was later on martyred during the 
1st century AD. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Hermes (2), Vol. II, p. 927] 
 
HERMES (The martyr) 
St. Hermes was born in Greece and was martyred in Rome during the 2 nd 
century (around 132 AD) though the circumstances of his martyrdom are not 
known. A magnificent Basilica was built over his grave around 590 AD by the 
Roman Pope Pelagius II (579-590 AD). The Pope restored it Adrian I  (772-
795 AD). Multitudes of believers go to get the blessing of this martyr.  The 
Church of the West celebrates him on the 28th of August. 
 [Butler: August 28] 
 
                                                 
1 ‘Dalmatia’ is located on the eastern Adriatic coast.

passages.text:
244 
 
entrusted him to resolve the problems referred to him by the congregation.  
With Julius Africanus: 
Pope Heraclas, by his virtuous life , drew not only the pagans of Egypt to 
Christianity but pagans from the foreign countries as well . The famous pagan 
Libyan Historian and traveler, Julius Africanus (160-240 AD), who authored 
the history of the world since the creation until the year 221 AD, came to visit 
St. Heraclas professed the Christian faith because of him. 
When the heart of Pope Heraclas felt comfortable about his people, and after 
he went through such a great l abor and strife for the sake of his love for the 
Lord Christ, he reposed. He departed to the dwelling places of the righteous on 
the 8th of Kiahk in the year 247 AD after he occupied the papal seat for sixteen 
years and one month. 
 [Fr. Tadros Yacob Malaty: The Early Fathers of the School of Alexandria]  
 [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Heraclas-Saint, by Aziz S. Atiya; p. 1219] 
 
HERACLEON 
Heracleon was a prominent Gnostic teacher, who represented  the Italian 
Gnostic School of Valentinian, centered in Rome during the 3rd quarter of the 
2nd century AD. Quotes of his interpretations of the Gospels were preserved in 
the writings of St. Clement of Alexandria (150-215 AD) and those of Origen 
(184-253 AD) in his interpretation of John's Gospel,  especially in volume 13. 
Heracleon used the symbolic approach in the interpretation of the events of the 
ministry of the Lord Jesus Christ. 
 [Hippolytus Haer, 6:35; 5-7] 
 
HERACLIDES (The martyr) 
St. Heraclides  was one of the students of the school of Origen . He was 
martyred in Alexandria in the year 250 AD. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Heraclides (1), Vol II, p. 902] 
 
HERAI (IRAEE) (Martyr) 
cf. the biography of St. Abadir (28 Tout). 
 
HERMAGORAS AND FORTUNATUS (The martyrs) 
St. Hermagoras and St. Fortunatus were among the martyrs of the 1st century

his heart was inflamed with Divine love. 
He asked the elder shepherd taking care of him, to let him spend the night 
in the monastery and come to bring him back on the next day. The shepherd 
reluctantly approved . The young saint spent the night happy and joyful, 
partook in the group prayers of the fathers , and continued praying until the 
morning. When he met with the Abbot of the monastery, he asked him to accept 
him there. Seeing the authenticity of his intention, and after explaining to him 
the toughness of monastic life, he allowed him. 
On the next day, the older shepherd was puzzled to find him refusing to go 
back without him. However, on encountering the parents and telling them what 
happened, the parents put him at ease and thanked him for taking care of their 
kid, which was something that he did not expect. 
Then, his parents carried many gifts and went to the monastery to meet their 
little boy Ehron, and to ask him to go back home with them. Ehron proclaimed 
to them his real longing for the monastic life, which brought comfort to their 
hearts, and they asked him to pray for them. 
His Seclusion: 
For ten years, he lived in the monastery growing in virtue, contemplation , 
and asceticism. All the monks loved him because of his piety and service to all 
of them. However, because the thought of seclusion was growing in his heart, 
he asked the Abbot of the monastery and the fathers to pray for him and bless 
him, and then he set forth to the wilderness to live in a cave on top of the 
mountain. 
There, St. ‘Ehron’ lived a life of complete asceticism, possessing nothing 
and eating only some herbs and few fruits he would find on the trees growing 
next to a little spring there. 
In Armenia: 
Three years after his seclusion, an angel of the Lord guided him to leave 
and move to the ‘Mountain of Armenia,’ where he would become a disciple of 
a sai ntly anchorite named ‘Gregorius the Hermit .’ There, he remained for 
another period of three years, practicing the monastic life of prayer and 
contemplation under the guidance of his new spiritual father. In addition, God 
granted him the gift of healing the sick and driving the demons out. 
In Jerusalem: 
Then, St. ‘Gregorius’ and his disciple ‘Ehron’ set forth to Jerusalem to get 
the blessings of the holy places , but Abba ‘Gregorius’ reposed in the Lord on 
their way and was mourned by his disciple. ‘Ehron’ continued his journey and 
moved between towns and villages, healing the sick and driving the demons

276 
 
HOR, THE ABBOT, ST. 
Abbot of Many Monasteries: 
This St. Hor was the Abbot of 1,000 monks. He had an angelic countenance 
and lived to be ninety years old. His long beard hanged downward on his chest 
and made him look so holy that all who saw him benefitted even without 
hearing a single word from his mouth.  
St. Hor lived first in a cave in the inner desert; Then, in a dream, he saw an 
angel of the Lord, telling him that he would become responsible for many 
monastic congregations. The angel assured him , saying: “Don't worry about 
food, from the time you sought the face of God until you depart from this 
world.” The saint set out to a place close to Shina, where he worshipped. He 
fed on the wild herbs, and during the days of fasting, he would eat once every 
week. Then, he became the Abbot of a few monasteries and managed to unify 
the monks under his supervision in great spiritual unity.  
An Illiterate who learned and Taught: 
St. Hor did not know the alphabet, but the Divine care taught him the Holy 
Scriptures, which he memorized by heart . With God' s grace, he was able to 
read with fantastic speed. And, he was granted the gif t of expelling the evil 
spirits. Once, St. Hor  claimed to know someone in the wilderness (most 
probably himself), who tasted no human food for three years; for an angel of 
the Lord used to bring him a Heavenly food once every three days, and put it 
into his mouth. Because of the sweetness of his talk, the monks used to gather 
around him to listen to him; and to sing hymns together in the church . They 
sounded as though a choir of angels singing in heaven. 
I Worship Christ Every Day: 
He also claimed that a mo nk, whom the demons intended to deceive, 
appeared to him in the form of horsemen escorting their king . Then, that king 
said to him: “Having proved to be perfect in everything , come now and 
worship me, and I will take you up to heaven like Elijah.” The monk answered 
him: “I worship Christ every day.” Then, he added: “You are not a king.” Right 
away, Satan evaporated before him. These stories happened to him personally. 
Because of his humility, he attributed them to someone else. 
 [The Paradise of Monks; p. 134]  
 
HORESIUS (Harsios) OF SOUL (The martyr) 
The Coptic Church celebrates St. Horesius of Soul on the 15th of Abib.

the Patriarch of Antioch,” despite never meeting the saint, that hermit thus 
prophesied Severus ascension to the patriarchal throne. 
And, it was also claimed that St. Leontius, the martyr, appeared to them like 
a mighty prince, with a girdle adorned with jewels, and seeing them terrified, 
he put their hearts at ease, then he disappeared. During his baptism, a shiny 
hand was put on Severus' head; and those present hear d a voice, saying: 
“Worthy, worthy, worthy,” and they were all amazed. 
His Monastic Life: 
After being baptized, he made significant spiritual progress, fasted every 
day, and spent most of his nights in the Church. 
After finishing his study of the Law, he s et forth to his hometown and 
worked as a lawyer for some time. Yet, deciding to visit the holy places in 
Jerusalem, there, he felt a longing to dedicate himself to ministry; and to 
exchange the robe of a lawyer with that of a monk. 
It was said that, while reading books of philosophy, St. Leontius, the martyr 
appeared to say to him: “Enough of this reading, O Severus! Come now and 
follow me, to go deep in studying the laws of God, which are read by the 
Fathers even at the time when they are about to repose. Wake up, Severus! 
Prepare yourself for the serious ministry in the Church. Walk -in monasticism 
to know how to strive with strength and to carry the shield of faith, by which 
you can quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one.” 
And it was also said that a hermit living outside the city saw Severus holding 
a shovel by which he was cleaning a fountain filled with mire and rot. As the 
saint approached him to seek his prayers, he recognized him, and said to those 
around him: “This man will be great among the wise, a martyr among the 
bishops.” He kept reading the Holy Bible and the books of the saintly Fathers 
unceasingly and in-depth. Then, he set forth to the monastery of Leontius, the 
martyr in Palestine, near Tripoli of Lebanon in the year 488 AD, where he was 
joined by some of his friends, who were previously his fellow -students in 
learning philosophy. 
His Seclusion: 
As his heart was kindled with longing for a life of seclusion, Severus, 
together with Athanasius from El-Roha, forsook the monastery and went to the 
desert of Eleutheropolis. There, he dedicated his time to worship and study; 
and wore out  his body intensely with fasting and watching the nights, to 
become ill, yet his illness did not quench the flame of his zeal.

‘Anthony,' among whom are: 
ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr: 
He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great 
zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then 
he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false 
gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was 
expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop 
assigned him to build a Ch urch, the pagans were stirred up against him and 
killed him. 
ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr: 
St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and 
merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to 
‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. 
The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. 
Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his 
Christ, he ordered him chained and se nt him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of 
Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ 
put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but 
God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' 
where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each 
other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with 
sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint 
received the crown of martyrdom. 
 
ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. 
He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family ’ and 
‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement ’ in the whole world, even though 
there have been some monastic movements prior to his. 
The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around 
the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his 
corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled 
toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the 
gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to 
the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me ” (Matt. 
19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched  his 
life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he 
proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its 
proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister 
also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed 
him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven 
flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the 
raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony 
to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church. 
St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic 
order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart

197 
 
The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying 
in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out 
to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of 
a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his 
head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned 
to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never 
get bored." That  came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand 
happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life. 
One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash 
their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they start ed to 
undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she 
answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, 
for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint 
said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He 
instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was 
around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to 
practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new 
location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of 
women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts. 
His Order of Seclusion: 
In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with  some 
beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He 
helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he 
was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept 
of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 
4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a 
member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he 
did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when 
Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his 
response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he 
said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of 
kings." However, when he was pressu red, he answered the emperor’s 
message, for the sake of the Church peace. 
5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy 
congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the 
Church. That is why he eventually came  down to help Pope Athanasius 
the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his 
entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants 
came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians 
came back to the Church.

the queen. After that, all stood with submissive and a contrite heart to pray and 
worship. Then, the monk came to give each of them what was needed for their 
hand-work. They worked in silence while singing praise until the ninth hour, 
when a servant brought food to them, which they ate after giving thanks to 
God. The hermit came to know that the king and the queen ate only once daily 
at sunset; watch the night praying  until midnight and live together  with a life 
of virginity. After having dinner with them, the saint bid them farewell, and the

St. Yusab returned to Scetis (el-Esqeet), beating his chest.  
And, he lived rejoicing until he reposed in peace. 
 [The Hermit Fathers, p. 25]  
 
YUSTUS ST. ANTHONY, THE MONK 
The monk Yustus (Justus) St. Anthony was born in the village called Zarabi 
near the M uĥarraq monastery in the province of Assiut in the year 1910 . He 
was given the name Naguib. He worked with his father as a tailor , and he 
learned and mastered the Coptic language . He was ordained as a deacon . 
Naguib went to the monastery of St. Paul in the Eastern desert. There, he spent 
two years as a novice. Then, he moved to the monastery of St. Anthony, where 
he was ordained as a monk in November 1941. 
He was always Expecting the Coming of his Master: 
From the very beginning, in his spiritual strife , he rarely closed his eyes . 
Still, he stayed all night wandering around inside the monastery, as though he 
was anticipating the coming of his Lord. And, whenever he needed some rest, 
he would sit underneath a tree for a short nap. In his early stages of strife, he 
used to lie down on the stem of a fallen tree on the ground, to keep himself 
from a comfortable sleeping, and to remain awake for praying all night long. 
Whenever he met with someone, he would ask him: “ What is the time 
now?” as though anticipating the time of his departure. At the beginning of his 
monastic life, he was fighting against evil thoughts. He was able to overcome 
them by staying awake and reciting the Lord’s Prayer in a loud voice, on and 
on, until they would go away. 
Concerning the Holy Bible, he memorized the Psalms and the epistles of 
Paul the Apostle by heart. And, he loved to read the Holy Bible in the Coptic 
language. Concerning his food, he used to eat just a little amount, mainly from 
the bread crumbles, which would fall off the main dinner table, after he would 
soak them in the water while he would give the rest of his food portion to the 
workers and the stray cats . Monk Yustus always lived poor. He never carried

of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St . Anthony what to 
do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on 
the ground and they dug the grave with their claws ; according to St. Antony's 
directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body. 
St. Anthony carried the garment of palm t ree fibers and presented it to 
Pope Athanasius who gr eatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every 
year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany , and Resurrection . Many signs 
were shown by that garment. 
In the location where St . Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery 
was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise 
for the Lord. 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.” 
 [The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25] 
 [Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

162 
 
According to St. Athanasius, while Abba Anthony was sitting one day by 
his monastery, he saw somebody ascending to heaven, and a multitude of saints 
was welcoming him. Inquiring about him, he was told that he was Abba Amon. 
Thirty days later, some hermits came over from Mount Nitria, to inform St 
Anthony that their father has departed to heaven. 
The C optic Church celebrates his feast on the 20 th of Bashons; and the 
Greek Church on the 4th of October. 
 
 
 
 
AMON, THE RYTHIAN, FR. 
He was called that way because he lived in the region of ‘Rythio’ by the city 
of ‘El-Tur’ in Sinai. He was an Egyptian monk who lived as an anchorite in the 
region of ‘Kanub’ (Abu Quir) at the beginning of the fourth century AD. When 
the persecution was stirred up by Emperor ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD), he was 
exiled to Palestine, and from there, he returned to the wilderness of Sinai. He 
witnessed by himself the invasion of the pagan Arabs on the monasteries of 
Sinai when they destroyed the monasteries and dispersed their monks. At that 
time, Amon set forth to ‘Rythio,' which became the center of a gathering of the 
monks of Sinai. He li ved there for a long time until Rythio ’ was invaded as 
well. And, he then left it and set forth to ‘Manf,' then to Scetis to live among 
its hermits as a disciple to Abba Bemen. When he once asked Abba Bemen 
about the evil thoughts; his answer was: “It is within the power of the enemy 
to bring them to our minds, but it is within our power not to accept them!” 
 
AMON, ABBA 
This saint was the disciple of Abba ‘Poemen’ (Bemoa). He came once to 
visit Abba ‘Sisoes’ (Shishoy) in wintertime. And he noticed that Abba  Sisoes 
was very sad and depressed after he left the life of seclusion in the wilderness, 
so he said to him: “Why are you so sad, O father? How could you have 
managed to live alone in the wilderness at your advanced age? ” The old man 
looked at him with admonishment and said: “What are you saying Amon?! Is 
feeling freedom in the desert not better than anything else?!” 
 
AMON, THE BISHOP OF HERMOPOLIS

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in 
prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 
7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who 
founded the system of congregations; as one of his disc iples and greatly 
rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of 
fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any 
particular order. 
8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to 
see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health 
until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 
9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet 
he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also 
drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could 
find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he 
answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the 
written text. 
When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book 
of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out 
seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. 
Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba 
Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it. 
Of His Words: 
 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have 
gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ. 
 Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack 
of discernment, they stayed away from God. 
 There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if 
they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are 
not like us. 
 Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over 
the beasts of the wilderness. 
The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba. 
 [The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated 
by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

(The martyrs) 
These saints were martyred in the 3 rd century AD in ‘Sebaste’ during the

161 
 
at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious 
monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone. 
His Personality and the Role of Nitria; 
Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or 
St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was 
characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away 
from the crowd and refrained from performing a ny miracles, claiming that he 
was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value 
of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in 
that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness 
of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused 
so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted 
to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. 
Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter 
migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba 
Amon. 
St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the 
repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, 
among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also 
found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the 
guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.  
His Miracles: 
Some farmers once came to Abba Amon, carrying a little child mauled by a 
dog and suffering severe pain. The saint asked them: “Why should you come 
to me to do something beyond my worthiness, when, in your hands, you have 
the healing medicine f or this child?! Now, give the stolen cow back to its 
widow owner, and the child will be healed." Having perceived that the saint 
revealed their hidden sin, they presented repentance and gave the cow back to 
its owner. The saint then prayed for the child, and the Lord healed him. 
St. Athanasius told that story about St. Amon: He was once with his disciple 
‘Tadros,’ and they needed to cross a river. Known for his great shyness, he 
sought from his disciple to go away from him, for each of them to take his 
clothes off and swim. Despite doing that, Abba Amon was too shy to take his 
clothes off, even in the absence of his disciple. In the middle of his confusion, 
he found himself all of a sudden on the other shore of the river. When his 
disciple saw him there with  his dry clothes, he was persistence to know how 
he crossed over. The saint told him, seeking from him not to tell it to anyone 
before his repose.

two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court . However, on his way 
to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened 
to be passing by . St. Paul asked himself: “Has t hat rich man taken anything 
from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he 
totally despised the temporal life . His heart was so i nflamed with the Eternal 
inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and  
entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking 
the Divine guidance. 
Then, an angel appeared to St . Paul and guided him to the wilderness in 
the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea . There he 
lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself 
in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration 
of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven . The saint lived 
all that time on that bread with s ome dates from the palm trees or herbs from 
the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring. 
An Encounter with Abba Anthony: 
One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to 
dwell in that wilderness . Then, an  angel of the Lor d appeared to Abba  
Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the 
world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers , God has 
lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain. 
On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St . Anthony set forth  with Divine 
guidance, to the cave of St . Paul. When he got there, St . Paul called him by 
his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their 
lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual  but carrying a whole loaf of bread . 
St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all 
along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, 
but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.” 
At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to 
bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius 
the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching . Abba 
Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment , and headed back to 
St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his s oul to 
Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God. 
On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling . 
For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to 
finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely 
mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.  
When St. Antony wanted to bury St . Paul, he wondered how he could dig 
the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body

‘Anthony,' he was of a wealthy pious family. He lost his parents while still in 
his youth and became under the guardianship  of his uncle. He desired to live 
as a virgin; his uncle betrothed for him a rich girl against his will. Not able to 
disobey his uncle ’s wish, he kept talking to his betrothed girl with spiritual 
conviction and through his holy behavior, he managed to have a good impact 
on her and made her love purity and planted in her heart the desire to dedicate 
her soul to be a bride for the real Groom Jesus Christ. The couple agreed to go 
along with the wedding plan, yet persisted on living together like brother and 
sister. They remained for 17 years, strict ly keeping their virginity. After that 
period, the wife departed to the eternal kingdom. In a night vision, the saint 
saw Abba Anthony calling him to put on the monastic ‘Eskeem.' Waking up, 
he went to St. Isidore who put on him the holy Eskeem. He stayed with him 
for some time; then, he set forth to Mount Tuna, where St. Anthony was 
dwelling. He lived a period with St. Anthony and became his disciple. He 
learned from him the holy monastic rules, then the saint built for him a cave in 
Mount Tuna and strove there in so many ways.  
The devil envied him and came to him in the form of a nun knocking at his 
door. When he opened the door and sought her to pray, the devil turned into a 
flame of fire and went away. Then, the devil seduced a loose woman to try to 
make the saint fall in sin. So, she put on her best attire and came at sunset and 
knocked on the saint’s door, saying: “I am a stranger traveler, who lost my way. 
It is now close to night time. Do not leave me outside, lest a beast may devour 
me, and you shall be responsible for my blood." The saint opened the door for 
her and recognized the trick of the devil who sent her, so he began to preach 
her from the Bible, to warn her about the suffering in hell prepared for the 
sinners and told her about the happines s prepared for the righteous. God 
opened up her heart; she understood his sayings and threw herself at his feet, 
weeping and supplicating to him to help her save her soul. He made her discard 
her luxurious clothes, had her head shaved, clothed her in a woo len garment

THEOGNOSTUS, FR. 
He was a priest from Alexandria, who was sent as a deputy of the 24th Pope 
Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to Constantinople, along with Fr. Sharmocinus 
the priest and Liontius the deacon [Cyril: Letters 37, 41] 
      [Smith & Wace; Vol 4, p. 990] 
 
THEOGNOSTUS 
Theognostus (Theogust) was a priest and a theologian in Alexandria in the 
3rd century AD. He was the Dean of the School of Alexandria, most probably 
before Fr. Peros. About him, we know very little through quotations that came 
in the writings of Fotius, Athanasius, and Gregory bishop of Nyssa. 
His doctrinal work “Hypotyposes” came in seven books, these books were 
available in the time of Fotius, but they have been lost later on . In his first 
book, he followed the style of Origen . In the second and third books, there 
were some Arian tendencies. In the fifth book, he denoted bodies to the angels 
and demons.While in the sixth and seventh books, he dealt with the Divine 
Incarnation in a sound Orthodox manner . The 20 th Pope Athanasius  the 
Apostolic considered his work as one of the best testimonies against Arianism. 
 
THEON, THE BLESSED ABBA 
This saint met with St. Jerome (347 -420) when he visited the region of 
Thebes. He was a monk who lived 30 years far from the city of Oxyrhync hus 
(El-Bahnasa)1 on the border of the extensive wilderness . He stayed in a little 
house he built by himself, keeping silent and practicing worship with such an 
enflamed heart, to be considered by the people as a prophet . And, with the 
spread of the sweet fragrance of Christ through his life, vast multitudes of 
people came daily to him carrying their sick . He used to stretch his hand on 
them from the window, and they were healed in the name of the Lord. 
It happened that some thieves, assuming that the hermit must have acquired 
plenty of gold from the gifts of his visiting people, so they came to kill him by 
night. Finding him standing in prayers, they were cast around as though 
chained by ropes and remained as such until the morning. When the multitudes 
came, as usual, they planned to punish them, but the saint sought from them to 
leave them alone, lest the Lord would take the gift of healing away from him . 
When they did, the thieves came to him with remorse and the fear of God and 
joined the rank of monks to practice the life of fellowship with God. 
 
1 ‘Oxyrhynchus’ (El-Bahnasa) is about 160 km south-southwest of Cairo in ‘El-Minya’ governorate…

IBRAHIM, THE ANCHORITE, ST. 
Ibrahim was a Pachomian monk whose feast is celebrated by the Church on 
the 30th of Baba. He was born in the city of Menuf to a wealthy pious family. 
He grew up despising every pleasure of this world. When he came to the proper 
age, he set out to Akhmim in Upper Egypt, and then from there , he went to 
where St. Pachomius resided. He revealed to him the longings of his heart . 
After being tested by St. Pachomius, he put on him the monastic attire.  
This saint practiced the life of communion and fellowship with loyalty and 
outstanding love toward his brothers’ monks for twenty-three years. Yet, when 
he started longing for a life of seclusion, he was allowed by St. Pachomius to 
live in a separate cave outside of the monastery. There, he led a strict monastic 
life, occupying himself with making fishing nets . Somebody from the 
community helped him by selling his hand -work, and buying him beans and 
giving the rest of the money to the poor. His daily food was a few beans wetted 
in water. His clothes, which he never replaced, were so worn out  that he used 
a piece of sackcloth to cover himself. He encountered no one and never came 
out of his cell, except to have the Holy Communion once every two or th ree 
years. 
Feeling that his time to depart from this world had come, he sent for his 
dear friend St. Tadros , the disciple of St. Pachomius . St. Tadros came and 
prayed with him for a while ; then, St. Ibrahim made the sign of the Cross on 
himself, and his soul departed into the Lord. 
       [The Synaxarion 30 Baba] 
 
IGNATIUS, THE THEOPHORUS, ST. 
He was born around the year 30 A.D. and was raised in Syria. Some scholars 
believe that he was the child whom the Lord Jesus Christ carried when He 
presented him as an example of humility (Matt. 18:2-4). 
Seeing his kindled zeal, the apostles ordained him a s a bishop on Antioch. 
However, there was a disagreement concerning which apostle has ordained 
him. According to some, Peter, the apostle, ordained Evodius as a bishop for 
the Christians from Jewish origin; and John, the apostle, ordained Ignatius for 
the Christians from Gentile origin . When bishop Evodius reposed, bishop 
Ignatius was put in charge of the region' s Christians from both origins. Being 
known for his eagerness for the salvation of souls, he gained so many new 
Gentiles for the Lord Christ. His i ntense love for his people was recorded in 
his conversation with those who came to welcome him in Smyrna, during his 
trip to Rome to be martyred. He kept mentioning his congregation to them and 
asked them to pray for his people.

424 
these thoughts and had understood the meaning of the rock, which is Christ. For she says: 
‘Show me your face, and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and  your 
countenance is glorious’ … And those who hear his sweet voice know the grace of the 
gospel—the ones who say, ‘You have the words of eternal life’ (John 6:68).”1091  
538. Why does St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, call the Church “a congregation of love”? 
St. Ignatius the Theophorus says, “All these things are good together, if you believe in 
love.”1092 He also says that Christ is eternal life for He grants us life through His divine love, 
“for the drink of God is His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.”1093  
539. Why does St. Ignatius the Theophorus call the Church “a congregation of 
thanksgiving and praise”? 
Because in the Eucharist, the Church is manifested in two ways. The first way is through 
love, purity, unity, fellowship in immortality, along wit h joy and praise. The second way is 
by resisting the devil and conquering him. St. Ignatius the Theophorus says, “Take heed, 
then, often to come together to give thanks to God, and show forth His praise. For when you 
assemble frequently in the same place, the powers of Satan are destroyed, and the destruction 
at which he aims is prevented by the unity of your faith.”1094  
540. How does Christ work in the members of His Church? 
Origen says, “When the Churches of God which are instructed by Christ, are carefully 
contrasted with the assemblies of the districts in which they are situated, they are as beacons 
in the world.”1095  
541. What is the Church’s role in the hearts of believers? 
According to a Syrian author, the role played by the Church, here on earth, is to inflame 
our hearts with longing to the heavenly Church: “It is befitting for us not to despise the seen 
church, which begets every one of us as children. Let us also not despise the church of the 
heart, which strengthens those who are sick. We must long to the high er (heavenly) church 
which perfects all the saints.”1096  
 
1091 St. Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory of Nyssa: Homilies on The Song of Songs, ed., Brian E. Daley S.J. and 
John T. Fitzgerald, trans., Richard A. Norris Jr. (Society of Biblical Literature, 2012) 5: pp. 175–177. 
1092 St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Philadelphians 9 (LCL 24:293). 
1093 St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Romans 7 (LCL 24:279). 
1094 St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Ephesians 13 (LCL 24:233). 
1095 Origen, Against Celsus 3.29 (ANF 4:476). 
1096 Book of Steps 1.3.

which he declined. After promising to give him many honors if he denied his 
Christ, he rejected them and held fast to his faith . Then, they started torturing 
him. They whipped him, pressed him by the Henbazin, cut some of his limbs, 
and burned his sides with fire . In all this, he endured for his love of the Lord 
Christ. And, the Lord sent his angel to strengthen and comfort him . Finally, 
they cut his head off, and he received the crown of martyrdom.  
The Church celebrated his feast on the 28th of Amshir. 
 
THEODORE, SON OF JULIUS EL-AQFAHSY (The martyr) 
This St. Theodore  was the son of the great martyr Julius el-Aqfahsy, the 
writer of the biographies of the martyrs . Together with his father, his brother 
Unias, their servants, the governors of Samannoud and Atrib, with a  great 
multitude of 1,500 believers were martyred all together. His body and those of 
his father and brother were moved to Alexandria on the 22nd of Tout. 
 
THEODORET, THE NESTORIAN HISTORIAN 
This Theodoret was a bishop of Cyrus (Cyrrhus)1, a citizen of Antioch, and 
educated in Antioch Monastic School. He distributed his possession on the 
poor and joined the Nicerte monastery around the year 416 A D when he was 
about 23 years of age. He was ordained as a bishop in Syria in the year 423 AD 
against his own will , and he was a strong adversary against paganism , In the 
controversy between the 24th pope of Alexandria St. Cyril the Great (412-444) 
and the heretic Nestor (428-431 AD), he took the side of his friend Nestor. But 
contrary to his friend Nestor, who refused to call the Virgin Mary, by the title 
Theotokos, namely (the Mother of God), Theodoret accepted it as a symbolic 
meaning. In the Council of Ephesus (431 AD), he strongly opposed pope Cyril 
the Great and the decrees of the Holy Council; although St. Cyril himself has 
accepted earlier a decree of faith, craftily written by Theodoret in the year 430.  
In the year 448 AD, he was accused by the 25 th pope of Alexandria St. 
Dioscorus I (444-454) that he made the Lord Christ as two Persons, for which 
he was considered as a heretic and was exiled from his throne. He was released 
from exile after appealing to Emperor Marcian (450-457). He then took part in 
the Chalcedonian Council in 451 AD against St. Dioscorus I. 
The Western Church tried to defen d him by claiming that he forsook the 
Nestorian heresy after the year 451 AD... 
This Theodoret left several works, among which were the interpretations of 
the Books of the Old and the New Testaments. Some of those were in the form

wherein He delighted, and I was daily His delight before His face at all
times.” (Prov. 8: 30) Since, therefore, the Father is eternal the Son also is
eternal, Light from Light.
Eusebius makes frequent use of Dionysius’
letters as an important source of the history of his life and times. He sent a
letter to Novatius who was illegally ordained the Bishop of Rome. In his
letter, he tactfully asked him to retire from the post even if he would be
martyred, for avoiding schism is more glorious than martyrdom.
“For in the
one case a man is a martyr for the sake of his own single soul, but in the
other for the sake of the whole Church."
[314]
Another letter he addressed to Basilides,
Bishop of Pantopolis in which he answers several questions regarding the
duration of Lent and the physical conditions required for the reception of the
Eucharist.
The third letter is addressed to Fabius,
Bishop of Antioch, in which he deals with the vexing problem of forgiveness
after apostasy during persecution. In his letter, he recounts the following:
I shall set forth for you this one example that happened amongst us:
There was a certain Serapion amongst us, an old man and a believer, who lived
blamelessly for a long time, but in time of the trial fell. This man oftentimes
besought (absolution), and no one paid him heed. For indeed he had sacrificed.
And, falling sick, he continued for three successive days speechless and
unconscious; but on the fourth day he rallied a little, and calling his
grandson to him, he said: “How long, my child, do you hold me back? Haste you,
I pray, and grant me one of the presbyters.” And having said this he again
became speechless. The boy ran for the presbyter. But it was night, and he was
unwell and could not come. Yet since I had given an order that those who were
departing this life, if they besought it, and especially if they had made
supplication before, should be absolved, that they might depart in hope, he
gave the little boy a small portion of the Eucharist, bidding him soak it and
let it fall in drops down into the old man’s mouth.
The fourth letter (
On Martyrdom
) is
addressed to the great master Origen
[315]
who was in prison at Tyre.
Finally, Eusebius mentions the Paschal
letters written every year by Dionysius in which he announces the date of
Easter and the beginning of the Lent. These letters took the form of pastoral
letters exhorting the congregation to observe Lent and the Easter season
spiritually. He also took the occasion to discuss important church questions of
the time.
Because of
widespread persecution, historical sources differ in arranging the Deans of the
School during the 3rd century
[316]
especially among Theognostus and Pierius. Cove sees that Theognostus succeeded
Pierius while Routh sees the opposite. He was the successor to Dionysius the
Great as head of the school of Alexandria, which he directed from ca. 265 to
282.
Theognostus is an Alexandrian priest and
theologian about whom little is known. Only through quotations in the writings
of Photius,
[317]
Athanasius
[318]
and Gregory of Nyssa
[319]
do we learn about this saint. Eusebius and Jerome do not mention him.
Athanasius considered Theognostus' writings useful in his struggle against
Arianism.

of Alexandria, Interpreter of the Scriptures
is the
name given by Photius I of Constantinople to the seven-volume work also known
