in the book: ‘The Paradise of the Monks .’ These two phrases might seem 
contradictory, yet they were actually complementing each other. They were: 
+ Refraining from eating bread would calm down the body of the monk. 
+ The continuous hunger would make the monk frail, and might even lead 
him to lose his mind.  
The saint was calling upon us to live an ascetic life and to refrain from eating 
too much of the necessary bread; yet this should be handled with wisdom and 
discernment, lest fasting would lose its goal, and might result into one’s 
weakness both physically and mentally. 
 [W. Budge: The Paradise; Vol. 2, p. 21: 253] 
 
THEODOTUS, BISHOP OF ANCYRA 
Bishop Theodotus was a supporter of the Nestorian theology of the heretic 
Nestor. However, in the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 AD, he reversed 
his position and becam e a prominent supporter of the 24th Pope St. Cyril of 
Alexandria (412-444) against Nestor.  This bishop  was defrocked by the 
Nestorians at their Synod of Tarsus in th e year 432 A D. Bishop Theodotus 
wrote so many articles, among which were: Essays against Ne stor (lost); an 
explanation of the Nicene Creed of Faith; several essays on the feast of 
Nativity; and on the Purification . Also, there is a mymar which has been 
attributed to him, dealing with the martyrdom of St. George and his miracles... 
 
THEODULUS AND AGATHOPUS (The martyrs) 
At the beginning of the 4th century AD, St. Agathopus the deacon and St. 
Theodulus the lector (reader), were martyred in the city of Thessalonica during 
the reign of Emperor Maximianus  (286-305). Faustinus, governor of the city, 
put them under arrest and sought from them to deny their Christ. On refusing 
to do so, he cast them in jail. There, the Lord wanted to put them at ease, so He 
allowed them to see a vision: They were as though sailing in a ship, which did 
encounter a violent storm that broke the ship and brought it down. Swimming 
along, they both reached a rock and ascended a hill peacefully. The two saints 
perceived that they would be encountering a great tribulation that would end 
up in their meeting with the Lo rd Christ – the True Rock – and to ascend to 
His Heavenly Paradise. Indeed, by refusing to deliver the books of the Church 
to the governor, after torturing them, he ordered to tie massive rocks to their 
necks and to cast them into the sea . There, their bodies were discovered later 
on in a miraculous way. They were martyred on the 4th of April 303 AD.

In Troas: 
He was taken in a boat from Smyrna to Troas, where he wrote three more 
letters to Philadelphia, Smyrna, and St. Polycarp. From Troas , he sailed to 
Neopolis, to Philippi, then to Epirus and Tyrone. Finally, he arrived at the 
region of Portus, where he met with the brethren, whose joy to see him was 
mixed with the sadness of his close departure. He received them with love, 
asking them to have the courage and show him true love. 
He knelt and prayed to God to put an end to the wave of persecution against 
His Church and to increase the love of the brethren toward each other. 
Finally, the guards rushed him to the arena and released the wild beasts, 
which he received with a cheerful countenance. Two lions jumped on him and 
devoured him to leave off his body, only a few bones. The believers gathered 
his precious relics and sent them to Antioch. His martyrdom took place around 
the year 108 AD. The Church celebrates him on the 7th of Abib. 
[Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty: The Two Martyrs: Ignatius and Polycarp; 1964] 
 
INNOCENT, BISHOP OF TORTONA, ST. 
This saint was born in Tortona in the north of Italy . His heart  was so 
inflamed with the love of God, that he was called before the judges charged of 
being a Christian. On refusing to deny his faith, he fell under torture and was 
finally included in a list of the condemned to be burned alive. However, before 
his execution, he saw in a dream his father asking him to go at once to Rome 
to find safety. When he woke up, he found the guards sleeping deeply, and he 
managed to flee quickly. 
In Rome, St. Innocent was received kindly by Pope Militiades (311-314 
AD) bishop of Rome . Then, his successor Pope Sylvester I (314 -335 AD) 
ordained him as a deacon. After the accession of the Emperor Constantine the 
Great (306-337 AD), the pope sent back  St. Innocent to Tortona as a bishop . 
During the twenty-eight years of his pastoral service as a bishop, St. Innocent 
cared to spread the faith among pagans and to convert the pagan temples , 
which became vacant of worshippers, into churches , as well as to build new 
churches. He departed around the year 350 AD. 
 [Butler's Lives of Saints, p.112 - April 17] 
 
INNOCENT I, POPE OF ROME 
This Roman pope was born in Albano near Rome, and succeeded St. 
Anastasius (399-401 AD) on the Seat of Rome around the year 401 . During

His Writings: 
This St. Theophilus  was one of the Christian apologists . However, only 
three books survived out of his many written works . Those books were 
dedicated to his pagan friend Autolycus, in which he introduced the Christi an 
thoughts about God and His creation before the pagan world with its wrong 
diverse fantasies. Among his lost writings were essays against Marcion and the 
heresy of Hermogenes. 
Of his Sayings: 
+ No one can see God except those who are capable of seeing Him, when their 
souls’ eyes are open wide . When there is dirt on a mirror, man cannot see 
his face in it. Likewise, it is with the sinful. He cannot see God. 
+ I indeed honor the emperor, yet not by worshipping him, but by praying for 
him. 
 
THEOPHILUS, The 23rd POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
The word Theophilus is of a Greek origin, meaning (the Lover of God) . It 
is being driven from two words: ‘Theo’ (=God) and ‘Philo’ (=Lover) . 
According to St. Athanasius the Apostolic; Abba Anthony the Great , in his 
youth was called Theophilus, because of his righteousness in the Lord and for 
his continuous conquests in his spiritual strife. Pope Theophilus (385-412 AD) 
was the third successor of the 20th Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373), 
and he was the predecessor of his nephew the 24th Pope Cyril the Great (412-
444 AD). He sat on the papal throne for 28 years of continuous activity that 
had a great impact on the history of the Church and the State, as well. 
His life was associated with three important events: 
1- He was u prooting the paganism in Egypt , something for which many 
historians commended him.  Even though some attempted to distort his 
image by showing him as a violent tyrant, in turning the pagan temples into 
churches. Yet, as testified by history, he did  so after those temples were 
already deserted.  
2- The struggle against Origen, having become an opponent to whoever 
supported the teaching of Origen, or used his name. Hence, those Origen’s 
advocates attempted to distort the pope’s image. 
3- His opposition towards St. J ohn Chrysostom. When St. John Chrysostom 
embraced The Tall Brothers the prominent defenders of Origen ; the 
Empress Eudoxia, the wife of the Eastern Roman emperor Arcadiu s (395-
408) used the pope’s hatred against the Origenism  to lure him to send St.

Tadros the Bishop:  
The one thing we know about this saint is that he wrote to St. Augustine 
(354-430) requesting his advice about what to do with the priests who 
apostatized from the heresy of Donatism. That heresy caused a dis agreement

records.question: What does the Coptic Orthodox Church teach about purgatory?
records.answer:
The Coptic Orthodox Church does not have a doctrine of purgatory as understood in some other Christian traditions. Instead, it teaches about the state of the soul after death and the immediate consequences of one's earthly life. According to the Church's teachings, once a person dies, their soul is separated from the body, and they cannot repent or change their fate. The body and soul are seen as working together during life, and they receive their respective rewards or punishments together after death. This is emphasized in the Catechism, which states, "the two also receive what they deserve together, whether entry into heaven, or deprivation of the vision of God" [1].

The fate of the soul after death is determined by the life lived on earth. Righteous souls are taken by holy angels to a place of comfort, while wicked souls are taken by evil angels to a place of torment, as illustrated in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus [1]. This reflects the belief that there is no intermediate state of purification like purgatory; rather, the soul's destination is immediate based on its earthly actions and faith.

In summary, the Coptic Orthodox Church teaches that there is no purgatory; instead, the soul's eternal fate is determined immediately after death, with the righteous being welcomed into heaven and the wicked facing separation from God.

462. Do the so-called saints make up the Church? 
The believers who make up the Church are called by the Apostle Paul “to be saints” 
(Rom. 1:7; 1 Cor. 1:2, 24). They are saints because God calls them and thus, they are special 
among all their fellows. When they receive the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, they become 
consecrated to God. The Commemoration of Saints always includes priests who labored for 
the edification of the body of Christ and served the holy mysteries, so that the believers may 
be sanctified. It also includes sinful preachers who used God's Word to attract new members 
to the Church. Although the scribes and pharisees were corrupt, the Lord did not take away 
their honor from them but gave them authority despite t heir wickedness, because they 
themselves do not do what they teach others (Matt. 23:3). 
463. Can Church members who cannot be rectified be cut off from the Church? 
Although the Church, the body of Christ, portrays God’s love for humanity, there are 
limits that she will never exceed. A sinner is cut off from the fellowship of the Church since 
he isolates himself from the life and salvation that spring from her. Thus, the rebellious 
sinners who have trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the coven ant by 
which they were sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace (Heb. 10:29), 
who preserves salvation within the Church — outside of which there is no salvation — set 
themselves apart from Christ and His community, the Church, and thus b reak every 
relationship with her. 
On the other hand, the heretics who misinterpret the teachings of Christ and His holy 
apostles (even if they quote phrases from the true Gospel), are excommunicated and 
separated from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Thus St. Paul teaches, “But 
even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you than what we have 
preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again, if anyone 
preaches any other gospel to you than what you have received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 
1:8–9). St. John the Apostle forbids receiving anyone who comes and does not have the true 
teachings. It is necessary not to receive them in homes and not to greet them (2 John 10). In 
fact, St. Paul comma nds us, “Reject a divisive man after the first and second admonition, 
knowing that such a person is warped and sinning, being self -condemned” (Titus 3:10–11). 
Heretics, because of their inaccurate faith and their arrogance, persist in their false teachings 
and isolate themselves from the source of life; the faith in Christ, and so they grow lukewarm 
and are thus expelled. If we do not stand firm on the foundation of the Apostles, we will lose 
our foundation and will collapse. 932 And we become like those who wanted to return to the

The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement 
870. Is asceticism, as it is practiced in the Coptic Church, biblical? 
The Coptic Church is known for its ascetic inclinations, not only due to the monastic 
movement that started in it, but asceticism is also considered one of the essential 
characteristics manifested in her life as a whole and her worship. These inclinations exist not 
because asceticism is a goal in and of itself, nor on the basis that the flesh is evil in nature; 
but rather on a biblical and heavenly understanding: “For what profit is it to a man if he gains 
the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” 
(Matt. 16:26). “Go your way, sell whatever you have and give to the poor … and follow Me” 
(Mark 10:21, Luke 18:22). “But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when 
I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27). 
This biblical understanding was found to be sweet by the Copts, whose hearts were 
inflamed with eternal love. 
871. What is the goal of ascetic life according to the Copts? 
While most ancient civilizations were attached to the temporal life and so they pursued 
worldly pleasures, the Egyptian mind was consumed with the world to come. Ancient 
Egyptians believed in the so -called “resurrection,” which is the belief in the resurrection of 
the dead to eternal life, if certain rituals were performed. This is why bodies were mummified 
in sealed tombs, such that no one would be able to visit the tomb or live in it except for the 
soul. The tombs were supplied with one’s daily needs (clothes, food, drink, vessels, knives, 
chairs, weapons, chariots, jewelry, toys for children … etc.). 
When the Copts accepted Christianity, their longing for the world to come grew, and their 
hearts were inflamed with longing for it, but now on a biblical basis. Instead of being 
concerned with the souls’ return to their bodies in the tombs, they desired for their souls, 
thoughts, and hearts to be lifted up to enjoy the heavenly life even when their bodies were 
still treading on the earth. In other words, their longing for the world to come drove them to 
lead an ascetic life on a biblical basis. 
872. What is the motive of asceticism for the Copts? 
Asceticism in the Coptic Church is not a goal in its own, but it is one’s practical response 
to the divine love. If our Lord offered His life for us, it is fitting for us to desire to offer our 
lives as a sacrifice of love to God. We despise worldly pleasures as a sign of our inner longing 
to enjoy the eternal joy of the new life in Christ Jesus. Believers, especially monks, have a

New Testament and so he chanted saying, “this is none other them the house of God and 
this is the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17). 
Second: The era of the Mosaic Law and Prophets: The law explained in detail the 
sacrifices and their rituals as a symbol of Christ’s sacrifice. The prophets wro te many 
prophecies about the Savior, His birth, crucifixion, burial, resurrection, and ascension.  
Third: The era of the incarnation of the Logos until His ascension: The Lord revealed 
His divine love to us, so He fed the hungry, healed the sick, comforted the brokenhearted and 
revealed to them His providence even after His ascension when He sent them the Comforter, 
the Holy Spirit. He announced to them the Father’s love to all humanity and the Holy Spirit’s 
work to declare the divine truth and lead the Church to heaven as she struggles in the world.  
Fourth: The era between Christ’s ascension until His second coming: Here, He acts 
as a heavenly high priest. The Apostle Paul spoke about this era in his epistle to the Hebrews 
(Heb. 6:20) in which he compares between the high priests who were in need of redemption 
and the unique heavenly High Priest.  
453. Why does the Creed mention the Church after talking about the oneness of God 
and the Holy Trinity? 
The goal of the Orthodox Creed is not to mention some theoretical facts about God, the 
world, the Church, the final judgment, and the eternal life, but its main goal is to help the 
believer encounter God, enjoy His love as he struggles in the world, prepare him for the great 
day of the Lord, help him have com munion with the heavenly, and have eternal life. So, as 
we confess our faith saying, “ and in One Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church,” we are 
affirming our commitment to be in communion with the Holy God, to love one another, to 
have a relationship with our  friends in heaven as we join their praising choir and enjoy our 
sonship to God on an eternal level.  
Our knowledge of the Church drives us to look forward to our life in heaven when we 
depart and meet the heavenly Bridegroom who will welcome us in a joyfu l heavenly 
procession which the heavenly hosts look forward to saying, “thrust in your sickle and reap” 
(Rev. 14:15). We should not marvel that the heavenly hosts are earnestly looking forward to 
the day of the Lord, since they view our Church not as a social institution governed by some 
laws that are in place to ensure man’s happiness, but as the people of God who are being 
prepared to partake in the angelic life where the believer experiences God’s plan for him 
every day. Therefore, we should not be surprised if we hear about many of the saints such as 
St. John Chrysostom who felt that they were the happiest people in the world. The believer 
has his eyes fixed on his Creator and Savior and what He is preparing for him in heaven, so 
he is joyful in the midst of his hardships. The believer performs his job with all honesty and 
is faithful in his relationships with others, because he considers himself to be a child of God 
who does not know failure, despair, or greed as he is the ambassador of heaven on earth.

records.question: What does the Coptic Orthodox Church say about the Protestant principle of sola scriptura?
records.answer:
The Coptic Orthodox Church holds a distinct view regarding the relationship between Scripture and tradition, which contrasts sharply with the Protestant principle of sola scriptura, or "Scripture alone." This principle asserts that the Bible is the sole authority for Christian faith and practice, independent of church tradition. However, the Coptic Orthodox perspective emphasizes the integral role of tradition alongside Scripture.

According to the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Holy Bible is indeed the book of the Church, but it has been preserved and understood through the Church's tradition. This tradition is seen as a vital means by which the Church recognizes and canonizes the sacred texts, confirming their divine inspiration. For instance, St. Augustine stated, “For my part, I should not believe the gospel except as moved by the authority of the Catholic Church” [2]. This highlights the Church's role in affirming the authority of Scripture.

Moreover, the Church teaches that oral tradition was the primary means of transmitting the Christian faith before the New Testament was written. The apostles delivered the Gospel through both oral and written means, and this oral tradition is considered essential for understanding the fullness of the faith. St. Irenaeus, for example, emphasized the importance of tradition, suggesting that in the absence of Scripture, one should turn to the ancient Churches to learn the truth handed down from the apostles [6]. 

The Coptic Orthodox Church also asserts that tradition is not merely supplementary to Scripture but is foundational to the life of the Church. Tradition encompasses the teachings, sacraments, and practices that have been passed down through generations, which are essential for the Church's identity and continuity. St. Basil the Great noted that “the faith that is the object of their war... is to throw down the foundation of faith in Christ by dashing apostolic tradition to the ground” [1]. This indicates that tradition safeguards the integrity of the faith against misinterpretations that might arise from a sole reliance on Scripture.

In summary, the Coptic Orthodox Church does not accept the Protestant principle of sola scriptura. Instead, it teaches that Scripture and tradition are inseparable, with tradition serving as the living context through which the Scriptures are understood and lived out. The Church believes that without tradition, the authentic interpretation and practice of the Christian faith would be compromised.

St. Cyprian insists that outside the Church there is no salvation, either for heretics or for 
schismatics: “He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his 
mother.”243 Therefore, the true interpretation of Scripture and orthodox doctrines are found 
only within the true Church. The tradition of the true Church is the guardian of the Christian 
faith. 
74. What does St. Gregory the bishop of Nyssa say about tradition? 
In the writings of St. Gregory of Nyssa, we find: “it is enough for proof of our statement, 
that the tradition has come down to us from our fathers, handed on, like some inheritance, by 
succession from the apostles and the saints who came after them.”244 
75. What does St. Basil the Great say about tradition? 
a. This saint refers to many quotations from the writings of the Fathers as witnesses of 
the orthodox faith. 
b. He also speaks of oral tradition as safeguarding the sound interpretation of the Holy 
Bible, which the heretics try to destroy. He says, “in truth, it is the faith that is the 
object of their war, and their intention, shared by all who oppose and hate sound 
teaching (1 Tim. 1:10) is to throw down the foundation of faith in Christ by dashing 
apostolic tradition to the ground and to obliterate it. On account of this, like true 
debtors they cry out for proofs from the Scriptures and dismiss the non -scriptural 
witness of the fathers as worthless.”245

teaching of the Scriptures, and others we have received in mystery [1 Cor. 2:7] as the 
teachings of the tradition of the apostles. Both hold the same power with respect to 
true religion. 
“No one would deny these points, at least no one who has even a little experience of 
ecclesiastical institutions. For if we attempt to reject non -scriptural customs as 
insignificant, we would, unaware, lose the very vital parts of the Gospel, and even 
more, we would establish the proclamation merely in name.

”Learn also diligently, and from the Church, what are the books of the Old Te stament, and 
what those of the New.” 204 So also St. Augustine: “For my part, I should not believe the 
gospel except as moved by the authority of the Catholic Church.”205 St. Basil the Great says, 
”For were we to attempt to reject such customs as have no writ ten authority, on the ground 
that the importance they possess is small, we should unintentionally injure the Gospel in its 
very vitals.”206 
It is important to note that while Church tradition testifies to the Holy Bible, and the Holy 
Bible is itself a part of the Church’s tradition, none of this diminishes the unique value of the 
Bible. Tradition defends the Bible’s nature as the word of God, the eternal divine revelation, 
which addresses not only the present age but also the ages to come.  
Although tradition testifies to the Holy Bible, it cannot be its judge. On the contrary, a 
tradition is only accepted if it is founded on the Bible; it cannot be accepted if it disagrees 
with the Holy Bible.207 
Moreover, the Holy Bible is for every believer, that he may experience it and personally 
taste its beauty, appreciating its value and inspiration. However, no one can by himself 
determine the divine inspiration of the Holy Bible and the presence of the Holy Spirit within 
the Bible — only the Holy Spirit who lives in t he Church can do that.  It is not through any 
individual effort of a human deciding alone, but through adherence to the judgment of the 
Church.208 
Finally, the close relationship between the Holy Bible and the tradition of the Church in 
no way extinguishes o ne’s personal feelings towards the Holy Bible. On the contrary, the 
tradition of the Church reinforces the personal approach, and requires of us that we live the 
Bible in no way isolated from the Church.

“gospel of salvation,” the “word of hearing” or the “God’s salvific work,” which he had

you received it not as the word of men but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectively

the Church, not written on paper but through word of mouth, that they may deliver it to the 
Church by oral tradition, as well as written. 
On this note, Cyril Richardson says, “Hence Christian preaching was founded on the Old 
Testament and on the living tradition of Jesus, passed from mouth to mouth. This feeling for 
personal witness was very strong in the Early Church. Papias, for instance, records his disdain 
for books and his preference for ‘the living and abiding voice’.”196 
Many Western scholars are coming to appreciate this truth: oral tradition does not stand 
side by side with the written works as separate and distinct things; rather, they are one thing. 
What the Bible declares, the Church has received by oral tradition. 
F. F. Bruce, the professor of Biblical Criticism and Exegesis at the University of 
Manchester notes: “Whereas western Christians tend to set ‘script ure’ and ‘tradition’ over 
against each other, as though tradition were exclusively oral and not written, there is no 
reason why tradition should not take written form. If it is apostolic tradition, in due course it 
takes written form and becomes apostolic scripture. Whether Paul’s teaching was given orally 
or in writing, it equally carried apostolic authority; hence he can encourage the Thessalonian 
Christians to ‘stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by 
word of mouth or by letter’ (2 Thess. 2:15).”197 
In The New Westminster Dictionary of the Bible we find, “The term (tradition), however, 
came to be used in a good sense of the apostolic teaching handed down in the Church either 
by the oral word or by letter.”198 
J. N. D. Kelly says, “by tradition the fathers usually mean doctrine which the Lord or His 
apostles committed to the Church, irrespective of whether it was handed down orally or in 
documents … The ancient meaning of the term is well illustrated by Athanasius’ reference199 
to ‘the actual original tradition, teaching and faith of the Catholic Church, which the Lord 
bestowed, the apostles proclaimed and the fathers safeguarded.’”200

the Church enjoyed a wondrous unity until  the fifth century. No nation insisted that

Christian writings were translated into th e languages of other nations, while

The believer does not deny the importance of the advancement of science, but he 
understands that these are theories that are liable to revision. For example: for a long time, 
scholars were c onfident that the Gospel of John was not written by St. John the Disciple, 
for its style was more like that of the second century. But when the Nag Hammadi 
papyruses were discovered in 1948, manuscripts from the first century were among them 
that exhibit t he same style as this gospel. Also, some scholars doubted the historical 
accuracy of some of the events recorded in the Holy Bible, such as those of the Book of 
Daniel. But more recent archaeological discoveries have confirmed the record of the Holy 
Bible as historical facts.

Indeed, the Church received the “word of God” before it was written on paper. She 
enjoyed its good news and understood the deepest meaning of the word of God by the Holy 
Spirit through oral tradition, received not only by words but also as a way of life. She received 
this life more than twenty years before the New Testament began to be written . And when 
the evangelists and apostles did write the New Testament by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, 
the Church accepted it, venerated it, and understood it as the very life she had already been 
living. Thus, the Gospel is not a stranger to tradition , but its first component, for they both 
declare the “One Truth” and explain the nature of the Church. 
Perhaps one may ask whether oral tradition was annulled by the appearance of the books 
of the New Testament. We point to the apostles themselves who, in their letters to the early 
Christian communities, often reminded the believers of oral tradition from which they may 
gain an understanding of Christian truth. “Having many things to write to you, I did not wish 
to do so with paper and ink; but I hope to co me to you and speak face to face, that our joy 
may be full” (2 John 12). “I had many things to write, but I do not wish to write to you with 
pen and ink; but I hope to see you shortly, and we shall speak face to face” (3 John 13 –14). 
“And the rest I will s et in order when I come” (1 Cor. 11:34). “For this reason I left you in 
Crete, that you should set in order the things that are lacking and appoint elders in every city 
as I commanded you” (Titus 1:5). 
In many situations, the apostle Paul commands his disc iples to preserve the tradition, 
deliver it to others, and keep the traditions they were taught ― whether by word of mouth or 
by his epistles ― and to withdraw themselves “from every brother who walks disorderly and 
not according to the tradition which he received from us“ (2 Thess. 3:6). He also warns us to 
beware of every tradition of men which is inconsistent with the faith, “according to the basic 
principles of the world, and not according to Christ” (Col. 2:8). Moreover, in the early 
Church, converts to Christianity accepted the faith in many countries that had no versions of 
the Bible in their own languages and thus had no access to the truth except through oral 
tradition.201 
St. Irenaeus in the second century is the first to discuss the matter of tradition. He poses 
these questions: suppose we had no holy scripture, what would have happened? To whom 
should we turn? “Should we not have recourse to the most ancient Churches with which the 
apostles held constant intercourse, and learn from them what is certain and clear in regard to 
the present question? For how should it be if the apostles themselves had not left us writings? 
Would it not be necessary, [in that case,] to follow the course of the tradition which they 
handed down to those to whom they did commit the Churches?”202

Early History of Christian Doctrine (London: Methuen 1920): pp. 55–56.

Conclusion 
The Church and  Tradition are but two aspects of the life of Faith. They cannot be 
separated from each other, neither can we know one without the other. Through tradition, the 
Church comes into being, is acquainted with her Bridegroom, practices His saving work, and 
receives His divine mysteries. Through tradition, we come to know the Gospel of the Church, 
and we embrace it, preserve it, live by its rules, and preach it. Through tradition, we 
understand the sacramental life of the Church, with its liturgies, hymns, and ri tes. Through 
tradition, we meet the saints and fathers of the Church, learn of their lives in Christ Jesus and 
their writings, take the blessings of their prayers, and enjoy our fellowship with them in Christ 
Jesus. Through tradition we understand the cano ns of the Church and relate to its holy 
Councils and their works. 
In brief, tradition is the nervous system of the Church, and her life. Without it, she could 
not exist, nor practice the apostolic life, nor her continual renewal, nor her unity, nor live her 
authentic character.

records.question: What is the filioque clause and why did the Coptic Church reject it?
records.answer:
The filioque clause refers to a phrase added to the Nicene Creed by the Western Church, stating that the Holy Spirit proceeds "from the Father and the Son." This addition has been a significant point of contention between the Eastern and Western branches of Christianity. The Coptic Orthodox Church, which adheres to the original formulation of the Creed established at the Council of Nicaea, rejects this clause for several reasons.

Firstly, the Coptic Orthodox Church emphasizes the original wording of the Creed, which states that the Holy Spirit proceeds "from the Father." This aligns with the teachings of the early Church Fathers and the theological understanding of the Trinity, which is central to Coptic belief. The Church believes that the addition of "and the Son" alters the understanding of the relationship within the Holy Trinity, potentially implying a hierarchy that undermines the equality of the three Persons of the Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [3][4].

Moreover, the Coptic Orthodox Church views the filioque as a theological innovation that was not present in the early Church's teachings. The Church holds that the original Creed reflects the apostolic faith and should remain unchanged to preserve the integrity of Christian doctrine [2][5]. This rejection is also tied to a broader historical context, where the Coptic Church has maintained its distinct theological identity, particularly in response to the developments in Western Christianity that diverged from the early ecumenical councils' decisions.

In summary, the Coptic Orthodox Church rejects the filioque clause because it believes it distorts the original understanding of the Trinity as articulated in the Nicene Creed, which affirms that the Holy Spirit proceeds solely from the Father. This position is rooted in a commitment to the teachings of the early Church and the desire to maintain the unity and integrity of the Christian faith as it was originally expressed.

97. What is the Apostles’ Creed (Symbolum Apostolicum)? 
St. Hilary says, “We are compelled to attempt what is unattainable, to climb where we 
cannot reach, to speak w hat we cannot utter. Instead of the bare adoration of faith, we are 
compelled to trust the deep things of religion to the perils of human expression.”276 
The Lord Christ questioned his disciples about their faith in him, so Peter confessed that 
“He is the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). Perhaps this declaration of faith 
provided the main idea for the creation of a creed of faith for the Church that declares “the 
truth of the Lord Christ, the Savior.” Another time, the Lord gathered his disciples and gave 
them authority to preach, teach, and baptize, saying, “Go therefore and make disciples of all 
the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy 
Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), thus providing them with a formula  for a trinitarian creed related to 
baptism. Thus, the New Testament records for us a formula of faith in Christ and a formula 
of faith in the Trinity. These two formulas are the essence of the faith of the Church. 
F. L. Cross says of the Apostles’ Creed, “Though it is much later than the Apostolic age, 
it can so far claim to be Apostolic that its articles one and all express the faith of apostolic 
times.”277  
Patrology278 offers us many texts of creeds found in the writings of both Eastern and 
Western Fathers. Among these are creeds found in the writings of: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, 
180 A.D.; Tertullian of Carthage, 200 A.D.; Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, 250 A.D.; Novatian 
of Rome, 250 A.D.; Origen of Alexandria, 250 A.D.; Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, 270 
A.D.; Lucian of Antioch, 300 A.D.; Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, 325 A.D.; Marcellus of 
Ancyra, 340 A.D.; Cyril of Jerusalem, 350 A.D.; Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, 3 74 A.D.; 
Rufinus of Aquileia, 390 A.D.; and the creed found in the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles. 
The Eastern texts differ from those of the West in that they are generally longer and more 
diverse. They have a metaphysical dimension (what lies beyond physical nature) and include 
a number of educational expressions in response to heresies that were widespread in the East. 
98. How did the Creed of the Church evolve?279 
In the apostolic era, as the Church set out to evangelize and preach salvation to the world, 
it was required of the catechumens to publicly confess their faith using a brief formula before 
being received as members of the body of Christ; that is, immediately before their baptism. 
 
276Anne Fremantle (ed.), A Treasury of Early Christianity (Viking Press, 1953): p. 325.

different text to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed used by the Coptic Orthodox Church.

101. What did our Fathers of the Middle Ages transmit to us? 
The libraries of Europe overflow with medieval manuscripts from Egypt, in both the 
Coptic and Arabic languages, that reveal the theological richness of the Coptic Church of the 
Middle Ages. This motivates me to present a sample of their writings about the Creed.  
Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis , a priest from Manyat Bani Khusib (now called Minya), 
who died in 1357 A.D., has an exposition of the Creed in about fifty large manuscript pages 
attributed to him. He wrote this at the request of Anba Gabriel, the bishop of Qus, in reply to 
a Jewish person who criticized the Creed saying, “Where did you get this text? And why 
have you inscribed it among the books of the church?” Thus, the book contains a collection 
of texts from the Old Testament to substantiate each of the Creed’s clauses.  
This work differs in its aims from other medieval Coptic expositions of the Creed: those 
of Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (around 940 A.D.); and a commentary at the beginning of the 
second chapter of Abu al-Barakat ibn Kabar’s  work titled Mișbâḥ al-ẓulma wa-îḍâḥ al-
khidma (The Lamp in the Shadows and the Illumination of Service , about 1310 A.D.). Abu 
al-Barakat quotes mostly from the New Testament. The Rev. Dr. Samir Khalil says that “the 
three Coptic commentaries complement each other in a felicitous manner.”282 
A summary of the text of Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis’ exposition:283 
1. We believe in one God:  he cites the Torah (2 quotations), Isaiah  (2 quotations), 
Jeremiah, and the Gospel (2 quotations; these are the only quotations from the New 
Testament). 
2. The Father almighty, [Pantocrator] of all things visible and invisible:  quotations 
from Zechariah (2), Nahum, and the books of Kings. 
3. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only -begotten, born of the Father before all 
ages: quotations from Isaiah (2), David, Solomon (2), and Micah. 
4. Light of light, true God of true God, begotten not made:  quotations from Isaiah, 
Jeremiah, Isaiah, and David. 
5. For us, he came down from heaven: quotations from David, Isaiah (3), Esdras (Ezra), 
Jeremiah, David (2), an unnamed prophet, and Isaiah. 
6. He was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary:  quotations from Isaiah 
(2), Ezekiel (2), Nahum, Zephaniah, Zechariah, Daniel, and Isaiah (2). 
 
282 Samir Khalil, “Abu Al-Majd Ibn Yu’Annis” in The Coptic Encyclopedia, vol. 1, Atiya, Aziz Suryal, ed. 
(Macmillan, 1991), 21–23: p. 21. 
283 See Samir Khalil, “Abu Al-Majd Ibn Yu’Annis” in The Coptic Encyclopedia, vol. 1, Atiya, 
Aziz Suryal, ed. (Macmillan, 1991), 21–23: pp. 21–22.

will see how Anatolius of Constantinople and others refused to call the Pope of Alexandria 
a heretic.  
Some scholars have been in the habit of attributing violence to the Alexandrian fathers 
and theologians, even to Athanasius and Cyril. 
St. Dioscorus and the Council of Chalcedon: although the Council of Chalcedon was 
thought to have been convened to try Eutyches, in the event, its attention turned to attacking 
Pope Dioscorus of Alexandria, rather than the old monk. Eutyches was not even present at 
the council, having been exiled to north Syria before the council met.  
In fact, Dioscor us was condemned not because of any theological heresy, but due to 
political circumstances which dominated this council.  
The Greek Professor Fr. Romanides says, “Dioscorus was considered quite orthodox 
in his faith by such leading Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon as those represented 
by Anatolius of Constantinople.” 19 Metropolitan Methodios of Aksum also says, 
“Information, which we possess, does not depict Dioscorus as a heretic. From available 
information it is obvious that he was a good man and even Bishop Leo himself tried to take 
him to his side … Likewise Emperor Theodosius in a letter to Dioscorus calls him a man 
who radiates the Grace of God, a humble man and of orthodox faith. 
“Several times in the course of the Council Patriarch Diosco rus declared his faith. He 
was not condemned because he was heretical but because he refused to communicate with 
Leo, the Archbishop, and because he refused to come to the Council although he was invited 
to do so three times. 
“This evidence is sufficient for us to look for other reasons for Dioscorus’ condemnation. 
Rome was annoyed by the extraordinary vitality of the Church of Alexandria and its active 
Patriarch.”20  
The emperor accepted the council’s decision and exiled Pope Dioscorus to the island of 
Gangra in Asia Minor. He remained in exile for five years, occupying his time in guiding the 
lost and healing the sick. He departed to the glorious realm in the year 457 A. D. 
What impact did the Council of Chalcedon have on the catechism of the Church?  
a. The rise of strong theologians, such as Philoxenus of Mabbug, Pope Timothy, and the 
great teacher St. Severus of Antioch, who preserved the orthodoxy of the faith. Fr. 
 
19 See “DISCUSSION: Concerning the paper of Professor Karmiris” in The Greek Orthodox Theological 
Review 10 (1965): p. 77. 
20 Metropolitan Methodios Fouyas, “Inter-Orthodox Theological Commission for Dialogue with the Non-
Chalcedonian Churches” in Theological and Historical Studies: A Collection of Minor Works, ed. 
Methodios Fouyas (Athens, 1985): p. 15.

15 
faithful, leading to many being killed. Rather, it will suffice to present an extremely concise 
rectification of the accusations levelled against St. Dioscorus.18 
St. Dioscorus and Eutyches : Eutyches was an archimandrite and the abbot of a 
monastery in Constantinople with about three hundred monks under his guidance. He was an 
old ascetic, gifted with eloquence of speech; but he was not a true theologian. He played a 
significant role in the split that occurred in the Church in the fifth century.  Eutyches enjoyed 
great fame throughout the see of Constantinople: within monastic circles, the imperial court, 
and among the people. This was due to his intelligence, eloquence, his ascetic life, and his 
close relationship with the emperor, especially through his relative Chrysaphius, the chief 
minister. 
In reality, Eutyches represented neither Alexand rian theology nor Antiochian 
theology. His extreme zeal against the Nestorianism that was rife in this region, and his 
defense of the Alexandrian formula led him to another heresy: he fell into the error of saying 
that there were two natures before the uni on; but only one nature after it, for  the divine 
nature absorbed the human nature, and the latter ceased to be.  
It is not difficult for any scholar to discover the character of Eutyches  and his theology 
by simply reading his responses during his trials at the  councils of Ephesus in 448 and 449 
A. D. He was not by nature a theologian and he was largely ignorant of th e system of 
Alexandrian theology. He would sometimes use  orthodox expressions that contradict his 
main ideas. Perhaps this was because his theological understanding was shaky, or perhaps he 
intended to deceive, or perhaps he feared losing his fame, position, or priesthood.  
Eutyches’ appeal to the emperor and bishops:  Leo, the bishop of Rome wrote to 
Eutyches, lauding his zeal in defending against Nestorian dualism. At the same time, he wrote 
to Flavian, urging him to be kind to Eutyches. But Leo later changed his mind, perhaps when 
he heard that the emperor had written to St. Dioscorus, the pope of Alexandria, inviting him 
to convene a council to discuss this matter. Leo, who had no real knowledge of the nature of 
the conflict between Alexandrian and Antioc hian Christology, sent his tome (letter) to 
Constantinople on June 13, 449 A. D.; not to reconcile the parties, but to undermine the 
position of the Alexandrian theologians. 
The Second Council of Ephesus in 449 A. D.: Emperor Theodosius II, who convened 
the council, appointed  Dioscorus to preside over the council,  and appointed Juvenal of 
Jerusalem and Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia to co-preside with him. 
St. Dioscorus did not say one word against Rome from the beginning of the council to its 
end. Leo, in his letters, refers to our pope as the “Egyptian Murderer” and the “Teacher of 
Satan’s Falsehoods” who always tries his best to spread blasphemy against his brethren. We

‘Anthony,' among whom are: 
ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr: 
He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great 
zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then 
he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false 
gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was 
expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop 
assigned him to build a Ch urch, the pagans were stirred up against him and 
killed him. 
ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr: 
St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and 
merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to 
‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. 
The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. 
Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his 
Christ, he ordered him chained and se nt him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of 
Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ 
put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but 
God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' 
where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each 
other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with 
sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint 
received the crown of martyrdom. 
 
ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. 
He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family ’ and 
‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement ’ in the whole world, even though 
there have been some monastic movements prior to his. 
The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around 
the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his 
corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled 
toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the 
gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to 
the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me ” (Matt. 
19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched  his 
life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he 
proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its 
proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister 
also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God 
667 
old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed 
him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven 
flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the 
raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony 
to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church. 
St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic 
order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart

197 
 
The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying 
in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out 
to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of 
a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his 
head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned 
to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never 
get bored." That  came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand 
happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life. 
One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash 
their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they start ed to 
undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she 
answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, 
for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint 
said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He 
instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was 
around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to 
practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new 
location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of 
women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts. 
His Order of Seclusion: 
In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with  some 
beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He 
helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he 
was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept 
of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 
4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a 
member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he 
did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when 
Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his 
response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he 
said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of 
kings." However, when he was pressu red, he answered the emperor’s 
message, for the sake of the Church peace. 
5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy 
congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the 
Church. That is why he eventually came  down to help Pope Athanasius 
the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his 
entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants 
came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians 
came back to the Church.

According to St. Athanasius, while Abba Anthony was sitting one day by 
his monastery, he saw somebody ascending to heaven, and a multitude of saints 
was welcoming him. Inquiring about him, he was told that he was Abba Amon. 
Thirty days later, some hermits came over from Mount Nitria, to inform St 
Anthony that their father has departed to heaven. 
The C optic Church celebrates his feast on the 20 th of Bashons; and the 
Greek Church on the 4th of October. 
 
 
 
 
AMON, THE RYTHIAN, FR. 
He was called that way because he lived in the region of ‘Rythio’ by the city 
of ‘El-Tur’ in Sinai. He was an Egyptian monk who lived as an anchorite in the 
region of ‘Kanub’ (Abu Quir) at the beginning of the fourth century AD. When 
the persecution was stirred up by Emperor ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD), he was 
exiled to Palestine, and from there, he returned to the wilderness of Sinai. He 
witnessed by himself the invasion of the pagan Arabs on the monasteries of 
Sinai when they destroyed the monasteries and dispersed their monks. At that 
time, Amon set forth to ‘Rythio,' which became the center of a gathering of the 
monks of Sinai. He li ved there for a long time until Rythio ’ was invaded as 
well. And, he then left it and set forth to ‘Manf,' then to Scetis to live among 
its hermits as a disciple to Abba Bemen. When he once asked Abba Bemen 
about the evil thoughts; his answer was: “It is within the power of the enemy 
to bring them to our minds, but it is within our power not to accept them!” 
 
AMON, ABBA 
This saint was the disciple of Abba ‘Poemen’ (Bemoa). He came once to 
visit Abba ‘Sisoes’ (Shishoy) in wintertime. And he noticed that Abba  Sisoes 
was very sad and depressed after he left the life of seclusion in the wilderness, 
so he said to him: “Why are you so sad, O father? How could you have 
managed to live alone in the wilderness at your advanced age? ” The old man 
looked at him with admonishment and said: “What are you saying Amon?! Is 
feeling freedom in the desert not better than anything else?!” 
 
AMON, THE BISHOP OF HERMOPOLIS

stayed alive in the frozen lake, including a young man called Melito. The 
governor ordered to break the hands and legs of those who were still alive, 
and to cast them into fire. So, the guards did what they were orde red and 
carried the saints’ broken bodies in a wagon to be burned. However, they kept 
Melito until the end, with the hope that he might change his mind when he 
would find out that he became alone. But his mother, a poor widow, 
admonished the guards on their wrong consideration and approached her son, 
who smiled at her with thanksgiving. With the power of the Holy Spirit, she 
exhorted her son to abide until the end, then carried him and cast him by 
herself into the wagon among his fellow martyrs. The guards burned the 
bodies of the martyrs and threw the ashes in the river, but the believers 
managed to haul some of the precious relics, and kept them in Caesarea. 
 [The Synaxarion: 13 Baramhat] 
 [Butler: March 10] 
 
MARTYRS OF ST. ANTHONY MOUNTAIN 
On the 26 th of Baba, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of seven 
martyrs who were martyred at the hands of the Barbarians, on the Mountain 
of St. Anthony, the Father of all monks. 
 [The Synaxarion: 26 Baba] 
 
MARTYRS OF THE ARIAN HERESY 
When the Arian Emperor Constan tius II (337 -361 AD), the son of 
Constantine the Great (306 -337 AD), approved the heresy of Arius (250 -336 
AD), he sent someone called Gregory of Cappadocia to Alexandria guarded 
by 500 horsemen, to be appointed as the patriarch of Alexandria, instead of 
the 20 th Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (328 -373 AD), who rejected and 
opposed that heresy. The emperor ordered his envoy to kill whoever would 
disobey him. When the people of Alexandria refused to accept him, he killed 
several thousands of them. In the mean time, Pope Athanasius fled away and 
hid for six years. Then, the pope went to Constantinople to face the emperor. 
However, the emperor ordered his men to place him on a boat without food 
or drink, with the hope he would perish of hunger and thirst or drown  along 
the way, through a miracle, the boat came to land in Alexandria peacefully, 
where his people greatly rejoiced, brought him to the Church; and drove 
away Gregory the intruder and all his followers. 
During the whole period (337 -361 AD) of the reign of  Emperor 
Constantius II, the Arian persecution against the Orthodox prevailed over the

279 
 
did not cease to visit all the Pachomian monasteries . He also had  very 
admirable spiritual sayings, few of which survived, in which he urged all t o 
study the Holy Bible and to observe the Pachomian rules.  
A Delegation to meet Pope Athanasius: 
When the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD) returned 
with honor back to his seat, according to a prophecy by St. Pachomius , St. 
Horsiesius sent a delegation of monks to greet him . In their way, when the 
delegation knew that St. Anthony the Great was in the outer mountain, they 
decided to visit him there to get his blessing . St. Anthony received them with 
a warm welcome, and getting to know that St. Pachomius had already reposed, 
he comforted and encouraged them . Then, the delegation continued on their 
way to Alexandria to meet the pope.  
Monastic Dissensions:  
As the plague spread, after claiming the lives of St. Pachomius , St. 
Petronius, and so many other Abbots of these Cenobitic monasteries, a sort of 
confusion spread among many of the brethren who sought to occupy those 
leading positions. This made the work of St. Horsiesius very difficult. He tried 
to provoke the spirit of humility among t hem by his spiritual sermons, in 
addition to his humility and compassion.  
It was Apollon, the Abbot of the monastery of Moncose  in the province of 
Qena, who ignited the first spark of dissension , seeking the financial 
independence of his monastery and the right to keep what would be more than 
its needs. St. Horsiesius tried to counsel him, sometimes by compassion and 
other times by firmness,  in particular, that other monastery Abbots tried to 
follow his example. The saint's heart was so grieved. 
St. Horsiesius soul became embittered , and he longed to relinquish the 
leadership to someone else or to have a partner to help him . He fervently 
prayed, and in a night vision, the Lord guided him to seek the assistance of St. 
Tadros, the disciple of Abba Pachomius. He was comforted by that vision , 
particularly that St. Tadros was much cherished by him and by all the others, 
because of the sweetness of his humility.  
St. Horsiesius called for an assembly of the Abbots of the monasteries, 
except for Fr. Tadros, and sought their counsel. They greatly rejoiced and sent 
to call Fr. Tadros to become co -head of the monasteries along with St. 
Horsiesius, who quietly retreated to the monastery of Chensbosque  until the 
matter was settled. Yet, he returned when Fr. Tadros insisted not to accept this 
assignment without having his blessing . Convincing Fr. Tadros to accept 
working with him, he set out to the monastery of Chensbosque. Then, he 
moved to the monastery of Moncose, from which the first spark of dissension

384 
 
of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St . Anthony what to 
do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on 
the ground and they dug the grave with their claws ; according to St. Antony's 
directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body. 
St. Anthony carried the garment of palm t ree fibers and presented it to 
Pope Athanasius who gr eatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every 
year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany , and Resurrection . Many signs 
were shown by that garment. 
In the location where St . Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery 
was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise 
for the Lord. 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.”

records.question: Who was St. Paul the First Hermit's wife?
records.answer:
St. Paul the First Hermit did not have a wife. He is known as the first hermit in Christian history, having lived a life of solitude and asceticism in the wilderness. According to the passages, he was born in Alexandria around 228 AD and, after a conflict with his brother Peter over their inheritance, he chose to flee into the wilderness to live a life dedicated to God. This decision was made during the persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius around 250 AD, which led him to seek solitude and a deeper spiritual life away from worldly distractions [2][3].

St. Paul is celebrated for his commitment to monasticism, which is a way of life that emphasizes ascetic practices, prayer, and devotion to God, often in isolation from society. He lived for nearly ninety years in the wilderness, sustained by divine providence, specifically by a raven that brought him bread daily [2]. His life exemplifies the ideal of monasticism, which encourages individuals to renounce worldly ties, including marriage, to focus entirely on spiritual matters and communion with God. Thus, St. Paul the First Hermit is recognized not only for his solitary life but also for his significant role in the early monastic movement, influencing many who sought a similar path [1][2].

A group of ninety-seven confessors: men, women , and children, were 
brought to the governor , and  he ordered  the executioners to burn the

then sear them with red hot metal. Afterward, he sent those courageous 
confessors to work as slave laborers in the mines of Lebanon. 
Another group from Gaza was arrested while gathering in prayer and 
listening to the Word of God. Among them was a girl named Thea (Tia), who 
rebuked the governor when he threatened to have her raped in public , and he 
ordered that she would be whipped and t ortured. When another girl from 
Caesarea of Palestine, named Valentina saw that, she rushed through the 
crowd to tell the governor: “Until when will you torture my sister?”  She was 
arrested and was taken to the temple of the idols . There, she kicked the al tar, 
and the governor ordered tying the two girls together and burning them alive. 
At the same time, the head of a Christian man name d Paul (Paulus) was 
cut off because he held fast to his f aith. That man showed an amazing love in 
the moments before his ma rtyrdom. After he requested the permission of his 
executioner, he stood up and with contrition prayed with a loud voice to God 
for his companions to support them in the moments of their s uffering; for the 
spreading of f aith; for t he sake of all who were pr esent and for that of the 
emperor, the governor and all the officials.  
His sufferings drew him to think not of himself but of the others, even the 
opponents and the persecutors, to pray to God to grant them Salvation. 
 [Eusebius: Ecclesiastical History, ch. VIII] 
 
PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA 
Through Divine care , St. Abba Anthony the Great the Father of the 
Monastic family and its founder in the whole world, encountered this St. Paul 
who preceded him by long years in monastic life in the wilderness, where no 
one but God knew anything about him . God kept sustaining him by half a 
loaf of bread, carried to him by a raven every day all along many decades; in 
which God smelled the sweet fragrance of his prayers and praise, to call him: 
“My beloved Paul.” 
His Upbringing: 
St. Paul the 1st hermit was born in Alexandria around the year 228 AD. His 
father passed away leaving a great wealth for him and for his older brother 
Peter. However, Peter conspired to acquire the greater portion of the 
inheritance for himself, and  when the disagreement escalated between the

In the apostolic age, many practiced a kind o f monasticism, seeking to enjoy the 
perfection of the Gospel. The eschatological direction of the Church made the believers long 
for the coming of their Bridegroom, so some preferred to live a life of virginity, consecrating 
all their time for worship to p repare themselves for the heavenly wedding. In the second 
century, the Christian virgins in Smyrna and Corinth used to walk in liturgical processions 
behind the priests and in front of the widows. Moreover, many groups of virgins were found 
living in Alexandria and in many cities around the world. Articles about virginity represented 
an essential aspect of the writings of the Church Fathers in the first three centuries. 
Virgins used to live together, while men preferred to leave the cities to live in simple huts 
in villages and were often called “consecrated.” Some people felt a thirst for the angelic life 
so they fled to the wilderness. We know of only a few of these, such St. Paul the Hermit who 
lived in the wilderness for almost ninety years (between 250–340 A. D.). 
St. Anthony established the monastic movement and is considered the father of all monks 
in the entire world, even though many preceded him. This is because of his strong relationship 
with St. Athanasius, who wrote about him to the Roman world. It is also because he opened 
his cave after twenty years of solitude to disciple monastic leaders, converse with 
philosophers in the simplicity of his faith, and receive rulers. He had an active role in the 
Church and went to Alexandria to support the martyrs and stand against the Arians. 
St. Pachomius, founder of cenobitic monasticism, felt that the order of solitude may not 
work for all those who want to become monks, so he started a monastic community within 
the walls of monasteries, and the hermits praised him for doing so. 
St. Macarius the Great, St. Ammonas and others started the order of communities (or the 
semi-eremitical order). Many came from around the world to practice the ascetic life in 
Egypt, and to write about it and take these orders back to  their countries. It is important to 
note that the leaders of the three orders were not biased for their monastic styles, but instead 
they used to visit each other and praise each other’s orders. 
The monastic movement of women started side by side with tha t of men, and monks 
helped build convents. Female leaders arose and had great influence, like Amma Sarah, 
Amma Theodora, and Amma Syncletica. Moreover, some Egyptian and foreign women were 
disguised in the apparel of men and led ascetic lives in monasterie s of men, and their 
asceticism, struggles, and spirituality exceeded many. 
875. Who were the most important monastic leaders? 
St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit):  St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 
375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and 
Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his 
parents. During the persecution of  Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness 
after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years

father's huge inheritance.  
By orders from the governor, he was stripped from his clothes, whipped , 
and had flames placed on his sides. They put iron tools in his mouth and ears; 
cut his tongue off and set poisonous serpents upon him , but God sent His 
Archangel Suriel to comfort, support , and heal him . The governor then sent 
him to Alexandria; and in the prison there, he met with his friend  ‘Isy’ (Ba-
isy) and his sister Tekla.  The three of them were exulted in spirit . The Lord 
Jesus Christ appeared to proclaim that the thr ee saints would testify to His 
Name and their bodies, as well as their souls, would stay together.  
The head of St . Paul was cut off on the seashore, where some believers 
came, shrouded his body and kept his relics with them. 
The church celebrates his martyrdom on the 9th of Amshir.  
 
PAULA, THE ELDER, ST. 
St. Paula is considered the most famous Roman woman as far as her piety 
and dedication to the Lord are concerned . Besides, she had vast wealth , 
honor, and sharpness of mind. She was born on the 15 th of May 347 AD to a 
very rich family among the Roman elites . Her man Toxotius  passed away 
when she was only thirty-two years old and a mother to a son and four 
daughters: 
1- The son was named Toxotius, after his father's name. 
2- The oldest daughter was  named Blesilla, after her maternal grandmother . 
She passed away three months after she completely changed her worldly 
lifestyle and lived in repentance . St. Jerome wrote a condolence letter to 
her mother, to assure her that she has gone to Paradise. 
3- The second daughter was Paulina, the wife of Pammachius.  After his 
young wife Paulina passed away, he distributed most of the possessions he 
inherited on the poor and he pursued an ascetic life, even though he was 
one of the elites. 
4- The third daughter was Eustochium , who accompanied her mother all the 
way on a very tough ascetic road that angered her relatives . When her 
mother passed away in Bethlehem ; she was on the brink of collapse . 
However, St. Jerome came to her support and exhorted her to complete the 
mission of her mother. 
5- The fourth daughter was Rufina, who passed away in her youth in 386. 
Her Widowhood: 
St. Paula lived with her husband an ideal family life, to become a role 
model in Rome for the virtuous matrimony in the Lord . The man she dearly 
loved passed away, when she was only thirty-two years old . She was so

389 
 
daughters. 
Paula's heart was day by day i nflamed with the longing to the Heavenly 
life; while the atmosphere in Rome was suffocating for her because of the 
fame of her noble fami ly and the criticism she got from her family elders , so 
she planned to leave Rome and go somewhere else to worship God in 
tranquility and peace away from her family and her old friends. 
In the year 385 AD, she sailed along with her daughter Eustochium  to 
Cyprus. There, they visited St . Epiphanius, the bishop of Salamis , and from 
there, they sailed to Antioch, where they met with St . Jerome. Then all of 
them set forth to the Holy places in Palestine , and from there, they went to 
Egypt to see some of its desert monks and hermits. 
In Egypt: 
St. Paula accompanied St . Jerome on his trip to Egypt and was most 
probably with him when he met with St . Didymus the Blind, the d ean of the 
School of Alexandria. She studied at his school for one month; then set forth 
together with St . Jerome to the wilderness of Nitria. In Nitria , they stayed a 
long time . St. Jerome described the effect of that period on the life of that 
saintly widow, he said that she was excited and joyful to see these saints and 
longed to imitate their lives. The fathers received her with joy, for which she 
glorified God and felt unworthy of such an honor . She met with the two 
Macariuses, St. Serapion and others . She visited them in their cells, 
prostrated herself at their feet, feeling that the Lord  Jesus Christ was in every 
one of them. She tolerated the harsh traveling between the cells and spen t the 
nights in the open wilderness with joy and enthusiasm beyond the endurance 
of any woman . She forgot her fatigue and all her needs because of her 
spiritual joy. 
In Bethlehem: 
In the next year, she set forth to Jerusalem to live in Bethlehem. There, she 
built a guest -house to gi ve hospitality to strangers, a monastery for monks 
and a convent for the nuns. 
In the convent, she  lived along with her daughter Eustochum  a serious 
monastic life, and according to the convent' s rules, all practiced the work of 
the hand, particularly sewing for the nuns or those outside. 
Paula lived among the nuns as a mother who drew them with her love, 
tenderness and she was their role model . Even though she and her daughter 
partook of ministry and work, yet she was firm . If, for instance, she noticed a 
nun talk too much or showing anger ; she would ask her to separate herself 
from the congregation, to pray outside , and to eat her meals alone for a 
certain period.

longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. 
He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness 
to become his disciples. 
St. Shenoute the Archimandrite: He was the abbot of the White Monastery in Athribis 
(or Atripe), in the wilderness of Thebes for over fifty-six years (fourth or fifth century A. D.). 
He led 2200 monks and 1800 nuns. He was called the “Archimandrite” as he practiced 
solitude from time to time, and he encouraged the monks at his monastery to retreat to the 
wilderness after practicing the life of fellowship. In the year 431 A. D., he accompanied St. 
Cyril the Great to the Ecume nical Council of Ephesus. He is known for  purifying Coptic 
literature of Hellenistic cultural influences, and did not allow any foreigners to join his 
monastic communities. For this reason, he was regarded as a political leader and a social 
reformer, besides the depth of his spirituality. 
Amma Sarah : The first monastic group of women in the world was in the city of 
Alexandria, following the rule of St. Syncletica. St. Athanasius documented her biography 
and teachings. Moreover, St. Pachomius established two convents for nuns, while many nuns 
lived in solitude in the desert. Many mothers came from foreign convents to Egypt, like St. 
Melania the Elder (374 A. D.) and her granddaughter Melania the Younger (418 A. D.). Also, 
we cannot forget to mention St. Mary of Egypt who repented in Jerusalem and lived for forty-
seven years in the wilderness across the Jordan not seeing the face of another human being, 
except St. Zosima twice in the last two years of her life.  
Many nuns were given the gift of true leadership and spiritual discernment, like St. Sarah 
of whom it was said that she lived for sixty years on the banks of a river, but never lifted her 
eyes to look at it. Many of her sayings were preserved in the sayings of the desert fathers and 
mothers.  
St. Hilaria: In the fourth century, the daughter of Emperor Zeno fled to Scetis where she 
led a life of asceticism in the attire of a male monk. When her sister, Theopiste, was possessed 
by an evil spirit, the elders of the wilderness sent her to St. Hilaria to pray for her, and did 
not know that St. Hilaria was a woman. She prayed all night for her and embraced her. 
Theopiste was healed, and she told the emperor about the monk, “Hilarion,” who healed her 
and was embracing her, so her father was disturbed. He called for her to come to the palace, 
where she revealed to him that she was his daughter after he had promised not to prevent her 
from going back to her cave. 
St. Syncletica: Some historians regard her to be the equal of St. Anthony, the star of the 
wilderness; for as St. Anthony was the father of all monks, St. Syncletica was a mother to 
that group of virgins which transformed the fertile valley of Egypt into a dwelling place for 
the grace of God. She was born to noble parents who settled in Alexandria to be close to the 
School of Alexandria. They had two sons and two daughters, so they wanted to educate them 
in all sciences, which were only offered in the School of Alexandria. This family was shocked
