records.question: St. Moses the Black
records.answer:
St. Moses the Black, also known as Moses the Ethiopian, is a significant figure in the Coptic Orthodox Church, renowned for his transformation from a life of crime to one of deep faith and asceticism. Originally, he was a notorious gang leader who committed numerous sins, including robbery and violence, which led him to be known as a "gangster" [4]. However, he experienced a profound conversion after encountering the monks of Scetis, where he sought to repent and change his life.

His journey towards holiness began when he was inspired to leave his life of crime and seek out the monks, believing that they could help him find salvation. Upon meeting St. Isidore, he openly confessed his past sins and expressed his desire to live a life dedicated to God [4][6]. This act of humility marked the beginning of his monastic life, where he faced intense spiritual struggles and temptations, particularly from the demons that sought to remind him of his past [6].

St. Moses's life was characterized by rigorous ascetic practices, which included fasting, prayer, and acts of service to others. He was known for his compassion and humility, often helping those in need and performing miracles, such as healing the sick [1][2]. His dedication to monastic life was so profound that he eventually became a priest and was later ordained as a bishop, despite initially refusing to be ordained by Arian hands, which he deemed unworthy [7].

His teachings and sayings reflect his deep understanding of humility and repentance. For instance, he advised others to focus on their own sins rather than judging others, emphasizing that "it would be unreasonable for a man to leave his dead son, and go to mourn that of his neighbor" [5]. This perspective highlights the importance of personal accountability and the need for self-reflection in the spiritual journey.

St. Moses's life culminated in martyrdom, where he chose to remain with his fellow monks during an attack rather than flee, demonstrating his commitment to his faith and community [8]. His legacy continues to inspire many within the Coptic Orthodox Church, symbolizing the power of repentance and the transformative grace of God.

Once four thieves tried to rob his cell, but he tied them together and 
carried them to the church. When the thieves r ealized that he was Moses, 
who used to be the head of a gang of thieves, they repented and wanted to 
become monks. St. Moses preached them with words that moved their hearts.  
Because of his great strife, the devils were stirred more against him, that 
his mentor Abba Isidore counseled him to moderate in his ascetic practices to 
keep them from causing him more troubles. He sought from him to deliver 
himself to God, and He alone would be able to alleviate that fight on him. 
Abba Isidore told him that, to keep  him from thinking that by his ascetic 
efforts, he could overcome the demons, but by humility and spiritual 
repentance, God would fight on our behalf.  
Ordained as a Priest: 
Because of his strife and virtues, they decided to ordain him as a priest. 
They arranged that the ordination would be performed at the patriarchate in 
Alexandria. However, the patriarch wanted to test Moses before ordaining 
him, so he ordered his priests that once they see him about to enter into the 
sanctuary, to drive him out saying: “Get out of here, O you with the 
blackface.” When they did that to him, the patriarch sent a deacon after him, 
and he heard him saying: “They did what you deserved Moses, for you are 
not a human, but dared to mix with men. Why then would you venture to sit  
among them?” St. Moses was ordained as a priest by the hand of the 23 rd 
Pope St. Theophilus (385 -412 AD), who heard at the time a voice saying: 
“Worthy, Worthy, Worthy,” and after putting the white robe on him, they said 
to him: “There you became all -white Moses.” He responded by saying with 
humility: “I wish this to be true on the inside as it is on the outside.” 
His Virtues: 
He lived denying himself that a governor, hearing about his virtues, 
longed to see him. When Moses knew about that, he ran away, bu t it 
happened that the saint passed by the governor in his way to the monastery, 
and he inquired from him about the location of father Moses' cell. St. Moses 
told him: “What do you want from such an old man, who is far from being 
upright.” The governor was disturbed and went to the monastery and told the 
monks about what happened. On understanding the monks how that monk 
looked like, they knew that it was no one but Fr. Moses, who denied himself.  
Because of his love, humility, strife, and intense asceticis m, he was 
granted by God to perform miracles and signs.  
A monk fell into a specific iniquity, and a meeting was held to discuss an 
appropriate penance. Moses was invited to attend, but he refrained from

256 
 
in the form of a girl. She managed to convince him to  spend the night at her 
place. Then, she claimed to him that she was the daughter of one of the kings 
and that she wanted him to marry her, quoting the honor of the marriage of 
the fathers: Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He accepted her request. Then, she 
claimed that she was a Jew, and he had to convert to her religion to be able to 
marry her. So, Moses was blinded, and he denied his Christ. Then, she (the 
deceptive devil) took him back to the wilderness, where a whole gang of 
devils ridiculed him and made so much fun of him. Finally, the hermit woke 
up and cast himself on the dust and kept crying and supplicating to the 
Compassionate God to forgive him. God sent him Abba Samuel, who told 
him that he would be departing after three days. Then, he took him to the  
church, where he gave him Communion in the Holy Sacraments after 
confessing all that the devil has done to him. St. Moses, the hermit, reposed 
in peace and was buried by Abba Samuel, who wrote his biography, and 
handed it to someone traveling to Alexandria for the benefit of the believers.  
 [The Hermit Fathers, Part 2, p. 25] 
 
MOSES, THE LIBYAN, ST. 
This saint was from Libya. He was so humble and compassionate all the 
time that God granted him the grace to perform the miracles of healing the 
sick. He once said: “When I was young, I lived in a monastery. There, it 
happened that eight monks dug a well, and seventy others built a wall around 
it, in the hope that they would get water from it. They dug it down to the 
depth of about twenty yards, but no water was found. They were very much 
grieved and intended to fill it up with dirt. However, by noontime, w hen 
Abba Pieour came over suddenly to the location of the well and was 
informed about what they were doing, he rebuked them saying: ‘Why did you 
despair, O you of little faith? ’ Then, he went down to the bottom of the well, 
and he prayed there. Afterward, he pushed an iron rod in the well bottom 
three times, saying: ‘O God of the saints, I pray, do not waste the effort of 
these men, but send them plenty of water.’ In a short while, the water erupted 
from the well and wetted everyone around.  
After praying a  thanksgiving prayer, Abba Pieour intended to go in his 
way. They tried to make him have a meal with them, but he said: ‘I have 
accomplished what I came here to do, I did not come here to eat.’”  
This was a good lesson for the brethren about faith and the trust in God.  
 [The Paradise of the Saints, p. 69]

240 
 
giving his sister Sarah in marriage and handing their whole wealth to her. 
However, when he discussed the idea with his sister, she responded to him by 
saying: “If you get married first, then I would follow suit.” He told her: “I 
have committed so many sins, which I intend to atone for by leading a 
monastic life, for I cannot get married and care for my salvation at the  same 
time.” She answered him: “How would you cast me in the snares of this 
world, and care only for your salvation?” Then, he answered her: “Whatever 
you choose will be yours.” She responded: “All that you would do, I shall 
also do, for we are of one fath er and one mother.” Then, they distributed all 
their wealth to the poor and the needy. St. Moises brought his sister Sarah 
into a house of virgins, and he joined a monastery near Alexandria, and for 
the following ten years, they did not see one another.  
Their Martyrdom: 
Then, when Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) incited persecution against the 
Christians, in the days of the 14 th Pope St. Dionysius the Great (246 -264 
AD), so many believers were martyred. At that time, St. Moises sent to his 
sister to bid her fa rewell, and let her know of his decision to be martyred in 
the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. She hastened to her mother -superior, 
sought to be released, got the blessings of her sisters, and joined her brother 
on his way to Alexandria. There, they both co nfessed together the Lord Jesus 
Christ, and after being tortured by many tools, they had their heads cut off by 
the sword, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.  
 [The Synaxarion: 26 Mesra] 
 
MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. 
St. Moises (Moses) was one of th e prominent fathers and saints of the 
church in the 8 th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and 
purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.  
St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Sce tis, 
where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during 
which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became 
known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), 
in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was 
an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of 
deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox 
faith. He used to spend most of his time in wors hip, that it was said that he 
did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

250 
 
master got rid of him. He turned into a gangster who lived on robbing and 
killing people. He had a large, muscular stature, which helped him to become 
the head of an evil gang.  
Having Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ: 
Even though an extreme evil -doer, yet he kept raising up his eyes towards 
the sun, believing that it was the true God, seeking fr om it to proclaim itself 
to him. Then, he heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to 
encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread all over 
the area at that time. He went there, carrying his sword, where he happened 
to meet with  St. Isidore (The Priest of the Cells ) coming out of his cell and 
heading to the church. Terrified by his appearance, the saint asked him: 
“What do you want from here, O brother?” Moses answered: “ I heard that 
you are a good servant of God . Therefore, I es caped and came to you to let 
God save me the way he saved you.” He continued in persistence and with 
submission, saying: “I want to remain with you, despite my countless sins 
and my great evils.” 
St. Isidore kept asking him about his past life and where he  has been. 
Moses confessed to him all the sins he committed. On seeing how he opened 
his heart to him, St. Isidore started to teach him and preached him at length 
the word of God, he told him about the judgment to come and then left him to 
contemplate.  
For hating evil and deciding to rid himself of it, Moses shed so many 
tears, and deep remorse swept his soul and disturbed his sleep, like a dreadful 
ghost. Then, he went to St. Isidore, prostrated himself before him, and in a 
loud voice, he confessed all hi s evil crimes again, with such contrition of 
heart that drew his compassion. He took him to Abba Macarius the Great, 
who put him under his care, taught him and guided him, gave him the grace 
of baptism, then put him back under the supervision of St. Isidore.  
His Monastic Life: 
After a while, Moses sought from Abba Isidore to make him a monk. 
However, Abba Isidore started to explain to him how tough the monastic life 
is with the constant fight against the demons and the other physical needs. He 
told him as a way of testing him: “It is better for you son, to go and live in 
the populated areas,” but after seeing his real intention and solid stand, St. 
Isidore sent him back to Abba Macarius the Great, the father of the 
wilderness.  
Moses stood in the church and  confessed publicly about all his sins and 
evil deeds. Abba Macarius said afterward that he saw during Moses 
confession a whiteboard with black writings, and with every sin Moses

would be unreasonable for a man to leave  his dead son, and go to mourn 
that of his neighbor. 
To die about your neighbor means to worry about your sins and not to 
care for the sins of any man, good or bad. You should not do wrong to 
anyone, or think bad about anyone else in your heart or despise anyone for 
doing wrong. You should not obey anyone who harmed his neighbor or 
rejoice for him. You should never slander anyone, but always say that God 
knows everybody's heart. Do not go along with the man who talks bad 
about his neighbor, because it would  make you fall in condemnation. Do 
not have hatred against anyone. Do not have a grudge in your heart against 
anyone, and do not hate the man who is hostile toward his neighbor. This 
would bring you peace. 
[Sayings of the Strong Saint Abba Moses, Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria-
Diocese of Los Angeles]

MOSES THE HERMIT 
St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of 
thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for 
twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went 
deep in the wilderness an d lived for thirty -five years in a spot having olive 
and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from 
the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended 
the wild beasts.  
His Multiple Falls and Repentances:  
Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older 
man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he 
repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five 
Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to 
him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the 
wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the 
hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his 
daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the 
brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his 
acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He 
could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the 
devil. He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.  
Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him

proclaimed, an angel wiped it out off that board until the board became all -
white. After Abba Macarius instructed him, he sent him back to the priest 
Isidore who clothed him in the monastic attire. He advised him: “Remain, my 
son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would 
leave it, all evil will come bac k to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure 
God will do mercy and grace on you and will crush the devil under your 
feet.” 
His Strife: 
St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the 
multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macari us to find for him a 
secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt 
tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for 
his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him 
of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand 
firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He 
mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept 
counseling him to stand fast until the dev il would get tired of him. He gave 
him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, 
seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to 
it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the 
thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he 
went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he 
refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it. ” Father. Abba 
Isidore too k him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” 
There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though 
preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he 
saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly an gels, about whom the saint 
said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against 
those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are 
against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and 
returned to his cell.  
Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body 
by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To 
discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks 
at night, take t heir water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far 
distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils 
caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to 
move, until some brethren happened to com e to the well, and they carried 
him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he

Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the 
queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the 
Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by 
the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, 
she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens 
accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those 
united tribes.  
Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands: 
On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop 
who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20 th Pope St. Athanasius 
the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then , 
St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even 
though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response 
to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never 
accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my 
beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I 
shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, 
then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.” 
The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they 
failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk 
Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take 
the monk to the nearest location o f the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he 
was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed 
with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant 
opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.  
Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, 
dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the 
opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not 
having a steady residence, teaching, preach ing, and converting multitudes to 
Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to 
establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of 
Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in  the 
year 372 AD.  
 [The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347]

For some reason, it was proclaimed an obligation in the Scetis to fast for a

himself. We shall talk to him about it.” When they got to know the facts, they

but kept that of God (i.e., giving hospitality to strangers).”  
His Martyrdom: 
Then, it happened that the Barbarians came to attack the monastery, an 
incident St. Moses knew by Spirit beforehand, and he sought from the 
brethren to escape. However, seven brethren stayed behind, and they asked 
him: “Are you not going to escape, father?” He answered: “For a long time, I 
waited for this day, for the words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be fulfilled: “ All 
who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). They said to 
him: “We shall stay with you and will not escape.” H e told them: “There, 
they are already at the gate.” The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed 
them all. However, when one of the seven escaped to the stronghold out of 
fear, he saw seven crowns coming down from heaven on the seven martyred

records.question: Jesus Prayer
records.answer:
The Jesus Prayer, also known as the Arrow Prayer, is a profound and simple invocation that embodies the essence of Christian prayer in the Coptic Orthodox tradition. It typically takes the form of "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner." This prayer is designed to facilitate a constant dialogue with God, allowing the believer to maintain a state of prayer throughout their daily activities. The goal of this practice is to foster closeness to God and to live in continual remembrance of His presence in one's life [1][4].

The Jesus Prayer is deeply rooted in the teachings of the Desert Fathers, who emphasized its power and simplicity. St. Augustine referred to it as "the arrow prayer," highlighting its ability to pierce through distractions and temptations, thereby keeping the believer focused on God [1]. This prayer can be recited at any time—during work, meals, or even while asleep—making it a versatile tool for spiritual growth [1][3]. 

The practice of the Jesus Prayer is not merely about reciting words; it involves a heartfelt engagement with the name of Jesus. St. Macarius the Great encouraged believers to remember the name of Jesus as a precious jewel, which brings sweetness and spiritual reward [7]. This prayer is also seen as a means of spiritual warfare, helping to dispel darkness and temptation, as noted by Origen, who spoke of its power to cast out demons and heal the suffering [7][8].

Moreover, the Jesus Prayer is intended to be a source of inner joy and peace. St. Cyril the Great emphasized that prayer should not be viewed as a burdensome duty but rather as a joyful privilege to converse with God, akin to speaking with a loving father [2]. This sentiment is echoed in the teachings of St. John Climacus, who described prayer as a union with God that sustains the world and brings about reconciliation [4].

In summary, the Jesus Prayer serves as a vital spiritual practice within the Coptic Orthodox Church, enabling believers to cultivate a continuous relationship with God, seek His mercy, and experience the transformative power of His name in their lives.

Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven  
93 
6 
The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer 
960. What is the “Jesus Prayer”? 
The goal of sacred worship — and of prayer in particular — is closeness to God 
through constant dialogue with Him. Hence, both scripture and holy tradition provide a 
varied approach to prayer through which the believer is able to attain to constant prayer 
without ceasing. The believer begins with pray er in every work he undertakes; even before 
he sleeps. He participates in liturgies, prays the psalms, and his own personal prayers. To 
preserve his thought from distraction, he offers up prayers that cannot be counted with 
words or sentences, remembering always the presence of God in his life, so that he lives in 
a state of constant communication with Him; prayers that he can recite or repeat at any 
time, even when he is performing any kind of work. Being confident in the power of the 
name of Jesus, the believer repeats it often. This is what we call the Jesus Prayer. 
The Desert Fathers often recited this prayer or other short prayers, which represent a cry 
to the Lord. St. Augustine used to repeat this prayer: “Make haste, O God, to deliver me. 
Make haste to help me, O Lord” (Ps. 70:1); and he encouraged the faithful to repeat it on 
every occasion: at home; at work; while eating or drinking; while awake or asleep; in grief 
or joy; wh en spiritually zealous or lukewarm in worship — for this prayer is particularly 
helpful. St. Augustine used to call this short prayer, “the arrow prayer,” for it shoots an 
arrow into the heart of the devil and prevents him from distracting our thoughts so long as 
we pray it. St. John of the Ladder (Climacus) urges us to employ this short prayer saying, 
“Let your prayer  be completely  simple. For both the  publican and the prodigal son  were 
reconciled to God by a single phrase.”293 
961. Are there other short prayers that can be considered as arrow prayers? 
St. John Chrysostom gives us a few examples of short prayers: 
O Lord, of Your heavenly bounties, deprive me not. 
O Lord, forgive me if I have sinned in my mind or my thought, whether in word or in 
deed. 
O Lord, deliver me from every temptation and from eternal torments. 
O Lord, enlighten my heart which evil desires have darkened. 
 
293 St. John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent, trans., Colm Luibheid and Norman Russell (Paulist Press, 
1982) 28.5: p. 251.

its virtue in the cause of good. And so it  knows nothing save how to recall the  souls of the

possessed, to open prison-bars, to loose the bonds of the innocent. Likewise it washes away

high-spirited, escorts travelers, appeases waves, makes  robbers stand aghast, nourishes 
the poor, governs the rich, upraises the fallen, arrests the falling, confirms the standing. 
Prayer is the wall of  faith: her arms and  missiles against the foe who keeps watch over us 
on all sides. And, so never walk we unarmed. By day, be we mindful of Station; by night, 
of vigil. Under the arms of  prayer guard we the standard of our General; await we 
in prayer the angel’s trump … What more then, touching the office of  prayer? Even the 
Lord Himself prayed; to whom be honour and virtue unto the ages of the ages!”55 
St. Hesychius of Jerusalem  says, “‘Oh, that I my request  may be fulfilled  before the 
Lord.’ Should my prayers ascend on high, my enemies would perish, and the righteous 
person would stand firm (Wisd . of Sol.  5:1); the net would be broken, and the bird would 
be liberated  and fly freely (Ps. 124:7) ; the oppressors would bow their heads , and the

Second: Prayer propagates the spirit of inner joy. St. Cyril the Great says, “For it is, I

sons with a  father. Is not this then a privilege worthy of being valued by us most highly? 
For suppose that some one of those possessed of great earthly power were easy of access to

us draw near with praises, and rejoicing that we have been commanded to converse with the

accomplishment of our supplications. For the blessed Paul somewhere writes, ‘Grace be 
unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ ’ (2 Cor. 1:2) . 
And He somewhere Himself said to the holy apostles, ‘Hitherto you have asked nothing in

Book 2: Christian Dogma 
303 
406. Why is Jesus called “the Suffering Servant”? 
Isaiah the prophet gave us the praise of the Suffering Servant, who is the crucified Christ 
(Isa. 53). 
407. Why is Jesus called “the Judge”? 
Christ identifies Himself as the Judge (John 5:22) who will judge the living and the dead 
(1 Pet. 4:5); not to terrify them, but to reassure them. He will come to condemn the wicked 
and to prepare the marriage supper, where the Church will rejoice without any fear of the 
enemy who opposes her. The wicked will see His eyes as a flame of fire and in His m outh a 
sharp sword and He will rule them with a rod iron. As for His children, they will see Him as 
the “King of Kings and Lord of Lords” who protects and glorifies them (Rev 19:9–16). 
408. What is “the Jesus Prayer”? 
Let us conclude this survey of the names an d titles of Christ by mentioning the 
effectiveness of the “ Jesus Prayer” in our lives. When the believer experiences the power 
of the name of Jesus, he cries out with blind Bartimaeus, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy 
on me!” (Mark 10:47, Luke 18:38). This prayer is found in the biography of Abba Philemon 
(6th to 7th century). It is also found in the letters of Saints Barsanuphius and John  of Gaza 
(beginning of the 6 th century), Dorotheus of Gaza, and St. John Climacus. The Church 
employs it as a spiritual practice for her children, with the addition of part of the prayer of 
the tax collector who beat his chest saying, “God be merciful to me a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).  
St. Anthony the Great says, “Do not cease from reciting the name of the Lord Jesus, but 
hold onto to His name with your mind, repeat it with your tongue, and say in your heart: ‘My 
Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me; My Lord Jesus Christ help me.’ Also say: ‘I praise 
You, my Lord Jesus Christ.’”  
It was also known to St. Macarius the Great and St. Evagrius.790  
St. Macarius the Great says, “ Be attentive to the name of our Lord Jesus Christ with a 
remorseful heart and let it pour forth from your lips. Let the name reflect back upon you. Do 
not bury it in your thoughts only for display, but be alert whenever you cry it out, saying, “O 
my Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me!” Then, in serenity you shall see His divinity resting 
in you; He will bring to naught the darkness of pain that is in you; and He shall purify your 
inner man to be like the purity  of Adam dwelling in paradise. This is the blessed name that 
St. John the Evangelist called, “the light of the world” (John 8:12); the sweetness of which 
no one can ever have enough and the true “bread of life” (John 6:35).” 
 
790 See Michael O’Carroll, Verbum Caro: An Encyclopedia on Jesus, the Christ (The Liturgical Press, 1992) 
“Jesus Prayer, the”: p. 82; and Gordon S. Wakefield ed., The Westminster Dictionary of Christian 
Spirituality (Westminster Press, 1983) “Jesus, Prayer To”: pp. 223–224.

The Life of Prayer 
896. What is prayer? 
St. Clement of Alexandria says , “Prayer is, then, to speak more boldly, converse with 
God.”37  
St. John Climacus says, “Prayer by reason of its nature is the converse and union of 
man with God, and by reason of its action upholds the world and brin gs about 
reconciliation with God  … it is … a work of angels, the food of all the bodiless spirits , 
future gladness, unending activity, a source  of virtues, a means of obtaining  graces, 
invisible progress, food of the soul, the enlightenment of the mind, an axe against despair, a 
demonstration of hope, a cure for sorrow.”38  
“Let your prayer be completely simple. For both the publican and the prodigal son were 
reconciled to God by a single phrase.”39  
“The benefit of prayer can be inferred from the assaults of the demons during the divine 
service; and its fruit from the defeat of the foe.”40 
St. Basil the Great  says, “Thus will you pray without ceasing, if you not only pray in 
words, but unite yourself to God through all the course of life so that your life be made one 
ceaseless and uninterrupted prayer.”41  
The Letter to Diognetus says of Christians that “their days are passed on the earth, but 
their citizenship is above in the heavens.”42

St. Isaac the Syrian says, “Sit in the presence of the Lord every moment of your life, 
as you think of him and remember him in your heart. Otherwise, when you only see him

Second: Let the recitation of the name be from the soul’s inner depths, without 
loudness or violence, even internally. When Elijah was command ed to stand before the 
Lord and prepare to encounter Him, he was told, “‘Stand on the mountain’ … and behold, 
the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind tore into the mountains and broke the rocks 
in pieces, but the Lord was not in the wind. And after  the wind an earthquake, but the Lord 
was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire, 
And after the fire a small voice. When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, 
and went out and stood in the ent rance of the cave. Suddenly a voice came to him and said, 
‘What are you doing here Elijah?’” (1 Kings 19:1–13). 
Third: Recite your prayer in serenity and simplicity, or more specifically, with 
gentleness. As a bird that flies up to the height it intends an d then gently glides, flapping its 
wings only from time to time to maintain its altitude, so the soul, if it flies up to glide upon 
the thought of Christ Jesus and is sated by remembering Him, can cease to repeat the holy 
name and instead rest in other tho ughts; namely, thinking about Jesus. It is natural for 
moments of lukewarmness to intrude upon this practice. But if at any time you begin your 
recitation once more, you find the name of Jesus upon your lips spontaneously, and 
returning to your thoughts co ntinually, silently, and internally. Thus, you will experience 
the verse: “I sleep but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). However, this prayer cannot be 
prayed inattentively: “Because of the fragrance of your ointment, the virgins love you. 
Draw me away; the daughters of Jerusalem will run after you” (Song 1:3–4). 
Fourth: We should be drawn toward the name of Jesus by the guidance of the Holy 
Spirit, so that calling on the name of Jesus becomes in our lives one of the fruits of the 
Holy Spirit Himself. 
Fifth: We should be careful not to despise other forms of prayer.  
Sixth: We must forget ourselves and put our egos to death while the name of the Holy 
God comes alive in our spirits: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). 
Seventh: Repetition of the Jesus Prayer should not lessen our participation in the divine 
liturgy or in other Church rites such as the Midnight Praises. 
Eighth: The best kind of prayer is that which is prayed when we are moved by the Holy 
Spirit.  
Ninth: The goal of the Jesus Praye r is to praise Him, crying out with Thomas the 
apostle: “My Lord and God!” (John 20:28). We should be concerned most of all with the 
Lord of glory, Jesus, being present in our lives.  
Tenth: Calling on the name of Jesus grants us salvation in every kind of  need in our 
lives.

969. How did the scholar Origen experience the power of invoking the name of Jesus 
Christ? 
The scholar Origen often spoke of the power of the name of Jesus, and his confid ence 
in achieving conquest and victory over sin and the devil, and over all the powers of 
darkness. He says, “Through His name, many demons are cast out of people; especially if it 
is prayed in a spiritual and sound manner with all confidence. Great is the  name of Jesus , 
and effective and blessed.  The name of Jesus heals those who are suffering mentally, 
dispels the spirits of darkness, and grants healing to the sick.” 
970. How did St. Augustine practice continual prayer through the name of Jesus? 
Having experienced the power of the name of Jesus in his repentance from sin, St. 
Augustine proclaimed, saying, “No one can pray in the name of the Savior if he is praying 
for something other than salvation.” 
971. What does St. Anthony say about the practice of the Jesus Prayer? 
“If you sit in your cell, work with your hands, while repeating the name of Jesus. Hold 
it fast in your heart and mind and sing it with your tongue: ‘My Lord Jesus, help me,’ ‘I 
praise You my Lord Jesus Christ.’” 
972. What did St. Macarius the Great say about the practice of the Jesus Prayer? 
“Always remember the holy name, our Lord Jesus Christ. This is the pearl which the 
wise merchant purchased (Matt. 13:45 –46) by selling all the desires of his heart, brought 
into the inner rooms of his hou se, and found it sweeter than honey in his mouth. He who 
keeps this jewel in his heart shall be granted a great reward in the glory of our Lord Jesus 
Christ.”

records.question: eucharist
records.answer:
The Eucharist, also known as the Holy Communion, is a central sacrament in the Coptic Orthodox Church, embodying the mystery of uniting the faithful with Christ through partaking of His Body and Blood. This sacrament is considered the pinnacle of Christian worship because it allows believers to actively participate in the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, thus receiving spiritual nourishment and grace for their lives.

The Eucharist is described as a "mystery of uniting us the faithful with the Savior" [4]. When believers partake of the Eucharist, they are not merely engaging in a ritual; they are experiencing a profound spiritual reality where their whole being is sanctified and blessed by Christ's eternal glory. St. John Chrysostom emphasizes the transformative power of the Eucharist, stating that it is the "medicine of immortality" and that through it, believers are cleansed and filled with hope for eternal life [1][2].

Moreover, the Eucharist is viewed as a sacrifice. The Church teaches that it is not a new sacrifice but a remembrance (ἀνάμνησις, anamnesis) of the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross. This understanding is rooted in the teachings of St. Paul and the early Church Fathers, who affirmed that the Eucharist is a pure sacrifice, fulfilling the Old Testament sacrifices through Christ's redemptive act [4][8]. St. Basil notes that receiving Communion is a way to remember Christ's obedience and to live for Him who died and rose again [7].

Participation in the Eucharist is also linked to the believer's spiritual growth. St. Cyril the Great teaches that regular participation is essential for retaining and growing in spiritual life, while irregular participation can deprive one of eternal life [5]. The Eucharist is not only a personal communion with Christ but also a communal act that invites believers to share the love of God with others, reflecting the openness and care that should characterize the life of a Christian [2][3].

In preparation for receiving the Eucharist, believers are encouraged to examine their consciences and approach with humility and repentance, recognizing their need for God's grace [8]. This sacrament is a profound gift that invites the faithful to a deeper relationship with Christ and a transformative experience of His love and sacrifice.

767. Is it possible to partake of the eucharist every week? 
There are two main reasons that some people offer for excusing themselves from 
receiving the eucharist every week. The first reason is feeling unprepared; while the truth is 
that to be prepared for communion is simply to feel unworthy, while sincerely praying for 
the work of God’s grace through repentance and prayer. The  second reason is when people 
lose the meaning of the eucharist because they pray the Divine Liturgy merely as a routine. 
The eucharist is the medicine of immortality. He who feels the need for this medicine should 
not stop partaking of the eucharist, or praying, or studying the Holy Bible, or striving to keep 
the divine commandments. Doing these things prevents us from practicing the rituals in a 
literal manner that is void of spirit, and instead fills the heart with love for God and love for 
others.  
768. Is it permissible for a person to receive the body and blood of our Lord every day? 
St. Basil talks about praying the Divine Liturgy daily: “Now, to receive Communion 
daily, thus to partake of the holy Body and Blood of Christ, is an excellent and advantageous 
practice; for Christ Himself says clearly: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has life 
everlasting’ (John 6:54). Who doubts that to share continually in the life is nothing else than 
to have a manifold life? We ourselves, of course, receive Communion four times a week, on

766. Why is the Sacrament of the Eucharist considered to be the pinnacle of Christian 
worship?  
In the sacrament of the eucharist, the believer, along with his heavenly friends, sets off 
to Golgotha where he sees his soul’s heavenly Groom, offering His blood as a dowry. The 
believer then remembers the death and resurrection of His  life-giving Groom, not just in 
words and thoughts but by actively partaking of His body and blood that are offered for him; 
the secret of his life and his continuous spiritual growth. 
In the sacrament of the eucharist, the Holy Spirit offers us the crucified body of the Lord 
who rose from the dead, and His precious blood, to be in Him and He in us. Through Him, 
we are worthy to enter before His divine throne, abiding in Christ’s righteousness, as 
members of His body. Christ the Lord says, “For My fle sh is food indeed, and My blood is 
drink indeed. He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him … so he 
who feeds on Me will live because of Me” (John 6:55 –57). The Church hides in this Holy 
Sacrifice, and therefore bears Christ’s holiness and righteousness.

The Sacrament of the Eucharist 
764. What is the mystery of communion in the eucharist? 
It is the mystery of uniting us the faithful with the Savior by partaking of His Body and 
Blood which He gave up for us. Thus, our whole being, including our bodies, is sanctified 
and is blessed by His eternal glory.  
765. Is the eucharist a sacrifice?  
First: The Church was introduced to the idea of sacrifice at the time of the apostles, for 
St. Paul says, “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to 
eat” (Heb. 13:10). In his epistle to the Hebrews (Chapter 10), he speaks of the Old Testament 
sacrifices as symbols fulfilled in Christ’s redemption and in the eucharist. He also speaks of 
the eucharist as an offering when he compares the holy table of God to that of demons (1 
Cor. 10:20–21). 
Second: Around the year 100 A. D., the author of the Didache mentions the eucharist as 
a pure sacrifice. 1471 This was further confirmed by Fathers of the Church 1472 such as St. 
Ignatius, St. Justin, St. Irenaeus, St. Cyril of Jerusalem, St. Cyprian, and St. Augustine.  
Third: The Church uses two Greek words to refer to the eucharist: θυσία (thysia; 
sacrifice), and προσφορά (prosphora; offering). When talking about the eucharist, St. 
Ignatius refers to the Church assembly as the eucharistic θυσιαστήριον (thysiastirion; place 
of sacrifice or altar.1473 St. Clement of Rome says that the work of the bishop is the offering 
of the προσφοτερια (prosfoteria; the oblations).1474  
Fourth: The Fathers often used 1475 the word τράπεζα ( trapeza), which means table, to 
refer to the altar. This term does not contradict the fact that the eucharist is a sacrifice, but it 
gives the sacrificial act of the eucharist a new meaning. In the New Testament, senseless 
animals were unwillingly slaughtered by the people on the altar for a sacrifice. However, on 
our altars, the Sacrifice offers Himself out of His immense love, to grant us life. He is not

Thirteen: The declaration of Himself.  St. Augustine  says, “Ah yes, brothers and 
sisters, but where did the Lord wish to be recognized? In the breaking  of bread. We’re all 
right, nothing to worry about; we break bread, and we recognize the Lord. It was for our

you, if you’re not called a Christian for nothing, if you don’t come to church pointlessly, if 
you listen to the word of God in fear and hope, you may take comfort in the breaking of 
bread.”1508  
Theophylact of Bulgaria says, “The eyes of those who receive the holy bread are opened 
to know Christ, for within the Body of the Lord is His great incomprehensible power.” 
Fourteenth: Acknowledging the mystery of the Christian Passover. St. Melito of 
Sardis says, “But the mystery of the Lord … through the body which was able to suffer … 
For, he himself led as a lamb and slain as a sheep, he ransomed us from the world’s service 
as from the land of Egypt, and freed us from the devil’s slavery as from the hand of Pharaoh; 
and he marked our souls with his own Spirit and the members of our body with his own 
blood.”1509 
The mystery of the Passover has been completed in the body of the Lord. For He who 
was led away as a lamb, and who was sacrificed as a sheep, by  himself delivered us from 
servitude to the world as from the land of Egypt, and released us from bondage to the devil 
as from the hand of Pharaoh, and sealed our souls by his own spirit and the members of our 
bodies by his own blood. 
Fifteenth: Continuous spiritual growth. St. Cyril the Great says, “The acquisition of 
a spiritual life through the Eucharist requires regular participation in the sacrament. The 
believer retains his spiritual life and grows in the Spirit as long as he is attached to Christ, 
not only spiritually but also by regularly participating in the communion of the body and

St. Basil the Great believes that Christ offered us His Body and Blood, which He gave 
up in obedience to His Father to the point of death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8). 
Thus, we are prepared for communion, by obedience.1537 He says, “With what understanding 
is it necessary to eat the body and to drink the blood of the Lord? Unto the remembrance of 
the Lord’s obedience until death: so that the living no longer live for themselves but for the 
one who died and was raised on their behalf.”1538 
He also says, “it is necessary for the one wh o receives the holy things to praise the

And, “Let him who receives Communion remember the death and resurrection of Christ, 
and that he ought to be adorned by the purity of the body and soul, and to manifest his death 
from sin, the world and the ego by his life with God and with Christ our Lord.”1540 
We cannot receive the Messiah’s banquet, the partaking of the Lord’s body and blood, if 
we have not first understood the significance of this banquet through our understanding of

769. Why do we believe in the one Sacrifice that is offered on multiple altars? 
There are no multiple sacrifices like the High Priest used to offer in the past, for we offer 
the same sacrifice every day, or in other words we fulfill the remembrance of the sacrifice

not offer every day? We offer indeed, but making a remembrance of His death, and this

records.question: Anthony the Great
records.answer:
St. Anthony the Great, often referred to as the "Father of Monasticism," is a pivotal figure in the history of the Coptic Orthodox Church and Christian monastic life. Born around 251 A.D. in the village of Kom Al-Aros, Egypt, he was raised in a wealthy family. His transformative journey began at the age of eighteen when he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21) [1][3]. This message deeply resonated with him, prompting him to sell his possessions, place his sister in a convent, and dedicate his life to God.

Anthony's life as a hermit began in earnest when he retreated to the desert, where he sought solitude and spiritual growth. He lived in a tomb carved into the mountains and later moved to the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir, where he attracted many disciples who sought his guidance [3][5]. His commitment to asceticism—self-discipline and abstention from indulgence—was profound, as he faced numerous spiritual battles against temptations and demons during his years in seclusion [5]. 

Despite his preference for solitude, Anthony was not disconnected from the Church or the world. He felt compelled to support the Christian community, particularly during times of persecution. He visited Alexandria to encourage the martyrs and to stand against Arianism, a theological controversy that questioned the divinity of Christ [3][5]. His influence extended beyond his lifetime, as he inspired countless others to pursue monastic life, establishing a model for future generations.

St. Anthony's teachings emphasized the importance of community, prayer, and work. He believed that a monk should engage in manual labor to avoid idleness, which he viewed as a gateway to temptation [5]. His life and writings, particularly the "Life of Anthony" by St. Athanasius, have had a lasting impact on Christian monasticism, shaping the practices and ideals of monastic communities throughout history [6][8].

In summary, St. Anthony the Great is celebrated not only for his ascetic lifestyle and founding of monasticism but also for his role in defending the faith and guiding others in their spiritual journeys. His legacy continues to inspire those who seek a deeper relationship with God through prayer, solitude, and community life.

‘Anthony,' among whom are: 
ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr: 
He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great 
zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then 
he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false 
gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was 
expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop 
assigned him to build a Ch urch, the pagans were stirred up against him and 
killed him. 
ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr: 
St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and 
merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to 
‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. 
The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. 
Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his 
Christ, he ordered him chained and se nt him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of 
Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ 
put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but 
God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' 
where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each 
other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with 
sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint 
received the crown of martyrdom. 
 
ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. 
He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family ’ and 
‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement ’ in the whole world, even though 
there have been some monastic movements prior to his. 
The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around 
the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his 
corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled 
toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the 
gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to 
the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me ” (Matt. 
19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched  his 
life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he 
proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its 
proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister 
also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed 
him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven 
flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the 
raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony 
to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church.

order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying 
in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out 
to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of 
a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his 
head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned 
to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never 
get bored." That  came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand 
happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life. 
One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash 
their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they start ed to 
undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she 
answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, 
for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint 
said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He 
instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was 
around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to 
practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new 
location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of 
women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts. 
His Order of Seclusion: 
In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with  some 
beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He 
helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he 
was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept 
of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 
4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a 
member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he 
did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when 
Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his 
response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he 
said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of 
kings." However, when he was pressu red, he answered the emperor’s 
message, for the sake of the Church peace. 
5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy 
congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the 
Church. That is why he eventually came  down to help Pope Athanasius 
the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his 
entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants 
came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians 
came back to the Church.

GALLICANUS (The martyr) 
Gallicanus was a deputy of Emperor Constantine the Great (306-337 AD) 
and a leader in his army , known for his courage and bravery . He led two 
victorious military campaigns: the first against the Persians and the second 
against the Scythians. In the second campaign, he converted to Christianity on 
the hands of two Christian brothers: John and Paul. 
When St. Gallicanus enjoyed the Christian faith, his heart opened with love 
for God and men, and his soul bowed by the spirit of humility to serve every 
weak, poor, and stranger. After his return to Rome, he went into seclusion in 
Ostia,2 where he built a church. Feeling the inner freedom, he could not endure 
having any slaves, and he gave freedom to all of his slaves. Then, he expanded 
his mansion and made it more significant to receive as many pilgrims as he 
could. He was accompanied in that task by a friend named Hilarinus. When he 
became quite famous in the East and West , multitudes of people came to see 
by their own eyes, how that former deputy and friend of the emperor was 
washing the feet of the pilgrims, preparin g the tables for them, tending to the 
sick and offering himself as a living role model for the exalted Christian values. 
Then, God allowed for his life to be crowned by martyrdom . So, when 
Emperor Julian, the Apostate (360-363 AD), ordered him to choose be tween 
burning incense to the idols or to be exiled, he decided to be exiled to Egypt 
where he lived in seclusion among a group of hermits . Yet, the persecution 
followed him into the desert  of Egypt, where his head was cut off around the 
year 362 AD, while his friend Hilarinus was tortured to death. 
         [Baring-Gould: The Lives of the Saints, Vol. 6, June 25]

He was a bishop of Constantinople (458-471 AD), and he was an interpreter

Around the year 459 AD, he held a council to fight against the Simon ism

His sermons were lost, except for some paragraphs of his attack against St.

GENTIANUS, FUSCIANUS, and VICTORICUS  
(The martyrs) 
Gentianus was a heathen; however, through the preaching of his two friends 
Victoricus and Fuscianus, who took refuge in his house, he believed in the Lord 
Jesus Christ. He loved God so much, and his soul became  attached to Jesus 
Christ, his Savior. The three of them were eventually arrested . They pushed 
through their ears and skulls burning nails , their eyes were plucked out,  and 
spears were aimed at them . Finally, their heads were cut off in the year 303 
AD. Relics of their bodies are kept in the cities: Amirns, S. Quentin, and in the 
church of Notre Dame in Beaugency, in the diocese of Orleans.  
The anniversaries of these saints are celebrated on the 11th of December.

HISTORY AND BIOGRAPHIES OF THE 
FATHERS 
Despite our great love to write down the biographies, spiritual works, and 
heritage of the saints; and to show their thoughts, as a spiritual work that affects 
our life, we hesitated many times to produce this encyclopedia. We started then 
stopped many times because we feel inadequate to create what we have in our 
hearts and minds concerning this task. For the life of saints essentially is not 
apparent works, as much as it is an inner life and a spiritual kindling, according 
to the saying of the Lord: “I came to send fire on the earth, and how I wish it 
were already kindled” (Lk 12: 49); and, “For indeed, the kingdom of God is 
within you” (Lk 17: 21). Such an inner flame, or divine kingdom, is not easily 
expressed by any tongue. But, as the holy will of God allowed us to present 
this little work, we wish to clarify specific important points in offering fathers’ 
and saints’ lives, which would be difficult to do in every separate biography. 
 First:  Concerning  the  Saints:  
In the Arabic language, the word ‘Kudos,’ corresponding to the word 
‘Kodoosh’ in Hebrew; ‘Hageos’ or ‘Agios’ in Greek, concerns God alone, and, 
in his love for His creation, not only makes man who dedicates his heart to 
Him, a saint, but the location assigned to worship God, holy, and even the tools 
used in it, spiritual.  
 Saints, therefore, in truth, are men of God who delivered their hearts, lives, 
and works, to God, as a work of love. That made Paul the Apostle to call the 
believers of Philippi, Colossae, Ephesus, and Rome, “saints,” in the 
introduction of his epistles to them, being members in the body of Christ “the 
Holy One,” those who became the new people of God, consecrated to Him. 
According to Origen, he who studied philosophy, for example, was counted

records.answer:
The difference in the dates of Coptic Easter and Catholic Easter primarily arises from the calendars used by the two traditions. The Coptic Orthodox Church follows the Julian calendar for its liturgical calculations, while the Catholic Church uses the Gregorian calendar. This divergence leads to a difference of thirteen days between the two calendars today.

The Julian calendar, which was established by Julius Caesar, has a slight inaccuracy in its calculation of the solar year, leading to a gradual drift in the dates over centuries. In contrast, the Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582, corrected this drift by adjusting the leap year system. As a result, the Coptic Church continues to calculate Easter based on the Alexandrian computus, which combines solar and lunar cycles, while the Catholic Church uses a different method that aligns with the Gregorian calendar [1][7].

Moreover, the Coptic Church's observance of Easter is also tied to the Jewish Passover, as the date of Easter must fall after this festival. The Jewish calendar is lunar, which adds another layer of complexity to the calculations. The Coptic Church ensures that Easter is celebrated in a way that reflects its historical and theological roots, maintaining a connection to the early Christian traditions established by the Church Fathers [1][8].

In summary, the difference in the dates of Easter between the Coptic Orthodox Church and the Catholic Church is primarily due to the use of the Julian calendar by the Copts and the Gregorian calendar by Catholics, along with the theological significance of the timing related to the Jewish Passover.

The Protestants broke away from the Roman Church in the sixteenth c entury. This was 
the same century in which the Roman Pope Gregory XIII  requested that the Jewish 
Passover not be taken into account in the computation of the Christian Pascha, but that it is 
sufficient only to take into account the time of  the spring equinox. Protestants continued to 
use the Alexandrian computus until 1775 A. D., that is for about two centuries. 
1091. What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian 
calendar? 
The Copts inherited the ancient Egyptian calendar from thei r ancestors, and with some 
slight modifications , used it to order their liturgical  Church life and their daily affairs , 
especially agriculture. The Coptic liturgical day begins at sunset, like that of the Jews and 
the Greeks ; and each week consists of  seven days , the first of which is  the Lord’s Day 
(Sunday). 
In the fourth century, many Copts were martyred,  and they therefore considered the 
reign of Diocletian as a golden age. They set the year in which Diocletian became emperor 
(November, 284 A . D.) as the first year of their calendar. They introduced the term, “The 
Year of the Martyrs”  (Anno Martyrum), abbreviated as A.  M. The scholar Tertullian  said, 
“If the martyrs throughout the world were to be put in one side of the scales and the Coptic 
martyrs alone were to be put in the other, the latter would outweigh the former.”637 
1092. What are the names of the Coptic months? 
Certain papyri dating from the fifth century B . C. discovered on the island of 
Elephantine indicate that the Egyptians of the time celebrated great feasts in honor of the 
gods whose names were given to the months of the ancient Egyptian calendar.  The Copts 
preserved the names of the ancient Egyptian months, despite the fact that they are the 
names of pagan gods or their feasts. The names of the months are: 
1. Thout (begins 11th September / 12th September in a leap year): God of wisdom and 
knowledge, inventor of writing, protector of scribes , and designer of seasons and 
months. Thout presides over t he “House of Life ” and is the source of  all the texts 
necessary to preserve and renew life. 
2. Paopi (10th/11th October): The Feast of Opet. Amun-Ra was accustomed  to 
travelling from the Temple of  Karnak to  the Temple of  Luxor to celebrate this 
famous festival. 
 
637 Iris Habib El-Masry, The Story of the Copts: Book 1, (Southern California, U.S.A: St. Anthony Coptic 
Orthodox Monastery, undated) 1.9.99: p. 100.

On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy 
790. What are the features of Egyptian liturgy? 
The East in general, and Egyptian Church in particular, still retains the spirit of the 
apostolic patristic Liturgy. The liturgical texts that are used have not changed very much 
since the fifth century, which gives the study of the Egyptian liturgy particular importance. 
In his book “The Early Liturgy,” Father Jungmann says, “especially in the general structure 
of the Mass, the Oriental rites have kept many primitive characteristics which have 
disappeared from the Roman rite … Whereas our Mass changes day after day, the Orient 
constantly repeats the same invariable formulary.”1546 Fr. Dix, the Anglican monk, says, “The 
main lines of all the Eastern traditions had been reached before the end of the fourth century, 
and after this the process in all of them is no more than one of adjustment and developmen t 
of detail. No new principle arose in the fifth century, as it did in the West …” 1547 
791. Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use? 
a. The Liturgy of St. Basil the Great. The Coptic Liturgy differs from the Byzantine 
Liturgy of the same name. This Liturgy is the one that is most often used.  
b. The Liturgy of St. Gregory the Theologian.  Often used on special occasions and 
feasts. Prayers of this Liturgy address the hypostasis of the Son. It is not unique in 
doing so because there are other liturgies with the same style, such as other Egyptian 
liturgies, three Ethiopian liturgies, the Syrian Liturgy of Saints Addai and Mari, and 
the Syrian Liturgy of St. Jacob. 
c. The Liturgy of St. Cyril (St. Mark the Evangelist).  St. Cyril of Alexandria 
compiled it and edited the older Liturgy of St. Mark; so it came to be named after 
him. Its use is less widespread than the previous two. 
792. What are the main sections of the Coptic Liturgy? 
The Liturgy can be divided into three services:  
a. Offering of the Lamb. The Lamb is chosen from among the offered loaves of bread. 
The priest anoints it with wine in the name of the Holy Trinity. The offering of the 
Lamb was once part of the Liturgy of the Faithful, but just before the fifth century, 
this rite was moved to the begin ning of the Liturgy instead, in order to prepare the 
congregation for the renewal of their covenant with God by listening to God’s word 
and partaking of the sacraments. It is the beginning of the journey where the Church

addition to this, the surviving Coptic monuments do not represent the true quality of Coptic 
art, since the most prized and valuable pieces were ru ined or lost in the unceasing waves of 
persecution,1230 as the historian Al-Makrizi describes. To this effect, K. Wessel says, “At the 
height of the medieval period, Arab writers described magnificent paintings, those of the 
shrine of St. Menas for example, were especially famed, but little survives.” 1231 We can 
therefore only get a rough idea of what once was found in abundance in the Churches and 
Monasteries. 
629. What are the most important characteristics of Coptic iconography? 
They represent the life of joy. Our icons appear joyous. None of the Lord’s or martyrs’ 
sufferings are depicted in icons, except the victorious cross, where the Lord was hung as 
King of kings. There are no pictures of hell, only of heaven, heavenly creatures, and heavenly 
crowns. This shows the Church’s desire to grant hope to her children. 
They are full of the spirit of victory. Because the Church is seeking to create a spirit of 
confidence in her children, it does not depict paintings of demons; and if any are necessary, 
they appear small in size, lying down in weakness. 
They express the spirit of love and kindness . For example, in one of the icons, St. 
Mary’s cheeks are depicted to be touching the cheeks of her Son in gentle tenderness as they 
each place their hands on each other’s should ers, as though Christ is reconciling with 
humanity through His mother the saint.  
They express the strength of the spirit. Coptic iconographers focus on the inner 
strength of the spirit. The heads are enlarged as a symbol of God who is our heavenly Head, 
and the eyes are widened as a sign of spiritual sight. 
They represent people of prayer. Saints usually appear raising their hands in prayer to 
God ( orant) as if they are declaring that prayer is the mystery of their holiness.  It is the 
preferred position for many martyrs and saints at the time of their departure to paradise.  
They bear the cross. The majority of the icons of Alexandria depict Christ bearing a 
Coptic cross. 
They depict the Lord’s providence. The Lord is depicted hanging on the cross with His 
eyes open. Eulogius of Alexandria  says, “The Lord slept on the Cross for a brief time 
according to the flesh but according to His divinity, His eyes remained open.”

Consequently, a high religious court was held, attended by the Muslim sheiks 
in Egypt, the head of the Coptic church, and representatives of the Roman 
church. The high religious court issued a decision and was del ivered to the 
pope. The decision could be summarized as follows: “Whoever of the Copts 
changes his sect, and joins the foreign sect, should accordingly be punished by 
the officials, to make him an example to others.” 
In the year 1741 AD, the Roman Pope Ben edict XIV (1740 -1758 AD), 
ordained a ‘Coptic/Catholic’ priest in Jerusalem by the name of Athanasius, as 
a metropolitan on Egypt. Yet he did not come to Egypt, but spent the rest of 
his life in Jerusalem, leaving his deputy in Egypt, to a priest called Jus tus el-
Maraghy to represent him there. 
Among the most well-known personalities which the Catholics managed to 
lure them to their camp by the end of the 18 th century AD, was a young Copt 
called Raphael el-Tukhi of Girga. The Catholics took him while he was still a 
child, and sent him to Rome to study theology. Then, after he graduated, he 
was ordained by the Roman pope as a bishop on Arsinoe (Fayyum). However, 
he was excommunicated by the Coptic church and was opposed by the local 
authorities. Eventually, he was called back to Rome to help writing books in 
the Coptic language and to revise the books on the rites of the church. He lived 
in Rome until his death. 
The Coptic Pope John XVII, striving to keep his children in the fold of their 
mother Orthodox church, made a pastoral trip to the cities where the Catholics 
set their centers. There, he supported his priests, gave sermons to his people, 
and unceasingly send them messages and books he wrote, to urge them to be 
aware not to be seduced or to be diverted awa y from their faith; and to hold 
fast to that faith delivered to us by the saints. In all his writings, he concentrated 
on the following: 
 Our church is the church of the martyrs who shed their blood to keep the 
upright faith. 
 As long as Emanuel, our God is on our side; we have more on our team than 
those against us. 
 The tribulations could never be compared to the glory to come. 
 The tribulations are the way to enter into the heavenly glories. 
 These tribulations are only physical and temporary: “He who endures to the 
end shall be saved.” (Matthew 24:13). 
This great pope succeeded, to a great extent, and by the grace of the Holy 
Spirit, in keeping Coptic heritage, we received from our fathers. Among the 
essential manuscripts, this pope left to his church is the Psalms of the Agpeya, 
the Ten Commandments; the Seven Holy Sacraments; and the Evangelic 
advice.

Church, whose principles can guide her life everywhere in the whole world? If we return 
to the apostolic age, we find “many local church traditions” reflecting a variety of cultures. 
However, all these traditions are bound together by one mind, the mind of Christ; one spirit, 
the Spirit of the Lord; and one aim, our salvation.  
For this reason, the bishops of Alexandria did not hesitate to participate with the bishops 
of Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem, in one service and on one  altar, even if they differ in the 
details of their rites and traditions. For all of them received a single form of worship, in one 
spirit and one Tradition.  
So did all the apostles live in one open spirit of preaching. “For though I am free from all 
men, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win the more” (1 Cor. 9:19). When St. 
Mark preached in Egypt, he spoke about the One Christ. The Egyptians worshiped through 
their culture but in true apostolic spirit, and with the same spirit of worship as other 
bishoprics. For instance, the Coptic hymns differ from the Syrian and Latin ones … but all 
have the quiet and meek spirit, the spirit of the new heavenly hymn, reflecting the deepest 
true dogmatic and spiritual concepts and teachings. 
The Lights in the House of the Lord  are another example. All the apostolic Churches 
in the world use lights during worship by day and by night, especially during the reading of 
the Gospel. This is the spirit of tradition, which declares that “Christ is the Lig ht of the 
world.” However, Egyptian art emerged in the crafting of their oil lamps —kanadeel —
peculiar to the Coptic Church, while the Syrians, Latins, Greeks, etc., embody their own 
artistic traditions in the particular styles of their own lamps.  
Thus, w hile all who are called Christians across the world share a unity of faith and 
preserve the true, living tradition, every local church expresses this one faith through her own 
language, her liturgical rites, hymns, sacred clerical vestments, etc., without losing the unity 
of faith. The local character of Churches does not obscure the character of the Universal 
Church. In other words, the differences between traditions, in detail and not in essence, do 
not stop the realization of the unity of the Universal Church, as long as those traditions have 
all been established upon the unity of faith and life.  
Finally, we conclude this section with the following observations: 
a. The Orthodox Church, especially the Church of Alexandria, has more than others, 
preserved the holy tradition, both in its details and in its spirit. Perhaps this is because 
our Church has neither worldly authority nor does it interfere in politics. She lives in 
her spirituality far from the spirit of the world. The emergence of the monastic 
movement in Egypt has preserved the reverent, biblical, and ascetic spirit of the 
tradition of the Church. 
b. The unity that exists between the Non-Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches in our time 
provides a very practical case study for theologians interested in the ecumenical 
movement of how the concept of unity can be implemented. While these Churches
